records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Bring your own IaC](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-iac)
- [Isolated execution](/concepts/isolated-execution)
- [OpenTofu state](/concepts/terraform-state)
- [Elench](/concepts/elench)

records.title: Read the canvas
records.text: Read the canvas. What a card on the Architecture canvas tells you, how status and drift show without colour, and how collections and bring-your-own IaC modules are drawn.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.text:
The Architecture canvas draws one environment as cards, one per resource. It is fully grayscale,
so every state is carried by shape, structure and text, never by colour.

 ┌─ classification rule (top edge) ───────────┐
 │ [glyph] DATABASE ● status │ ← glyph, kind, status dot
 │ orders-db │ ← name
 │ Engine PostgreSQL 16 Capacity 0.5–4 │ ← the facts
 │ [aws] inherits core │ ← provider chip
 └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: The parts of a card
records.text:
- **Glyph and kind**, top left: what kind of resource this is.
- **Facts**, in the middle: the two or three settings that matter for that kind, for example
 `PostgreSQL 16 · 0.5–4 · 7 d` for a database or `private · on · 2 origins` for a bucket. A fact
 with no value shows a muted dash.
- **Provider chip**: the cloud account the resource lands in. Most resources inherit the project's
 account, and the chip says `inherits core`.
- **Classification rule**, the band across the top edge:

 Rule Meaning 
 --- --- 
 Solid, full ink **Root**: the project itself. 
 Solid, strong **Core**: must be on the project's cloud (network, cluster, data services). 
 Hairline **Periphery**: can be on another cloud (DNS, buckets, registry, secrets, GitOps). 
 Dashed **External**: not managed by this design (a bring-your-own chart or IaC module). 

The facts say how a resource really runs. On Hetzner, which has no managed data services, a
database card says `Runs as · CloudNativePG`. Caches run as Valkey and queues as RabbitMQ.

The cloud's own logo is the one thing in colour, because it belongs to the cloud.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: Status
records.text:
A dot shows the state, read by its fill and shape. A healthy resource shows only the dot; every
other state adds a short label.

 Dot State 
 --- --- 
 Solid **Live** or **Ready** 
 Hollow ring **Needs setup** or **Not deployed** 
 Haloed **Queued**, **Updating**, **Update pending** or **Destroying** 
 Blinking **Applying**: a runner is changing it now 
 Hollow centre **Failed** or **Unreachable** 
 Faint **Gated** or **Destroyed** 

When several states are true at once, the card shows the first that applies:

1. **Failed**.
2. In flight: queued, applying, updating or destroying.
3. **Needs setup**: the design is invalid, so the next deploy fails. This shows even on a live
 resource.
4. **Gated**.
5. **Destroyed**, then **Not deployed**.
6. **Unreachable**: the cluster's API server did not answer the last probe.
7. **Update pending**: live, but the design changed since the deploy.
8. **Live** or **Ready**.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: Drift
records.text:
Drift does not replace the state. A live resource whose cloud copy changed outside Alethia stays
**Live** and carries a chip such as `2 drifted`. Its **Status** tab lists the OpenTofu addresses
that drifted. Drift that cannot be traced to one resource is reported on the environment instead
of on a card.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: Gated resources
records.text:
A core resource placed on a different cloud from the project is **gated**. You can design it, but
the project does not provision until it is on the project's cloud.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: Collections
records.text:
Secrets collapse into one card, the vault. It shows the count, a few names, and the state of its
worst member, so a vault with one failed secret never reads **Live**. Open the vault to list,
filter, add or remove secrets, and to open one. Each secret is still its own resource, with its own
status and its own line in the plan.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: Bring-your-own IaC modules
records.text:
When an environment runs [your own OpenTofu module](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-iac),
Alethia draws the module's resources as dashed, read-only cards:

- Resources are grouped by kind and by module. An `aws_vpc` and its subnets become one
 **Network** card; the `aws_eks_*` resources become a **Cluster** card.
- A resource type that Alethia does not recognise goes into an **Other** card. Nothing is dropped.
- Open a card to see each resource's address, what the last plan does to it, its cost and its
 drift.
- After a scan, cards read `Source · declared`: what your code declares, so `count = 3` is still
 one resource. After a plan, they read `Source · planned`: the real, expanded resources.

**Sources** in the toolbar shows the repository, the ref, the commit the safety scan pinned (a
deploy applies that commit, not the branch), and the scan's verdict. A module the scan rejected
reads **Needs setup**.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: Zoom
records.text:
Zoom Shows 
 --- --- 
 Far out Glyph, name and status dot 
 Middle Header, name and the most important fact 
 Close in The full card

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not colour-code anything, so a status is never only a colour.
- It does not draw the cluster or the network as cards. Size them from the environment's name in
 the toolbar.
- It does not let you edit a bring-your-own IaC card. Change the module in its repository.

records.title: Read the canvas
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Use the canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas)
- [Use the inspector](/guides/design-project/node-inspector)
- [Drift](/concepts/drift)

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.text: Chart namespace admission. What the namespace of a bring-your-own chart refuses — Pod Security levels, the admission policy, and how a namespace moves from warning to enforcing.

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.text:
The ArgoCD project of a [bring-your-own chart](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts) decides which kinds the
chart may create; it cannot see the fields inside them. The chart's namespace checks those fields with
Kubernetes Pod Security Admission and a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, in one of two modes: `enforce` or
`warn`.

 Kinds{"Kind allowed by the AppProject?"}
 Kinds --> no SyncFail["Sync fails"]
 Kinds --> yes Mode{"Namespace mode"}
 Mode --> enforce Check["Pod Security baseline and the policy refuse"]
 Mode --> warn Report["Warn and record only"]
`} />

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.heading: Pod Security
records.text:
Each namespace carries Pod Security Admission labels pinned to the Kubernetes 1.33 version of the
standard:

 Mode Level Effect 
 --- --- --- 
 `enforce` `baseline` A pod that breaks the level is refused. 
 `warn` `restricted` The pod is created, with a warning. 
 `audit` `restricted` The pod is created, and the cluster's audit log records it. 

`baseline` refuses a pod that asks for its node: a privileged container, the node's network, process
or IPC namespace, a `hostPath` volume, a host port, or added Linux capabilities. A pod with no security
context passes. The namespace does not enforce `restricted`, because it also needs settings such as
`runAsNonRoot` and a seccomp profile that many public charts leave to you. The `restricted` warnings
show what your chart would have to change to pass it.

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.heading: Admission policy
records.text:
The policy refuses four kinds of object in the namespace:

 Refused Why 
 --- --- 
 A `Service` of type `LoadBalancer` or `NodePort` It answers outside the cluster, and a load balancer is billed to your cloud account. Use `ClusterIP` and an `Ingress`. 
 A `Service` with `spec.externalIPs` It captures traffic the nodes receive for those addresses. 
 A `Secret` of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` It holds a token that never expires. Pods already get short-lived tokens. 
 An `Ingress` annotation with `snippet` in its name A snippet configures the ingress controller, which serves every namespace. 

The policy needs Kubernetes 1.30 or later, which every version Alethia provisions has. On an older
cluster the deploy skips the policy, says so in its log, and Pod Security still applies.

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.heading: The two modes
records.text:
The namespace label `alethia.io/byo-admission` sets the mode:

- **`enforce`**: Pod Security enforces `baseline`, and the policy refuses.
- **`warn`**: Pod Security enforces only the cluster's own default, and the policy only warns and
 records.

 
 On EKS, GKE Standard and AKS the cluster's default is `privileged`, which refuses nothing. So a
 `warn` namespace there has no pod-level enforcement. Talos clusters on Hetzner enforce `baseline` in
 every namespace by default.

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.heading: How a namespace gets its mode
records.text:
Refusing in a namespace where a chart already runs would refuse its next pod after a restart. So the
mode comes from the history of the charts in this environment. On each deploy, Alethia reads each
chart's Application on the cluster. A chart has run if its Application exists, or if Alethia has ever
read it running; that record is never cleared, even when the cluster is provisioned again.

 The namespace Its charts Mode 
 --- --- --- 
 Exists, is not a bring-your-own namespace of this environment, and no Application of this environment deploys into it Any Refused: the chart is not deployed 
 Already has a mode Any Keeps it 
 Any At least one has run here, or moved out of `default` `warn` 
 Does not exist None has run `enforce` 
 Is a bring-your-own namespace of this environment None has run `warn` 

A chart cannot take over a namespace that is not this environment's: `enforce` would refuse the pods
of workloads already there, and the takeover would give those workloads this environment's secrets.
If the cluster's namespaces or a chart's Application cannot be read, the deploy fails before it
changes anything for bring-your-own charts.

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.heading: From warn to enforce
records.text:
A deploy never moves a namespace to `enforce` because of what it finds. While a namespace is in `warn`,
each deploy reports on the **Deploy** tab what `enforce` would refuse: the chart, the object and the
field. When the report is clean, turn on **Refuse in every BYO namespace** for the environment and
deploy again. See [Enforce chart admission](/guides/design-project/enforce-chart-admission).

You can also set one namespace's label to `enforce` with `kubectl`, and deploys keep it.

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not enforce `restricted`. It warns about it.
- It does not move a namespace to `enforce` on its own.
- It does not check objects that are not running at the deploy: a `CronJob` between runs or a workload
 scaled to zero is not in the report.

records.title: Chart namespace admission
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Bring-your-own charts](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts)
- [Enforce chart admission](/guides/design-project/enforce-chart-admission)
- [Troubleshoot bring-your-own charts](/troubleshooting/bring-your-own-charts)

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.text: Cloud abstraction. What Alethia can provision on AWS, GCP, Azure and Hetzner, which service backs each component on each cloud, and where the clouds differ.

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.text:
You design a project once, with cloud-neutral components such as a cluster, a database and a cache.
Alethia maps each component to a service of the cloud you chose and provisions it from that cloud's
OpenTofu template.

 Cat["Cloud catalog"]
 Cat --> AWS["AWS template: EKS, Aurora, ..."]
 Cat --> GCP["GCP template: GKE, Cloud SQL, ..."]
 Cat --> AZ["Azure template: AKS, Azure Database, ..."]
 Cat --> HZ["Hetzner template: Talos, in-cluster services"]
`} />

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
The cloud catalog lists which service backs each component on each cloud. The canvas, the
[conversion between clouds](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion) and a CI parity check all read it. A
component that a cloud cannot back is a documented exclusion: the canvas does not offer it there, and
a deploy that asks for it is refused rather than silently dropped.

The runner picks the template directory for the project's cloud and writes the design into it as
OpenTofu variables. See [Provisioning pipeline](/concepts/provisioning-pipeline) and
[Infrastructure templates](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates).

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.heading: Services per cloud
records.text:
Component AWS GCP Azure Hetzner 
 --- --- --- --- --- 
 Kubernetes EKS GKE AKS Talos (self-managed) 
 Network VPC VPC Network VNet Hetzner private network 
 Database Aurora Cloud SQL Azure Database CloudNativePG, in the cluster 
 Cache ElastiCache Memorystore Azure Managed Redis Valkey, in the cluster 
 NoSQL DynamoDB Firestore Cosmos DB Not offered 
 Queue SQS Pub/Sub Service Bus RabbitMQ, in the cluster 
 Topic SNS Pub/Sub Service Bus Not offered 
 Object storage S3 Cloud Storage Blob Storage Hetzner Object Storage 
 Container registry ECR Artifact Registry ACR Harbor, in the cluster 
 DNS Route 53 Cloud DNS Azure DNS Hetzner DNS 
 Secrets Secrets Manager Secret Manager Key Vault Vault, in the cluster 
 WAF AWS WAFv2 Cloud Armor Azure WAF Not offered 
 Managed certificate ACM Managed Certificate App Service Certificate Not offered 

You can replace the cloud's DNS, secrets, registry or observability with a tool you already run. See
[Connectors](/concepts/connectors).

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.heading: Hetzner is different in kind
records.text:
Hetzner sells servers, private networks, DNS and object storage. It sells no managed database, cache,
queue, registry or secret store. Alethia provisions the cluster and network with OpenTofu and installs
the other services in the cluster, each as its own ArgoCD application. You design the same canvas;
what runs is different:

- **You operate the data.** A managed database is backed up, patched and failed over by the cloud. An
 in-cluster one is backed up, patched and failed over by you.
- **The secret store is only as strong as the cluster.** Hetzner has no key management service, so
 the in-cluster Vault is sealed with a key stored as a Kubernetes Secret in the same cluster. Against
 a cluster admin, an etcd backup or a volume snapshot, it protects no more than a plain Secret. It
 still gives you an audit log of reads, leases, revocation and rotation. If you need a key held
 outside the cluster, connect an external secret store.
- **Credentials are an API token, not federation.** See [Security](/concepts/security#hetzner).

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.heading: Cache and database engines
records.text:
Not every cloud sells every engine, so the engine choice is narrowed per cloud rather than mapped.

 Cloud Redis Valkey PostgreSQL MySQL 
 --- --- --- --- --- 
 AWS Yes Yes Yes Yes 
 GCP Yes Yes Yes Yes 
 Azure Yes No Yes Yes 
 Hetzner No Yes Yes No 

The engine picker shows only what the selected cloud can build. A conversion to a cloud without the
engine switches it and tells you: a Valkey cache moved to Azure becomes Redis, and a MySQL database
moved to Hetzner becomes PostgreSQL.

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.heading: Cluster services after the apply
records.text:
After `tofu apply`, the runner installs a set of services in the cluster through ArgoCD. Some do not
apply to every cloud. For each one, the runner records whether it was installed or skipped, and why,
and the console shows that next to the add-on status.

 Service AWS GCP Azure Hetzner 
 --- --- --- --- --- 
 external-dns Installed (Route 53) Installed when the Workload Identity service account exists Installed when the managed identity exists Installed when a Hetzner API token is connected 
 External Secrets store Installed (Secrets Manager) Installed (Secret Manager) Installed (Key Vault) Installed (in-cluster Vault) when the project declares a secret 
 Ingress Installed (AWS Load Balancer Controller) Skipped: install the Traefik add-on Skipped: install the Traefik add-on, or use the Application Gateway Skipped: install the Traefik add-on 
 Default storage class Installed (gp3) Built in (`standard-rwo`) Built in (`managed-csi`) Installed (`hcloud-volumes`) 
 ArgoCD URL Installed (ALB ingress with an ACM certificate) Skipped: port-forward Skipped: port-forward Skipped: port-forward

records.title: Cloud abstraction
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not hide real differences. A component a cloud cannot back is refused, not faked.
- It does not offer NoSQL, topics, a WAF or a managed certificate on Hetzner.
- It does not move data between clouds. Conversion copies a design, not its data.

records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Multi-cloud conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion)
- [Infrastructure templates](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates)
- [Connectors](/concepts/connectors)
- [GitOps and ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd)

records.title: Cluster access
records.text: Cluster access. How Alethia hands out short-lived kubeconfigs without a cloud login, what each access tier allows, how long a credential lasts, how to revoke it, and what Alethia records.

records.title: Cluster access
records.text:
Alethia gives you a kubeconfig for a cluster it deployed without giving you a login to the cloud
account. A runner in your organization makes a short-lived credential and seals it so that only the
machine that asked can open it. To get one, see
[Get a kubeconfig](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).

 >CP: request: cluster, tier, lifetime, one-time public key
 CP->>CP: check your permission, write an audit record
 CP->>R: mint job
 R->>K: create or check the credential
 R->>CP: credential sealed to your one-time key
 You->>CP: collect (once)
 CP-->>You: sealed credential, then deletes its copy
 You->>You: open it with the one-time private key
`} />

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
1. The CLI or your browser makes a one-time key pair and sends the public key with the request.
2. The control plane checks your permission for the tier and writes an audit record.
3. A runner in your organization takes the mint job and gets the credential from the cloud or the
 cluster.
4. The runner seals the credential to your one-time public key and sends back only the sealed copy.
5. Your machine collects the sealed copy once and opens it. The control plane deletes its copy when
 it is collected, or 10 minutes after the request.

The control plane never sees the credential in plaintext and never stores it.

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: Access tiers
records.text:
Each tier is a separate permission, and a request gets exactly the tier it asks for.

 Tier Who can get it Identity in the cluster 
 --- --- --- 
 Read-only (the default) Roles with `cluster:access_readonly`: owners, admins and operators The `alethia-view` ServiceAccount in `alethia-system`, bound to the `alethia:view` ClusterRole 
 Admin (`--admin`) Roles with `cluster:access_admin`: owners and admins. People only, never a service token The cloud's own admin credential for the cluster. On Hetzner, an admin certificate from the Talos API 

Viewers get neither tier. A custom role can hold either permission. See
[Roles & permissions](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions).

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: What read-only allows
records.text:
`alethia:view` grants only `get`, `list` and `watch`. It is the built-in Kubernetes `view` role
written out rule by rule, plus nodes, namespaces and events. It does not aggregate from `view`, so a
role that someone aggregates into `view` cannot widen it.

 API group Resources 
 --- --- 
 core pods and their logs and status, services, endpoints, configmaps, persistent volume claims, replication controllers, service accounts, bindings, events, limit ranges, resource quotas, namespaces, nodes 
 `apps` deployments, replica sets, stateful sets, daemon sets (with `scale` and `status`), controller revisions 
 `batch`, `autoscaling`, `policy` jobs, cron jobs, horizontal pod autoscalers, pod disruption budgets, with `status` 
 `networking.k8s.io`, `discovery.k8s.io`, `events.k8s.io`, `extensions` ingresses, network policies, endpoint slices, events, and the legacy `extensions` objects 

It cannot read Secrets (so not the ArgoCD admin password), custom resources such as ArgoCD
`Application` objects, or RBAC objects. It cannot `exec`, `attach`, `port-forward` or `proxy`, and
it cannot change anything.

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: How long a credential lasts
records.text:
`--ttl` sets the lifetime, from `15m` to `8h`, default `1h`. For an admin credential it is a ceiling:
the cloud decides the real lifetime, and the CLI prints it.

 Cloud Read-only Admin 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS The TTL 14 minutes. An exec kubeconfig gets a new token when it expires. 
 GCP The TTL About 1 hour 
 Azure The TTL About 60 to 90 minutes 
 Hetzner The TTL About 1 hour (the cluster's admin certificate) 

Alethia refuses an admin credential that would last longer than 8 hours. A Hetzner cluster deployed
before the 1-hour certificate keeps a 24-hour one, so its admin requests are refused until its next
deploy. That deploy restarts no nodes.

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: Exec and static kubeconfigs
records.text:
An **exec** kubeconfig (the default on AWS, GCP and Azure) holds no credential. It runs
`alethia cluster token`, which mints a new one when the old one expires, so `kubectl` keeps working
and each new token checks your permission again. A copied file is useless without a signed-in CLI.

A **static** kubeconfig (`--static`, and always on Hetzner) holds the credential itself. It needs
only `kubectl`, works for anyone who has the file, and stops at expiry.

`alethia cluster token` caches each token until 60 seconds before it expires, so only the first
`kubectl` call per token waits for a runner. The cache is in the CLI's configuration directory
(`kubecache`, mode `0700`, files `0600`):

 OS Cache directory 
 --- --- 
 Linux `~/.config/alethia/kubecache` 
 macOS `~/Library/Application Support/alethia/kubecache` 
 Windows `%AppData%\alethia\kubecache` 

A machine that never ran `alethia cluster kubeconfig`, such as a CI runner, has none of your
choices: it mints read-only, 1-hour tokens in its active organization. A mint can only be collected
by the session or service token that requested it.

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: Revoke access
records.text:
A short lifetime is the main control. The others:

- **Remove the person** from the organization, or give them a role without `cluster:access_*`.
 They cannot get a new credential. A static file or a cached token works until it expires.
- **Revoke every read-only credential for a cluster** by deleting the ServiceAccount, with admin
 access: `kubectl -n alethia-system delete serviceaccount alethia-view`. Every token it issued stops
 at once. The next read-only request creates it again.
- **End access from one machine** with `alethia logout`. It deletes the session and the whole token
 cache. A static file is not in the cache, so it keeps working until it expires.

Admin credentials cannot be revoked through Alethia. They end at their real expiry.

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: What Alethia records
records.text:
Alethia writes an audit record before it returns a credential: one for the request and one for the
collection. Each holds who asked and from which IP address, the cluster, tier, shape and requested
TTL, the client (CLI or console), and the service token's ID if one was used. It never holds the
credential. Refused requests appear in [Activity](/guides/access/activity-log).

Every user maps to the same identity inside the cluster, so the cluster's own audit log cannot tell
your users apart. Alethia's records can.

records.title: Cluster access
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not proxy traffic. `kubectl` must reach the cluster's endpoint itself.
- It does not issue a kubeconfig for environments on a shared cluster, or for clouds other than AWS,
 GCP, Azure and Hetzner.
- It does not give a service token admin access.

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.text: Connection health and inventory. How the console checks each cloud connection and keeps a minimal, encrypted, expiring inventory of the resources in the account, without a runner.

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.text:
The console checks every cloud connection on its own, and keeps a small inventory of the resources
in each connected account. Both run in the console, not on a runner: a runner only provisions.

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
Cloud[Your cloud account]
 C -- inventory sweep, every hour --> Cloud
 F[Event forwarder, optional] -- change events --> C
`} />

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.heading: Connection health
records.text:
The console signs in to the account with a short-lived credential that it makes from the Alethia
OIDC issuer (Hetzner uses the stored token). It then runs a few read calls that stand for what
Alethia provisions. The account gets one of three states:

 State Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Connected** Sign-in works and the read calls pass. 
 **Limited permissions** Sign-in works, but some permissions are missing. They are listed, and a deploy can fail until you add them. 
 **Verification failed** Sign-in fails: the trust was removed, the trust no longer names the Alethia issuer, or the token is wrong. 

The check runs when you connect, again when it is more than 10 minutes old, and when you select
**Re-verify**. It is a direct API call, so it answers in about a second.

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.heading: Asset inventory
records.text:
The inventory lists networks, subnets, network interfaces, Kubernetes clusters, databases, caches,
queues, topics, NoSQL tables, container registries, secrets, storage buckets, DNS zones and regions.
The canvas uses it to offer existing resources, such as an existing VPC. The verification agent
uses it for context.

 When What happens 
 --- --- 
 On connect A first sync fills the inventory. 
 Every hour A sweep lists the resources again, adds new ones, marks missing ones as removed, and fills accounts that were never synced. It is on by default and needs no external scheduler. 
 On a change event (optional) A forwarder that you deploy in your cloud sends each change within seconds: EventBridge and Lambda on AWS, Cloud Asset Inventory, Pub/Sub and a Cloud Function on GCP, Event Grid and a Function App on Azure. It sends only `{ kind, native_id, region, deleted }`, never a credential.

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.heading: How the inventory is stored
records.text:
The cloud stays the source of truth. The inventory is a reduced copy:

- **Reduced.** It keeps the resource ID, name, region, kind and a few low-risk fields. It does not
 keep tags, because tags often hold email addresses or secrets. Only the `Name` tag becomes the
 row's name.
- **Encrypted.** CIDRs, IP addresses, endpoints and DNS domains are sealed with AES-GCM in one field
 per row, and decrypted only when a feature needs them.
- **Expiring.** Removed rows are deleted after `ALETHIA_INVENTORY_RETENTION_DAYS` days (default 7).
 Disconnecting an account deletes its whole inventory.

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not run on a runner, and a runner does not test connections, list resources or cache
 resource lists.
- It does not hold a standing cloud credential. A stolen inventory row gives no cloud access, because
 access still needs the trust that you created in your account.

records.title: Connection health and inventory
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Manage connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections): re-verify or disconnect an account.
- [Security](/concepts/security): the keyless model behind the health check.
- [Troubleshoot: connect a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect): fix **Limited permissions** and **Verification failed**.

records.title: Connectors
records.text: Connectors. How a project uses a provider you already run — Cloudflare DNS, Vault or another secret manager, an external registry, Datadog or Grafana — in place of the cloud's own service, and how its credential reaches a job.

records.title: Connectors
records.text:
A connector separates what a project needs, such as a DNS zone, secrets, a registry or observability,
from who provides it. You pick a provider per component; Alethia composes that provider's OpenTofu
module into the plan and skips the cloud's native resource.

 provider chosen Mod["Provider module added to the plan"]
 Comp --> native Native["Cloud's own resource"]
 Cred["Connector credential, encrypted"] --> decrypted at claim Job["Runner job, in memory"]
 Job --> Mod
`} />

To connect an account, check it or remove it, see [Connectors](/guides/connectors).

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Terms
records.text:
A **connector** is a provider type in the catalog, such as Cloudflare DNS. An account you connect to
a cloud is a **cloud identity**, not a connector. See the [glossary](/reference/glossary#connectivity).

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Categories
records.text:
Category Providers 
 --- --- 
 DNS Cloudflare 
 Secrets HashiCorp Vault, Doppler, Infisical, 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager in another account, and more 
 Container registry Docker Hub, GitHub, GitLab, Quay, Harbor, DigitalOcean, Scaleway, a generic registry, and ECR, Artifact Registry or ACR in another account 
 Helm chart registry HTTPS and OCI registries, including Docker Hub, GitHub, GitLab and ECR 
 Observability Datadog, Grafana Cloud 

Each provider is declared once in a catalog that the console's forms, the database and the runner all
read, so the set cannot drift between them. Observability adds to the cluster; it replaces nothing.

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Credentials
records.text:
API-key credentials are stored per organization, with secret fields encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM).
Non-secret fields, such as a Vault address, are stored in clear. A connector for another cloud
account, such as ECR in a second AWS account, uses a role or service account instead of a key.

The [configuration snapshot](/concepts/provisioning-pipeline#2-snapshot) of a job holds only the
chosen provider, never a secret. When a runner claims the job, the control plane decrypts the
credentials the project uses and sends them with the claim. The runner passes them to OpenTofu in
memory and never holds the encryption key.

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: In the plan
records.text:
For each component with a provider chosen, the runner copies that provider's module into the work
directory, wires it with its variables, and sets a guard variable such as `dns_provider`. The cloud
template skips its native resource when the guard names another provider. Before planning, the
provider checks that the combination makes sense and refuses one that does not.

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not put a credential in the job's snapshot or logs.
- It does not give the runner the encryption key.
- It does not connect a cloud account. That is a [cloud identity](/guides/connectors).

records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Connectors guide](/guides/connectors)
- [Pluggable connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable)
- [Cloud abstraction](/concepts/cloud-abstraction)

records.title: Cost estimation
records.text: Cost estimation. Where Alethia's cost figures come from — Infracost on every plan for the environment's real cost, and a list-price estimate for designs that have not been planned.

records.title: Cost estimation
records.text:
Alethia shows two cost figures. An environment's cost comes from Infracost, run on its last plan; a
design that has not been planned yet gets an approximate figure from list prices.

 list prices Est["Approximate estimate"]
 Design --> Plan["tofu plan"]
 Plan --> Infracost Break["Per-resource breakdown"]
 Break --> Chip["Cost chip and Plan tab"]
 Break --> Gate["Promotion cost gate"]
`} />

records.title: Cost estimation
records.heading: After a plan: Infracost
records.text:
When a runner plans an environment and an Infracost API key (`INFRACOST_API_KEY`) is configured, it
runs Infracost on the plan JSON. The breakdown is stored with the plan job:

- The **cost chip** on the canvas shows the environment's monthly total from its last plan. An
 environment never planned shows **Not priced**, not `$0.00`.
- The **Plan tab** lists each priced resource with its monthly and hourly cost, most expensive first.
- The [promotion cost gate](/concepts/promotions#protection-gates) compares this total with the
 target's previous one.

Without an Infracost key, plans have no cost figure. See [Cost](/guides/design-project/cost).

records.title: Cost estimation
records.heading: Before a plan: list prices
records.text:
The assistant's design proposals and the provider comparison show an approximate monthly figure
before anything is planned. It covers the main cost drivers: the control plane, nodes, NAT gateways,
databases and caches. On AWS it uses live on-demand list prices from the public AWS pricing API,
cached for 24 hours; on other clouds, and when that API fails, it uses the prices in Alethia's cloud
catalog. A month is 730 hours.

 List-price estimate Infracost 
 --- --- --- 
 When While you design After a plan 
 Accuracy Approximate, main drivers only Every resource in the plan 
 Use Comparing options Reviewing before you apply

records.title: Cost estimation
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not price usage. NoSQL, messaging, object storage requests and data transfer depend on use,
 and neither figure includes them.
- It does not update the cost chip when you change the design. Plan again.
- It does not price capacity created outside OpenTofu, such as nodes Karpenter launches.

records.title: Domain model
records.text: Domain model. The objects Alethia works with — organization, project, environment, component and job — how they relate, and the states each moves through.

records.title: Domain model
records.text:
Alethia organizes infrastructure as organizations that own projects, projects that own several
environments, and environments that declare components. A job is one unit of work a runner does on
one environment. For the canonical name of each term, see the [Glossary](/reference/glossary).

 owns many Proj["Project"]
 Proj --> uses one CI["Cloud identity"]
 Proj --> owns many Env["Environment"]
 Env --> Comp["Components: cluster, network, databases, caches, ..."]
 Env --> Jobs["Jobs: plan, deploy, destroy, ..."]
`} />

records.title: Domain model
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
- An **organization** is the tenancy boundary. Every project, runner, connection and job belongs to
 exactly one, and the database refuses a query for another organization's rows. See
 [Security](/concepts/security#row-level-security).
- A **project** is one infrastructure application. It uses one
 [cloud identity](/reference/glossary#connectivity) (a connected cloud account) and has a default
 region.
- An **environment** is a target you provision on its own, such as `staging` or `production`.
- A **component** is a resource an environment declares: a cluster, a network, a database, a cache.
- A **job** is the work a runner does for one environment.

records.title: Domain model
records.heading: Environments
records.text:
A project owns several environments, not one. Each environment has its own OpenTofu state, its own
components and its own status, so deploying `production` never changes `staging`.

 Property Meaning 
 --- --- 
 Name Unique in the project. It is part of the OpenTofu state key and of the URL. 
 Stage `development`, `staging` or `production`. The stage sets template defaults such as instance sizes and high availability, and the order [promotions](/concepts/promotions) follow. 
 Default One environment per project is the default. Single-value views, such as the project list's status column and the CLI, show it. 
 Lifecycle `persistent`, or `ephemeral`. An ephemeral environment has an expiry, and Alethia queues a destroy for it when the expiry passes. 
 Region Empty means the project's region. 

Where an environment's infrastructure comes from is a separate choice: see
[Fabrics and placement](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement).

records.title: Domain model
records.heading: Components
records.text:
Some components exist at most once per environment: the network, the cluster, the DNS zone,
observability, the GitOps repository and a [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac)
module. Others can exist many times, each with its own name: databases, caches, queues, topics, NoSQL
tables, container registries, secrets, storage buckets and [add-ons](/concepts/gitops-argocd).

Each component has its own status, so a cluster can be `ACTIVE` while a database you just added is
`CREATING`.

 Component status Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `PENDING` Declared, not provisioned yet. 
 `CREATING` Being created by `tofu apply`. 
 `ACTIVE` Provisioned. 
 `UPDATING` A change is being applied. 
 `FAILED` Creation or update failed. 
 `DESTROYING` Being removed. 
 `DESTROYED` Removed.

records.title: Domain model
records.heading: Environment status
records.text:
DRAFT
 DRAFT --> QUEUED: plan or deploy
 QUEUED --> PROVISIONING: a runner claims the job
 PROVISIONING --> ACTIVE: apply succeeds
 PROVISIONING --> FAILED: apply fails
 FAILED --> QUEUED: retry
 ACTIVE --> QUEUED: deploy a change
 ACTIVE --> DESTROYING: destroy
 DESTROYING --> DESTROYED
 DESTROYING --> FAILED
`} />

`DRAFT` means the design was never submitted. `FAILED` can be retried.

records.title: Domain model
records.heading: Jobs
records.text:
A job references one project, one environment and one cloud identity, and records the runner that
claimed it. It moves `QUEUED → CLAIMED → PROCESSING → SUCCESS` or `FAILED`; a queued or claimed job
can also be `CANCELLED`. A promotion adds no job type: it runs a plan, then a deploy. The full list of
job types is in [Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types), and how a job is claimed and recovered is in
[Job queue](/concepts/job-queue).

records.title: Domain model
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- An environment does not inherit components from another environment. Each declares its own.
 [Promotions](/concepts/promotions) copy structural changes on purpose, behind gates.
- A project does not span cloud accounts. To run the same design on another cloud, see
 [Multi-cloud conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).

records.title: Domain model
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Fabrics and placement](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement)
- [Provisioning pipeline](/concepts/provisioning-pipeline)
- [Glossary](/reference/glossary)

records.title: Drift detection
records.text: Drift detection. How Alethia runs scheduled refresh-only OpenTofu plans to find live infrastructure that no longer matches its state, and what the drift posture on the Evidence page means.

records.title: Drift detection
records.text:
Provisioning proves an environment matched its design at the moment of the apply. Drift detection
keeps checking: on a schedule, a runner compares each environment's OpenTofu state with the live
cloud and records whether anything changed.

 Job["DETECT_DRIFT job"]
 Job --> Plan["tofu plan -refresh-only"]
 Plan --> Post["Drift posture"]
 Post --> Ev["Evidence page, CLI, MCP"]
 Post --> opt-in Heal["Auto-heal"]
`} />

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: Schedule
records.text:
A loop in the control plane queues a `DETECT_DRIFT` job for each environment whose last check is
older than its cadence:

 Stage Cadence 
 --- --- 
 Production Every 6 hours 
 Staging Every day 
 Development Every 7 days 

An environment never checked is due at once. An environment with a drift job already queued or
running is skipped, so checks do not pile up. To check one environment now, open the canvas **Run**
menu and select **Detect drift**.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: The check
records.text:
The job copies the configuration of the environment's latest successful deploy. The runner prepares
the template (or clones your [bring-your-own module](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac) at its pinned
commit), reads the state through the [state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state), and runs
`tofu plan -refresh-only`. This asks each provider what the live resource looks like and compares it
with the state. It never applies and changes nothing in the cloud.

A refresh-only plan still runs provider plugins. For a bring-your-own module on a managed runner, the
job runs only inside the [container sandbox](/concepts/isolated-execution).

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: The posture
records.text:
Each drifted managed resource is classified:

 Kind Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `modified` It exists, but its live configuration differs from the state. 
 `deleted` It was deleted outside OpenTofu and is still in the state. 
 `other` Any other kind of change. 

The posture records whether the environment is in sync, how many resources drifted, each one's
OpenTofu address, type and kind, and when the plan ran. Alethia keeps the latest posture per
environment.

If an environment drifted, Alethia can heal it by deploying again. Auto-heal is off unless you turn it
on, and production stays behind approval.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: What you see
records.text:
The Evidence page and the **Drift** tab show one mark per environment:

 Mark Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **In sync** The last check found no drifted managed resource. 
 **N drifted** That many managed resources differ from the state. 
 **Not scanned** No check has run yet. This is an unknown, not a pass. 

The CLI (`alethia drift`) and the MCP tool `get_drift_posture` read the same posture.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not see resources OpenTofu does not manage. A resource created outside OpenTofu is not in
 the state, so a refresh-only plan cannot find it. The posture says this: its unmanaged count is
 marked as unknown, never as zero.
- It does not check app delivery. Drift between your apps repository and the cluster is ArgoCD's to
 report.
- It does not change anything, unless you turned on auto-heal.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Elench](/concepts/elench)
- [OpenTofu state](/concepts/terraform-state)
- [Drift in the CLI](/reference/cli/drift)

records.title: Agent harness
records.text: Agent harness. How Alethia exposes one set of tools to its own assistant and to external agents over MCP — what each audience sees, how approval stays with a person, and how agent memory is kept per tenant.

records.title: Agent harness
records.text:
Alethia defines each agent tool once and serves it to its own assistant and, read-only, to your agents
(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others) over MCP. Every call is checked against your permissions, and
no tool can approve an apply or a destroy.

 InApp["In-app assistant: all tools"]
 Reg --> Ext["External projection: read-only tools"]
 Ext --> MCP["MCP server at /api/mcp"]
 Ops["Operation tools: plan, request_apply, request_destroy, wait_for_job, get_job_logs, cancel_job"] --> MCP
 MCP --> Agent["Your agent"]
 Agent --> request_apply Pending["Pending approval"]
 Pending --> person approves in the console Deploy["Deploy queued once, for that plan"]
`} />

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: One registry, two audiences
records.text:
Every tool is marked with an audience:

 Audience Who sees it 
 --- --- 
 In-app Only the console's assistant: design proposals, canvas tools, and tools that queue jobs. 
 External or both Read-only tools that are safe for your own agents. 

A test fails the build if a tool has no audience, so the external set cannot widen by accident. The
audience decides only visibility: each tool still checks your permission when it runs.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The MCP server
records.text:
The MCP server serves the external tools and six operation tools: `plan`, `request_apply`,
`request_destroy`, `wait_for_job`, `get_job_logs` and `cancel_job`. Clients sign in with OAuth; the
token carries the scopes you approved and is bound to the server. The full list is in the
[tool reference](/agents/tools).

Approval happens outside MCP. `request_apply` records a pending approval bound to the plan's digest
and to the calling client, and returns a console link. A person approves it there. The agent then
calls `request_apply` again, and only that call queues the deploy, once, for that plan, through the
same checks every other path uses. So text an agent reads can lead at most to a pending request.

Evidence is readable too: `get_plan_result` returns a job's status and its [Elench](/concepts/elench)
verdict, and `get_drift_posture` returns an environment's [drift posture](/concepts/drift). Queuing an
audit stays in the console's assistant.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Agents and memory
records.text:
An agent is stored data, not a running process: a persona, a mission, a tool scope and a memory
namespace. Each turn runs on stateless compute that loads the agent and narrows the tools to its
scope.

Memory is kept per tenant: under the organization, or under one project in it. Every memory path is
checked, and a path that tries to leave its namespace (`..`, an absolute path, a backslash, a null
byte) is refused, so one tenant cannot read another's memory.

Each scope also has pinned context: custom instructions and knowledge documents, at the organization
and project level, plus facts derived from the project. They are added to the agent's instructions
before its first tool call. You edit them in the assistant's [knowledge panel](/guides/assistant/knowledge).

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not let any tool approve an apply or a destroy.
- It does not give external agents tools that write designs or queue jobs directly, other than the
 operation tools above.
- It does not give an agent more than the person it acts for.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Agents overview](/agents)
- [Security model for agents](/agents/security)
- [MCP server](/guides/assistant/mcp)
- [Assistant](/guides/assistant)

records.title: Elench
records.text: Elench. Alethia's verification layer — a deterministic check of every OpenTofu plan before it is applied, a signed receipt of the result, audits of infrastructure you bring, and drift and vulnerability posture after the apply.

records.title: Elench
records.text:
Elench is the check Alethia runs on every OpenTofu plan between `tofu plan` and `tofu apply`. Named,
versioned controls evaluate the plan JSON, a failing hard control stops the apply unless someone with
authority waives it, and the result is sealed in an evidence receipt.

 Eval["Controls: pass, fail, warn, not_evaluable"]
 Eval --> fail, not waived Stop["Deploy stops before apply"]
 Eval --> otherwise Apply["tofu apply"]
 Eval --> Rec["Evidence receipt"]
 Apply --> Drift["Drift and security posture"]
`} />

records.title: Elench
records.heading: The verdict comes from code
records.text:
The controls are deterministic code with no side effects: the same plan always gives the same
verdict, which is what lets a receipt be checked later. A language model may explain a failing control
or suggest a fix in the [assistant](/guides/assistant), but a fix is offered only if running the
controls again shows it resolves the failure without a new one. The model is never the gate.

The controls cover keyless access, least privilege and OIDC subject pinning on AWS, GCP and Azure, and
a Kubernetes set for manifests. Each control, what it detects and what it cannot see is in the
[control catalog](/reference/control-catalog).

records.title: Elench
records.heading: Statuses
records.text:
Status Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `pass` Evaluated, and the plan satisfies it. 
 `fail` Evaluated, and violated. On a deploy this stops the apply unless waived. 
 `warn` A concern that does not stop the apply. 
 `not_evaluable` The plan does not hold what the control needs. Never counted as a pass. 

The overall verdict is the worst status: `fail`, then `warn`, then `not_evaluable`, then `pass`. A
policy computed only at apply time, or an AWS managed policy referenced only by ARN, is
`not_evaluable` with a note saying why, never a silent pass.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: Plan and deploy
records.text:
On a plan, the report is shown in the Plan tab and stops nothing. On a deploy, the same check runs on
the reviewed plan, and a failing hard control stops the job before any resource changes.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: Overrides
records.text:
An override is an authorized, time-limited waiver of specific control IDs, never of the whole check.
Alethia records who granted it and when it expires, and the runner applies only the controls it names.
The verdict is not rewritten to `pass`: the waiver is sealed into the receipt as an exception. See
[Override a verify failure](/guides/jobs/verify-override).

records.title: Elench
records.heading: IAM Access Analyzer
records.text:
On AWS, the check can also ask IAM Access Analyzer whether a planned policy could grant any action from
a list of sensitive actions, before anything is deployed. It is off unless the runner sets
`ALETHIA_VERIFY_ACCESS_ANALYZER=1`. An error from the analyzer is `not_evaluable`.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: Receipts
records.text:
Every apply seals a receipt bound to the SHA-256 of the plan, the verdict, the control catalog version
and any exception. With a signing key it is signed with ed25519 and can be checked offline. See
[Receipts and signing](/concepts/elench/receipts).

records.title: Elench
records.heading: Audits of infrastructure you bring
records.text:
The controls work on any plan, so an `AUDIT` job can check a `tofu show -json` plan or Kubernetes
manifests that Alethia did not generate, with the same controls. It provisions nothing and writes the
report to the project's feed. Queue it from the assistant; it needs the `project:audit` permission.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: After the apply
records.text:
- **Drift.** Scheduled refresh-only plans check that live resources still match the state. See
 [Drift detection](/concepts/drift).
- **Vulnerabilities.** If the Trivy Operator add-on runs in the cluster, Alethia reads its
 vulnerability reports on each deploy and drift check and sums them by severity. The Evidence page
 shows the highest severity found, **Clean**, or **Not scanned** when there are no reports.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not prove compliance. A receipt is evidence that named controls passed on one plan; whether
 that meets a standard is an auditor's judgment.
- It does not judge what the plan cannot show. Those controls are `not_evaluable`.
- It does not let a model decide a verdict or apply a fix.
- It does not see resources outside the plan. Drift detection covers resources in state only.

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.text: Receipts and signing. What an evidence receipt records, how ed25519 signing makes it tamper-evident and checkable offline, who a signature can vouch for, transparency-log anchoring, and how waivers appear.

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.text:
Alethia seals an evidence receipt on every apply. It binds the Elench verdict to the exact plan that
was applied, and when a signing key is configured it is signed, so you can check it later without
trusting the console.

 SHA-256 Rec["Receipt: plan hash, verdict, catalog version, report, exception"]
 Rec --> ed25519 Sig["Signed receipt"]
 Sig --> opt-in Rekor["Transparency log anchor"]
 Sig --> CLI["alethia verify receipt"]
`} />

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.heading: What a receipt records
records.text:
Field Why 
 --- --- 
 `plan_sha256` Binds the receipt to the exact plan. 
 Verdict and the per-control report What was decided, including `not_evaluable` controls. 
 Catalog version A verdict means something only against the controls that produced it. 
 Exception Any waiver: the control IDs, the reason, who granted it, and when it expires. 
 OpenTofu version, runner, evaluation time Where and when it was produced.

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.heading: Signing
records.text:
With `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` set on the runner, each receipt is signed with ed25519 over its
canonical JSON, so any change breaks the signature. Without a key, the receipt is still attached,
unsigned: an apply is never blocked on signing.

 State Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Signed** Tamper-evident and checkable offline. 
 **Unsigned** A faithful record, not signed. 
 **—** No apply has sealed a receipt for this environment yet.

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.heading: Checking one
records.text:
alethia verify receipt --job 

The command checks the signature and exits non-zero when it cannot, so a pipeline can gate on it.
`alethia verify show --job ` prints the report. See [Verify commands](/reference/cli/verify).

A receipt always verifies under the public key it carries, whoever made it, so that alone proves only
that it was not altered. The CLI checks the signature against a key it trusts and says which:

 Trust The signing key is 
 --- --- 
 `pinned` A key you gave with `--key-file`, held outside Alethia. The strongest answer. 
 `org` A key registered for your organization. Registered, not proven to be held by you. 
 `platform` Alethia's platform key. The receipt says "Alethia asserted this". 
 `self` Only the receipt's own key. Proves it was not altered, not who made it.

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.heading: Transparency log
records.text:
An operator can turn on anchoring with `ALETHIA_REKOR_ANCHOR_ENABLED=true`. The control plane then
logs a hash of each signed receipt in a Rekor transparency log (only the hash; the receipt's contents
are not uploaded), so anyone can check offline that the receipt existed at that time. Anchoring never
blocks an apply: if it fails, the receipt stays unanchored.

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.heading: Waivers
records.text:
A waiver passes specific failing controls for a limited time. It is sealed into the receipt as an
exception, so the record shows the check was passed on purpose, not turned off. Active waivers are
listed on the Evidence page.

records.title: Receipts and signing
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not prove compliance, only what was checked on one plan.
- A platform-signed receipt does not prove that your organization asserted anything. Use your own key
 for that.
- It does not record the Git commit of a bring-your-own module. That is on the environment's source.

records.title: Fabrics and placement
records.text: Fabrics and placement. How an environment is separated from the infrastructure that hosts it — placed onto a Fabric as a namespace, a virtual cluster, or a dedicated cluster.

records.title: Fabrics and placement
records.text:
An **environment** is where you deliver your apps; a **Fabric** is the infrastructure that hosts it:
a cluster, its network, shared add-ons and its own OpenTofu state. A **placement** says how an
environment sits on a Fabric, so several environments can share one cluster.

 dedicated FabA["Fabric A: its own cluster"]
 Dev["dev"] --> namespace FabB["Fabric B: shared cluster"]
 Prev["preview"] --> vcluster FabB
`} />

records.title: Fabrics and placement
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
A project owns one or more Fabrics. A Fabric can come from an Alethia template or from
[your own OpenTofu module](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac). Each environment names the Fabric it is
placed on and its placement mode. A Fabric has at most one cluster, and every environment placed on
it shares that cluster.

records.title: Fabrics and placement
records.heading: Placement modes
records.text:
The modes form an isolation ladder. Each step isolates more and costs more.

 Mode What the environment gets Isolation 
 --- --- --- 
 `namespace` A Kubernetes namespace on a shared cluster. Soft. Same nodes and API server as its neighbors, bounded by `ResourceQuota`, `LimitRange`, `NetworkPolicy` and Pod Security Admission. 
 `vcluster` A virtual cluster on a shared cluster: its own API server, custom resources and Kubernetes version. Medium. Its own control plane, but its pods run on the shared nodes. 
 `dedicated` A whole cluster: the environment owns its Fabric. Hard. A separate cluster. 

`dedicated` is the default for a new project's first environment. An empty mode is treated as
`dedicated`. All three modes work on AWS, GCP, Azure and Hetzner. A deploy that cannot honor the
placement you chose fails; it never ignores the placement.

 
 A `vcluster` isolates the control plane, not the nodes. Do not use it as a boundary for untrusted
 workloads. Use `dedicated` for that, and `namespace` for targets of the same trust, such as `dev`
 and previews.

records.title: Fabrics and placement
records.heading: What each side tracks
records.text:
- **Infrastructure is per Fabric.** Each Fabric has its own [OpenTofu state](/concepts/terraform-state),
 and [drift detection](/concepts/drift) runs per Fabric.
- **Delivery is per environment.** ArgoCD syncs each environment's apps into its own destination: the
 namespace for `namespace` and `vcluster`, the whole cluster for `dedicated`. See
 [GitOps and ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).
- **Managed data is per environment.** A database belongs to the environment that declares it, also on
 a shared Fabric.

A `dedicated` environment is the simple case: infrastructure and delivery are the same cluster.

records.title: Fabrics and placement
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not give a kubeconfig for a `namespace` or `vcluster` environment. A kubeconfig for the
 shared cluster would reach every environment on it, so the runner refuses. See
 [Cluster access](/concepts/cluster-access).
- It does not make a `vcluster` a hard boundary.

records.title: GitOps and ArgoCD
records.text: GitOps and ArgoCD. What Alethia installs in every cluster it provisions — ArgoCD, the cluster services each cloud needs, and the Application that deploys your apps from Git.

records.title: GitOps and ArgoCD
records.text:
After a successful apply, the runner installs ArgoCD in the new cluster and hands it the cluster
services and your apps repository. From then on, Git is the source of truth: ArgoCD keeps the cluster
in sync with the repository.

 Out["OpenTofu outputs"]
 Out --> Facts["Infrastructure facts: cluster, DNS, endpoints, identities"]
 Facts --> Argo["ArgoCD installed with Helm"]
 Argo --> Plat["Platform Applications: external-dns, External Secrets, ingress, ..."]
 Argo --> Apps["apps Application: your apps repository"]
 Argo --> Add["Add-ons and your own charts"]
`} />

records.title: GitOps and ArgoCD
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
1. The runner reads the OpenTofu outputs: cluster name, endpoint and certificate, DNS zone, database
 and cache endpoints, and the cloud identities made for in-cluster controllers.
2. It writes a kubeconfig whose credential plugin is the runner itself. Each `kubectl` or Helm call
 mints a short-lived token from the job's keyless cloud credential. No cloud CLI is used and no
 long-lived kubeconfig is stored.
3. It installs ArgoCD with Helm and waits for its pods to be ready.
4. It renders the outputs into a values file, the *infrastructure facts*, and applies the platform
 Applications that use them.
5. It creates an `apps` Application that syncs your apps repository, at the environment's apps path or
 the repository root.
6. It records the ArgoCD address and cluster details on the environment. Passwords, kubeconfigs and
 generated secret values are never stored.

The ArgoCD admin password stays in the cluster, in the `argocd-initial-admin-secret` Secret. Read it
with admin [cluster access](/concepts/cluster-access):

kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
 -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' base64 -d

records.title: GitOps and ArgoCD
records.heading: Platform services
records.text:
Each service is an ArgoCD Application. A service that does not apply to a cloud renders nothing and is
skipped, and the console records why. The per-cloud result is in
[Cloud abstraction](/concepts/cloud-abstraction#cluster-services-after-the-apply).

 Service What it does Where 
 --- --- --- 
 external-dns Creates DNS records from your Ingress objects. Every cloud, when DNS is on with a domain and its identity or token exists. Uses Route 53, Cloud DNS, Azure DNS, Hetzner DNS, or Cloudflare when that connector is attached. 
 External Secrets Operator Syncs secrets from the cloud's secret store into Kubernetes Secrets. Every cloud. 
 cert-manager Issues certificates through a DNS challenge, and provides webhook certificates for add-ons that need them. Issuing on AWS, GCP and Azure with the cloud's own DNS. Webhook certificates on every cloud. 
 AWS Load Balancer Controller Turns Ingress objects into ALBs. AWS. 
 Application Gateway Ingress Controller Turns Ingress objects into rules on one Application Gateway. Azure, when the gateway is on. 
 Karpenter Launches nodes for pending pods. AWS, when enabled. 
 metrics-server CPU and memory metrics for autoscaling and `kubectl top`. AWS a

records.title: GitOps and ArgoCD
records.heading: Keyless identities for controllers
records.text:
Controllers that call the cloud use a workload identity, never a static key:

 Cloud Identity Bound with 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS IAM role for the service account (IRSA) `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn` annotation 
 GCP Google service account through GKE Workload Identity `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` annotation 
 Azure User-assigned managed identity with a federated credential on the AKS OIDC issuer `azure.workload.identity/client-id` annotation 

On Hetzner, external-dns and the cloud controller use the connected Hetzner API token, which is
stored in the cluster as a Secret.

records.title: GitOps and ArgoCD
records.heading: Your apps
records.text:
The `apps` Application syncs your apps repository with automatic sync, prune and self-heal. If the
repository is empty, the runner first commits generated manifests for your detected services: a
Deployment, Service and Ingress each, running as non-root with a read-only root file system and
resource limits. A repository that already has manifests is never changed.

Marketplace add-ons and [your own charts](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts) are Applications too, each
in its own ArgoCD project.

records.title: GitOps and ArgoCD
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not extract or store the ArgoCD admin password.
- It does not overwrite your apps repository.
- It does not install an ingress controller on GCP, Azure (without the gateway) or Hetzner. Install
 the Traefik add-on there.
- It does not expose the ArgoCD UI outside AWS. Elsewhere, port-forward to it.

records.title: Concepts
records.text: Concepts. A map of how Alethia works — the model, how infrastructure is provisioned, how runners execute jobs, and how access and verification are secured.

records.title: Concepts
records.text:
Alethia provisions Kubernetes clusters and their backing services into your own cloud account, from
a design you make in the console or the CLI. A runner does the work: it plans with OpenTofu, checks
the plan, applies it, and installs ArgoCD so your apps deploy through Git.

 design, plan, apply CP["Alethia control plane"]
 CP --> job R["Runner"]
 R --> short-lived credential Cloud["Your cloud account"]
 R --> tofu apply, then ArgoCD Cluster["Your cluster"]
 R --> logs, results CP
`} />

Read the sections in order. Each page explains one part and links to the guides that use it.

records.title: Isolated execution
records.text: Isolated execution. How Alethia runs your own OpenTofu or Helm on the managed fleet — a sealed container per job with no platform secrets, no cloud metadata, and egress only to allowed domains.

records.title: Isolated execution
records.text:
When Alethia runs your own code on its managed fleet, such as bring-your-own OpenTofu providers,
`external` data sources, Helm charts and their hooks, that code is arbitrary. Isolated execution runs
each such job in a fresh, sealed container, so the code cannot reach the platform's secrets, the cloud
metadata service or the open internet.

 Guard{"Platform secret in the child's environment?"}
 Guard --> yes Refuse["Refuse to start"]
 Guard --> no C["Per-job container: own PID namespace, dropped capabilities, read-only credential mounts"]
 C --> only route Proxy["Forward proxy: registries, Git hosts, the target cloud API"]
 C --> State["State proxy, per-job token"]
 Proxy -.blocked.-> IMDS["Cloud metadata, other hosts"]
`} />

records.title: Isolated execution
records.heading: Trusted and untrusted code
records.text:
- **Alethia's own templates** are reviewed platform code. They run in the runner process.
- **Your OpenTofu or Helm** runs, on a managed runner, in a container per job. The runner serializes
 the work, starts itself again inside the container, and reads the result from the job's work
 directory. The container is removed after the job, and a fleet VM runs one job.

Removing environment variables at the last moment is not enough: a child process in the runner's PID
namespace could read the parent's `/proc/1/environ`. Only a real namespace boundary contains it.

records.title: Isolated execution
records.heading: What the container gets
records.text:
The child receives an allowlisted environment and nothing else:

- the cloud credential settings: file paths and non-secret IDs, such as `AWS_CONFIG_FILE` or the
 `ARM_*` variables;
- a provider token the job needs, such as `HCLOUD_TOKEN`;
- the state proxy and egress proxy settings;
- `PATH` and locale.

The runner token, storage keys, the receipt signing key and any static cloud key are dropped. A guard
checks the final environment and refuses to start the container if a denied secret survived.
Credential files are mounted read-only as directories, so the runner's token refresh stays visible
during a long apply.

The container has its own PID namespace, no added capabilities, no privilege escalation, only the job's
work directory writable, and process and memory limits.

records.title: Isolated execution
records.heading: Secrets removed at the source
records.text:
- **State.** OpenTofu reaches state through the [state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state) with a per-job
 token; the runner holds no storage key, and one job's token reaches only its own state.
- **Cloud credentials** are minted per job and bound to it.
- **Fleet VMs** register with a short-lived bootstrap token minted for that VM, not a shared secret.

So a managed VM's boot configuration holds no long-lived secret, and the network control below closes
the last path rather than being the only one.

records.title: Isolated execution
records.heading: Network
records.text:
The child has no network route of its own. The VM's network has no gateway, and a forward proxy allows
egress by domain: package registries, Git hosts and the target cloud's API. The cloud metadata service
(`169.254.169.254`) and other hosts are unreachable by construction. A chart scan needs no network and
runs with none.

records.title: Isolated execution
records.heading: Availability
records.text:
The sandbox is turned on per fleet with `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container`. On a managed runner,
untrusted work runs only when egress enforcement is confirmed (`ALETHIA_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` and
`ALETHIA_SANDBOX_ENFORCE_MANAGED`); otherwise the job is refused, never run unsandboxed.
Bring-your-own Helm is also gated by `ALETHIA_BYO_HELM_ENABLED`, and bring-your-own IaC by
`ALETHIA_BYO_IAC_ENABLED`. See
[Managed provisioning](/self-host/fleet-sandbox).

records.title: Isolated execution
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It is not a general sandbox service. There is no API to run arbitrary code in it.
- It does not apply to self-operated runners, which run inside your own trust boundary.
- It does not sandbox Alethia's own templates.
- It does not fall back to running untrusted code without the sandbox.

records.title: Job queue
records.text: Job queue. How Alethia queues provisioning work as jobs in Postgres, how a runner claims each job exactly once, and how a job is recovered when its runner dies or stalls.

records.title: Job queue
records.text:
Every piece of runner work, such as a plan, a deploy, a destroy, a drift check or a scan, is a job in a
Postgres queue. Runners claim jobs atomically, run them and report the result, so the console and the
CLI never wait on the work itself.

 QUEUED
 QUEUED --> CLAIMED: a runner claims it
 CLAIMED --> PROCESSING: work starts
 PROCESSING --> SUCCESS
 PROCESSING --> FAILED
 CLAIMED --> QUEUED: recovered (runner died or stalled)
 PROCESSING --> QUEUED: recovered (runner died or stalled)
 QUEUED --> CANCELLED: you cancel
 CLAIMED --> CANCELLED: you cancel
`} />

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Queuing
records.text:
You plan, deploy or destroy in the console or the CLI, and Alethia adds a `QUEUED` job with the
environment's frozen [configuration snapshot](/concepts/provisioning-pipeline#2-snapshot). Connecting
a cloud account is not a job: the control plane does it. The job types are listed in
[Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types).

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Claiming
records.text:
A runner learns that a job is claimable from its wake stream, or from a 30-second poll when the
stream is down, and asks for one. The database picks the next job with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`: a
row another runner has locked is skipped, not waited on, so two runners can never claim the same job.

The pick also respects:

- **Priority.** Higher priority first, then oldest first.
- **Cloud.** A runner gets only jobs for the clouds it serves, and only jobs its cloud identity allows.
- **Self-operated jobs.** A job marked for a self-operated runner, such as a Hetzner job whose token
 stays in your runner, is never given to a managed runner.
- **Fairness and limits.** On managed runners, organizations share capacity fairly, and each plan's
 limit on jobs running at once applies. Extra jobs wait; they are not refused.
- **One job per environment.** Jobs on one environment run one at a time.

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Running and reporting
records.text:
The runner sets the job `PROCESSING`, mints a credential, runs it, streams logs, and reports `SUCCESS`
or `FAILED` with its results. For a deploy, the control plane then writes the cluster and database
endpoints onto the environment. See [Job execution](/concepts/runner/job-execution).

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Failure recovery
records.text:
A runner refreshes its liveness about every 10 seconds; after 45 seconds of silence it is marked
offline. A background sweep then recovers its job when:

- it was claimed over 15 minutes ago and its runner has sent no heartbeat for 5 minutes, or
- its runner is alive but the job made no progress for 30 minutes.

A recovered job goes back to `QUEUED` for another runner, which reads the state and continues. Two
cases fail instead:

- **The apply had started.** A retry would run the apply a second time, so the job fails with a
 message saying cloud resources may have changed. Check the environment before you deploy again.
- **It reached 5 attempts.** A job whose runner died or stalled five times fails, to protect the queue.

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not run one job on two runners.
- It does not retry an apply that may have started.
- It does not push job status to the browser. Status is polled; see
 [Real-time updates](/concepts/realtime#poll-everything-else).

records.title: Keyless database auth
records.text: Keyless database auth. How a service reaches a PostgreSQL or MySQL database with its cloud identity and a short-lived token on AWS, GCP and Azure, and what database role it gets.

records.title: Keyless database auth
records.text:
Keyless database auth lets a workload log in to its database with its own cloud identity and a
token that expires, instead of a stored password. It works for PostgreSQL and MySQL on AWS, GCP and
Azure; to turn it on, see [Use keyless database auth](/guides/design-project/keyless-database-auth).

 app ──► 127.0.0.1: ──► proxy sidecar ──TLS + token──► database
 │
 └─ token from the pod's cloud identity

records.title: Keyless database auth
records.heading: The proxy
records.text:
The application connects to a proxy sidecar on `127.0.0.1`, with no password. The sidecar gets a
token from the pod's identity and connects to the real database over TLS. The application never
sees the token.

- **GCP** uses the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy with `--auto-iam-authn`.
- **AWS and Azure** have no such proxy, so the pod runs `alethia db-authproxy`, a subcommand of the
 runner image. For each new connection it gets a token, connects over TLS with the token as the
 password, then copies bytes both ways. It does no pooling, routing or query parsing.

The token lives only in the sidecar's memory and is reused while it is valid. There is no token
file and nothing to rotate. Both engines check the token only when a connection opens, so an
expiring token never breaks an open session.

 Cloud Database Token from Alethia creates 
 --- --- --- --- 
 AWS RDS and Aurora, IAM database authentication The pod's IAM role for its service account (`rds-db:connect`, tokens of about 15 minutes) An IAM role for the app's Kubernetes service account. `rds-db:connect` is scoped to one database user on one cluster. 
 GCP Cloud SQL, IAM database authentication The pod's Workload Identity A service accou

records.title: Keyless database auth
records.heading: The database role
records.text:
The app's login maps to a least-privilege role, never a superuser:

- **PostgreSQL**: `CONNECT` on its own database, and `USAGE` and `CREATE` on the `public` schema.
- **MySQL**: `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, ALTER, INDEX, REFERENCES` on its own
 database. Never `*.*`, `GRANT OPTION` or `SUPER`.

A one-time setup Job creates the role. Alethia adds it to your GitOps repository as an ArgoCD
PreSync hook, so it finishes before the app deploys. It connects as the administrator, grants the
role, and deletes itself when it succeeds.

 Cloud PostgreSQL MySQL 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS A role in the `rds_iam` group A user `IDENTIFIED WITH AWSAuthenticationPlugin`. The IAM policy's user name is the link. 
 GCP OpenTofu creates the IAM user; the Job only grants The same, for the shortened MySQL login 
 Azure A login role with a `pgaadauth` security label holding the object ID `CREATE AADUSER` with the client ID 

The Job's own administrator credential:

- **Azure**: a separate admin managed identity gets an Entra token. No password exists, and the app
 identity has no admin rights.
- **AWS and GCP**: the External Secrets Operator fetches the existing administrator credential for
 t

records.title: Keyless database auth
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not fall back to a password. A database marked for IAM authentication on a cloud that
 cannot do it, for example after a move to Hetzner, fails the deploy with the reason.
- It does not pool connections.
- It does not give the app administrator rights.
