records.title: Multi-cloud conversion
records.text: Multi-cloud conversion. What changes when you duplicate a project onto another cloud — what Alethia maps, what it clears, and the warnings it shows before you submit.

records.title: Multi-cloud conversion
records.text:
When you duplicate a project and pick a cloud identity on another cloud, Alethia converts the design
for you. It maps each setting to the target cloud, clears what cannot carry over, and lists a warning
for each change so you can review it before you submit.

 Duplicate and edit Conv["Convert design"]
 Conv --> Map["Mapped: region, machine types, engines, sizes"]
 Conv --> Clear["Cleared: network ID, DNS zone, WAF rules"]
 Conv --> Warn["Warnings to review"]
 Map --> Dst["Draft project on cloud B"]
 Clear --> Dst
`} />

records.title: Multi-cloud conversion
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
1. Select **Duplicate & Edit** on a project.
2. Choose a cloud identity on another cloud.
3. Alethia converts the design and shows the warnings.
4. Review and change the draft, then submit it.

records.title: Multi-cloud conversion
records.heading: What is mapped
records.text:
Setting What happens 
 --- --- 
 Region Mapped to the nearest region on the target, for example AWS `us-east-1` → GCP `us-east4` → Azure `eastus`. With no match, the target's default region, with a warning. 
 Machine types Mapped to an equivalent, for example `t3.medium` → `e2-standard-2` → `Standard_B2s`. A mapping never picks a type too small to run the cluster add-ons, so it can pick a larger node. With no match, the target's default type, with a warning. 
 Kubernetes version Set to the target's default version. 
 Autoscaler Replaced with the target's equivalent, for example Karpenter → GKE Autopilot → the AKS cluster autoscaler. 
 Spot capacity Kept where the target sells Spot. On Hetzner, or on GKE Autopilot, the cluster uses on-demand nodes, with a warning. On Azure, Spot adds a separate Spot pool; the system pool stays on-demand. 
 Database engine Mapped, for example `aurora-postgresql` → `cloudsql-postgresql` → `azure-postgresql`. An engine the target does not offer switches, with a warning: MySQL on Hetzner becomes PostgreSQL. 
 Database capacity Kept inside the target's range. The unit changes: Aurora capacity units on AWS, vCPUs on GCP, vCores on Azure. A warning names t

records.title: Multi-cloud conversion
records.heading: What is cleared
records.text:
These identify resources in the source account, so they cannot carry over. Set them again on the
target.

- An existing network you reused. The draft provisions a new network instead.
- The DNS zone and domain. Select a zone in the target account.
- WAF rules. The rule formats differ between clouds.
- IAM roles, service accounts and cluster admin identities.

records.title: Multi-cloud conversion
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not move data. A converted project provisions new, empty resources.
- It does not submit for you. The converted design is a draft until you submit it.
- It does not offer a component the target cannot build. See
 [Cloud abstraction](/concepts/cloud-abstraction).

records.title: Promotions
records.text: Promotions. How Alethia carries a source environment's structural design onto a higher-stage environment — a plan, then protection gates, then a deploy or a wait for approval.

records.title: Promotions
records.text:
A promotion copies the structural design of one environment onto another environment of the same or
a higher stage. Alethia plans the result, checks the target's protection gates, and then deploys it
or waits for a person to approve.

 PENDING_PLAN
 PENDING_PLAN --> DEPLOYING: every gate passes
 PENDING_PLAN --> PENDING_APPROVAL: a gate needs a person
 PENDING_PLAN --> BLOCKED: a gate fails
 PENDING_APPROVAL --> DEPLOYING: approvals reached
 PENDING_APPROVAL --> CANCELLED: rejected
 DEPLOYING --> SUCCEEDED
 PENDING_PLAN --> FAILED: plan fails
 DEPLOYING --> FAILED: deploy fails
`} />

records.title: Promotions
records.heading: What is copied
records.text:
A promotion changes what a resource is, not how much of it there is.

- **Structural** fields are copied: engine, version, topology, whether a component exists. For
 example, a database promotes its engine, engine version, port and IAM authentication setting.
- **Environment-tunable** fields stay as the target has them: sizes, node counts, retention, and
 environment-specific domains and repositories.

So promoting "add a Redis cache" from `staging` to `production` adds the cache and keeps
production's own sizes. A promotion with nothing structural to copy is refused.

records.title: Promotions
records.heading: The steps
records.text:
1. You promote from a source environment to a target. Alethia checks that you may `deploy` the
 project, that the target's stage is the same or higher (`development` → `staging` → `production`),
 and that the target is not queued, provisioning, destroying or destroyed.
2. Alethia records the promotion with a fingerprint of the source design, writes the merged design
 into the target, and queues a plan for the target.
3. When the plan succeeds, Alethia checks the gates below.
4. If every gate passes, Alethia queues a deploy that reuses the plan's frozen configuration. When it
 succeeds, the promotion is `SUCCEEDED`.

A failed plan or deploy marks the promotion `FAILED`. Only one promotion can be in progress for a
target environment at a time; a second one is refused before the target's design is touched.

records.title: Promotions
records.heading: Protection gates
records.text:
Each target environment has protection rules. With no rules, or every rule off, it promotes freely.

 Gate Turned on by Passes when 
 --- --- --- 
 Predecessor healthy Require predecessor The predecessor environment is in sync (no drift) and has already deployed this exact design. 
 Verify Require verify pass The plan's [Elench](/concepts/elench) report has no failing hard control that is not waived. With no report yet, the gate waits. 
 Soak Soak minutes That many minutes have passed since the predecessor's last deploy. With no predecessor deploy, the gate fails. 
 Cost delta Cost threshold (USD per month) The plan's monthly cost minus the target's previous cost is not over the threshold. With no previous cost, the gate is skipped. 
 Manual approval Require approval Enough people have approved. 

The gates decide together: any **fail** blocks the promotion (`BLOCKED`); otherwise any gate that
waits moves it to `PENDING_APPROVAL`; otherwise it deploys. A cost over the threshold waits for
review; it does not block.

A [classification](/guides/classification) value on the target can force the approval or verify gate
on and raise the number of approvals needed. The strictest requireme

records.title: Promotions
records.heading: Approvals
records.text:
When the approval gate waits, Alethia opens one approval slot per required approval.

- **Approve** fills one slot and checks every gate again. When all pass, the deploy is queued.
- **Reject** cancels the promotion.
- **Cancel** stops a promotion in progress. The design already written into the target stays.

The protection rules name who may approve: listed people, or a role. Owners and admins always satisfy
a role requirement. With no list, anyone who may `deploy` the project may approve.

records.title: Promotions
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not promote down: a target of a lower stage is refused.
- It does not copy sizes, counts or environment-specific domains.
- It does not undo the design it wrote into the target when you cancel.
- It does not add a job type. A promotion is a plan and a deploy.

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.text: Provisioning pipeline. How a design becomes infrastructure — a frozen configuration snapshot, OpenTofu variables, a plan, the verification check, the apply, and the cluster setup that follows.

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.text:
When you plan or deploy an environment, Alethia freezes its design into a snapshot on the job. A
runner turns the snapshot into OpenTofu variables for that cloud's template, plans, checks the plan,
applies exactly that plan, and then sets up the cluster.

 Snap["Config snapshot on the job"]
 Snap --> Vars["tfvars for the cloud template"]
 Vars --> Plan["tofu plan"]
 Plan --> Gate["Elench check"]
 Gate --> Apply["tofu apply of that plan"]
 Apply --> Post["Kubeconfig, ArgoCD, app manifests"]
`} />

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: 1. Design
records.text:
You design the environment on the canvas, in the CLI, or from a proposal. A proposal comes from
scanning your source repositories: Alethia reads each repository without running it, detects its
services (a monorepo gives several), and proposes the components they need. You review the proposal
before anything is saved.

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: 2. Snapshot
records.text:
When a job is queued, Alethia reads every component of the environment and stores the result on the
job as its configuration snapshot. The job runs that snapshot, even if you edit the design afterwards.
When a signing key is configured, the snapshot is signed, and the control plane fails a job whose
snapshot changed after it was queued instead of handing it to a runner. The snapshot carries identifiers, never secrets: the Git token and
connector credentials reach the runner separately, at claim time.

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: 3. Variables
records.text:
The runner reads the snapshot and maps each field to the variable names of the cloud's template, for
example the cluster version to `eks_cluster_version`, `gke_cluster_version` or
`aks_cluster_version`. It writes them to `terraform.tfvars.json`. No templating engine edits the
`.tf` files: the templates are plain OpenTofu with `variable` blocks.

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: 4. Plan
records.text:
The runner initializes OpenTofu against the [state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state), runs
`tofu plan`, and saves the binary plan with the control plane. If an Infracost key is configured, it
also prices the plan (see [Cost estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation)).

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: 5. Check
records.text:
[Elench](/concepts/elench) evaluates the plan before anything is applied. On a plan job the report is
shown in the Plan tab. On a deploy, a failing hard control that no one waived stops the job before
`tofu apply`.

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: 6. Apply

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: 7. Cluster setup
records.text:
After the apply, the runner reads the OpenTofu outputs, writes a kubeconfig that mints short-lived
tokens (no cloud CLI), checks that the cluster answers, installs ArgoCD and the cluster services, and
generates manifests for your detected services. It commits manifests only to an empty apps
repository, so it never overwrites yours. See [GitOps and ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).

The control plane then records cluster endpoints, database endpoints and the ArgoCD address on the
environment and sets it `ACTIVE`. Passwords, kubeconfigs and tokens are removed from the job's
results before they leave the runner.

records.title: Provisioning pipeline
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not apply a plan nobody reviewed, when the deploy names one.
- It does not store secrets in the snapshot.
- It does not overwrite an apps repository that already has manifests.
- It does not create resources it can reuse: a component marked existing, such as a network, is read
 with a data source instead. See [Reuse existing resources](/guides/design-project/network#use-an-existing-network).

records.text:

records.title: Real-time updates
records.text: Real-time updates. How the console streams job logs and support messages live over Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY and server-sent events, and why everything else refreshes by polling.

records.title: Real-time updates
records.text:
A stream that must feel instant, such as a job's log or a support thread, is pushed to the browser:
Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, relayed over server-sent events (SSE). Everything else, such as job status,
the runner list and environment status, is polled, and polls fast only while something is in flight.

 L["Runner log buffer"]
 L --> POST batch DB[("job_logs")]
 DB --> NOTIFY jobId, logId C["Console LISTEN"]
 C --> SSE B["Browser"]
`} />

records.title: Real-time updates
records.heading: Log streaming
records.text:
1. The runner captures OpenTofu's standard output and standard error in two buffers.
2. It sends a buffer to the control plane within about 100 milliseconds of a write, when it passes
 10 KB, and at the end of the job. A 1-second timer backs this up.
3. The control plane inserts each chunk into the job's log, and the database emits a notification on
 the `job_logs` channel with only the job and row IDs, because a notification is capped at 8 KB.
4. Each console instance holds one `LISTEN` connection per channel. On a notification, the job's SSE
 route reads the rows newer than the last one it sent and writes them to the stream.
5. The browser appends each chunk. A dropped connection reconnects on its own and resumes from the last
 row it received, so no chunk is lost or shown twice.

From OpenTofu writing a line to the browser showing it takes about 200 milliseconds. Standard error
chunks are shown in the error color.

Support threads use the same path on the `support_messages` channel. Each stream route checks that you
may see the job or case before it opens. Because each instance listens for itself, this works with
several console instances and no message broker.

The runner also

records.title: Real-time updates
records.heading: Poll everything else
records.text:
Data Refresh 
 --- --- 
 Jobs page Every 5 seconds while a listed job is in flight, otherwise every 30 seconds 
 Shared job list (palette, overview, notifications) Every 5 seconds while any job is in flight 
 One job Every 3 seconds while it is `QUEUED`, `CLAIMED` or `PROCESSING` 
 Runners Every 10 seconds while the tab is focused 
 Environment status on the canvas Every 4 seconds while a job runs on it, otherwise every 30 seconds

records.title: Real-time updates
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not push job status, runners or environment status. A change shows on the next poll.
- It does not send log contents in the notification, only IDs.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.text: Cloud credentials. How a runner gets a short-lived credential for each job — keyless federation on AWS, GCP and Azure, and an API token on Hetzner that you can keep inside your own runner.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.text:
A runner gets a cloud credential at the start of every job and removes it when the job ends, even if
the job fails. On AWS, GCP and Azure the credential is keyless: the runner exchanges a short-lived
assertion from Alethia's own OIDC issuer. Hetzner has no federation, so it uses an API token.

 Id["Read the job's cloud identity"]
 Id --> Mint["Fetch an assertion (10 min or less) from the control plane"]
 Mint --> File["Write it to a token file the provider re-reads"]
 File --> Tofu["OpenTofu exchanges it for a ~1 h cloud session"]
 Tofu --> Refresh["Re-mint into the file every few minutes"]
 Refresh --> End["Job end: stop refreshing, delete the files"]
`} />

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
The runner asks the control plane for an assertion for the job's cloud, writes it to a token file,
and points OpenTofu's provider at that file. The cloud checks the assertion and returns a session of
about an hour. A background refresher writes a new assertion into the file every few minutes, so an
apply longer than one session keeps working. Why the cloud trusts the assertion is explained in
[Security](/concepts/security).

 Cloud What the connection stores What the runner does 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS The role ARN Writes an AWS profile with `web_identity_token_file` and `role_arn`, and points OpenTofu at it with `AWS_CONFIG_FILE` and `AWS_PROFILE`. AWS STS returns the role's session. 
 GCP The project ID and the Workload Identity Federation configuration: pool, provider, service account Points the configuration's credential source at the token file. Google STS exchanges it for an access token. 
 Azure The tenant ID, subscription ID and the client ID of your user-assigned managed identity Sets `ARM_USE_OIDC`, the IDs and `ARM_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE_PATH` (and `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`). The provider exchanges the assertion for an Azure Resource Manager token. 

No access key, service accou

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Hetzner
records.text:
Hetzner authenticates with one API token. You choose how Alethia gets it when you connect:

- **Store a scoped token.** Alethia stores the token encrypted and decrypts it only when a runner
 claims the job. The runner sets `HCLOUD_TOKEN` for the job and clears it after.
- **Keep the token in your runner.** The connection stores no token. Its jobs are marked for a
 self-operated runner, and managed runners cannot claim them. Your runner reads `HCLOUD_TOKEN` from
 its own environment, so the token never enters Alethia's database.

Either way the token is long-lived and scoped to a whole Hetzner project. Hetzner is not keyless.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Connector credentials
records.text:
Credentials for a [connector](/concepts/connectors), such as a Cloudflare token, are decrypted by the
control plane at claim time and sent with the job. The runner uses them in memory for that job only.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not keep a credential after the job.
- It does not share a session between jobs: each job gets its own.
- It does not hold the issuer's signing key. Only the control plane does.
- It does not make Hetzner keyless.

 Property How 
 --- --- 
 Time-bounded An assertion lasts 10 minutes or less; the session it buys about an hour. 
 Scoped A credential has only the permissions of your role, service account or managed identity. 
 Revocable Delete the role, the federation provider or the managed identity, and the next exchange fails.

records.title: Runners
records.text: Runners. What a runner is, where it runs — Alethia's managed fleet or your own infrastructure — and how it claims a job, gets credentials, runs OpenTofu and reports back.

records.title: Runners
records.text:
A runner is the agent that does Alethia's work: it claims jobs from the queue, gets a short-lived
credential for your cloud, runs OpenTofu, installs ArgoCD and streams logs back. It is one Go binary
in a container image, and it holds no storage key and no long-lived cloud key.

 Reg["Register with the control plane"]
 Reg --> HB["Heartbeat every 30 s"]
 Reg --> Wake["Wake stream (SSE)"]
 Wake --> Claim{"Claim a job"}
 Poll["Safety poll every 30 s"] --> Claim
 Claim --> job Cred["Mint a per-job cloud credential"]
 Cred --> Exec["Run the job (sandbox seam)"]
 Exec --> Logs["Stream logs"]
 Logs --> Report["Report the result"]
 Report --> Claim
`} />

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Where a runner runs
records.text:
Managed Self · deployed Self · registered 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Who runs it Alethia, in the platform account You, in your cloud account You, anywhere 
 How it starts The [warm-pool scaler](/concepts/runner/scaling) creates Hetzner VMs that register themselves A `DEPLOY_RUNNER` job provisions it, on AWS as an ECS Fargate service You start it, for example with `alethia runner start`, and register it for a token 
 Cloud credentials Keyless, minted per job Your runner's own cloud identity Your runner's own cloud identity 
 Billing Provisioned runner hours Your own cloud bill Your own infrastructure 

A self-operated runner keeps credentials inside your infrastructure. It is also the only way to run
[bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac) without the managed sandbox, and the only runner
that can claim a Hetzner job whose token you keep to yourself. See
[Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated).

The process reads its role from `ALETHIA_RUNNER_OPERATOR` (`managed` or `self`) and the control plane
address from `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN`.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Running a job
records.text:
1. **Claim.** The control plane pushes a wake signal over a server-sent events stream when a job is
 claimable; a 30-second poll covers a dropped stream. The claim is atomic, so one job runs on one
 runner. See [Job queue](/concepts/job-queue).
2. **Credentials.** The runner mints a short-lived credential for the job's cloud identity, without a
 stored key, and clears it when the job ends. See [Cloud credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).
3. **Run.** The runner runs the job through a sandbox seam. Alethia's own templates run in the runner
 process. Your own OpenTofu or Helm runs, on the managed fleet, in a per-job container. See
 [Isolated execution](/concepts/isolated-execution). What each job type does is in
 [Job execution](/concepts/runner/job-execution).
4. **Logs.** OpenTofu output streams to the job page within about a second. See
 [Real-time updates](/concepts/realtime).
5. **Report.** The runner posts the result: status, OpenTofu outputs with secrets removed, the
 [Elench](/concepts/elench) report and timings.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Heartbeat
records.text:
A runner sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds with its version and the clouds it can serve. The
response lists jobs cancelled on the server, as a fallback when a cancel on the wake stream was
missed. The wake stream also refreshes the runner's liveness about every 10 seconds; a runner silent
for 45 seconds is marked offline. What happens to its job is in
[Job queue](/concepts/job-queue#failure-recovery).

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Shutdown
records.text:
On `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` a runner stops claiming, lets its current job finish for up to 10 minutes,
and exits. The managed fleet drains a runner before it destroys its VM, so the stop signal reaches a
runner that already finished.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: The image
records.text:
Each image starts from a shared base (Alpine 3.21, non-root `runner` user) and adds one cloud's
template, already initialized so no provider downloads happen at job time. The base holds the runner
binary, OpenTofu 1.9.0 (checksum-verified), `kubectl`, Helm, Infracost 0.10.39, and a rootless
container runtime that stays unused unless the sandbox is turned on. It holds no `aws`, `gcloud` or
`az` CLI: cluster tokens are minted inside the runner process.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Repository URLs
records.text:
The runner checks every repository URL before it clones, pulls or pushes:

- The URL uses `https://`. A bring-your-own IaC repository can also use `ssh://` or
 `git@host:owner/repo`, for a deploy key. Other schemes, such as `file://`, `git://` and
 `http://`, are refused.
- The URL holds no credentials. A private repository is read through its connected git account.
- The host is a public name that resolves only to public addresses. `localhost`, `*.local`,
 `*.internal`, and private, loopback, link-local and carrier-grade NAT addresses are refused.

A self-operated runner that uses a Git server on a private network allows it with
`ALETHIA_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`: a comma-separated list of host names (`git.corp.example`), wildcard
suffixes (`*.corp.example`), IP addresses or CIDR ranges (`10.20.0.0/16`). It is empty by default,
and the scheme and credential checks still apply. If an entry cannot be read, the runner refuses
every clone until it is fixed.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not keep cloud credentials between jobs.
- It does not hold an object-storage key. State goes through the [state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state).
- It does not verify cloud connections or keep the asset inventory. The control plane does that when
 you connect. See [Connection health and inventory](/concepts/connection-health).

records.title: AWS template
records.text: AWS template. What the AWS OpenTofu template builds — EKS, Karpenter, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB and the rest — and the Karpenter and node group settings you can change.

records.title: AWS template
records.text:
The AWS template (`infra/templates/project/aws/`) builds an EKS cluster and the AWS services your
design declares, in your account. Pods reach AWS through IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA), never
static keys.

 EKS["EKS cluster and node groups"]
 EKS --> K["Karpenter NodePools"]
 EKS --> IRSA["IRSA roles for controllers"]
 VPC --> Data["Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, SQS/SNS, S3, ECR"]
 Edge["Route 53, ACM, WAFv2"] --> EKS
`} />

records.title: AWS template
records.heading: What it builds
records.text:
File Resources 
 --- --- 
 `networking.tf` VPC, public and private subnets, NAT and internet gateways, route tables, security groups 
 `eks.tf` EKS cluster, the default and extra managed node groups, the OIDC provider for IRSA 
 `karpenter.tf` Karpenter's interruption queue (SQS) and EventBridge rules, and the EC2 Spot service-linked role when `ec2_spot_service_role` is set 
 `irsa.tf` IAM roles for service accounts 
 `rds.tf` Aurora PostgreSQL or MySQL cluster and instances 
 `elasticache.tf` ElastiCache Redis replication group 
 `valkey.tf` ElastiCache Serverless Valkey cache 
 `dynamodb.tf` DynamoDB tables with KMS encryption 
 `sqs.tf` SQS queues (standard and FIFO) and SNS topics 
 `s3.tf` S3 buckets with encryption, versioning and lifecycle rules 
 `ecr.tf` ECR repositories with lifecycle policies and scan on push 
 `route53.tf` Route 53 hosted zone 
 `acm-certificate.tf` ACM certificates with DNS validation 
 `waf.tf` WAFv2 web ACL with managed rule groups 
 `custom_secrets.tf` Secrets Manager secrets with generated passwords 

These files call modules under `modules/` for EKS, RDS, Redis, Valkey, DynamoDB, ECR, S3, SQS and
SNS, WAFv2, ACM, Route 53 and password generation.

records.title: AWS template
records.heading: Karpenter NodePool
records.text:
With `enable_karpenter`, the runner applies a Karpenter `NodePool` named `default` after the cluster
is up. It decides which EC2 instances Karpenter may launch. Set these keys in the cluster's
`provider_config`; with none set, the defaults apply.

 Key Default Allowed values 
 --- --- --- 
 `karpenter_capacity_types` `["on-demand"]` `spot`, `on-demand`, or both. With both, Karpenter prefers Spot. 
 `karpenter_architectures` `["amd64"]` `amd64` only. Use `karpenter_arm64_nodepool` for arm64. 
 `karpenter_instance_categories` `["t", "m"]` EC2 categories such as `c`, `m`, `r`. An empty list removes the requirement. 
 `karpenter_instance_families` `[]` Families such as `c7i`, each in one of the categories. 
 `karpenter_cpu_limit` `100` Total vCPU the pool may launch, 1 to 1000. 
 `karpenter_node_labels` `{}` Labels on every Karpenter node. 
 `karpenter_node_taints` `[]` Taints, each `{ key, value, effect }`. 
 `karpenter_arm64_nodepool` `null` Adds an `arm64` pool. Fields: `instance_families` (Graviton, not `a1`) and `cpu_limit` (default `100`). 

Keys in the `kubernetes.io`, `k8s.io`, `karpenter.sh` and `karpenter.k8s.aws` domains are refused for
labels and taints, except `node-restri

records.title: AWS template
records.heading: Node groups
records.text:
The [node pool keys](/reference/node-pools) build these on
EKS:

- `node_labels` reach the default node group and every extra one. `node_taints` reach the extra node
 groups only.
- Each entry in `extra_node_pools` is a managed node group named ` - `.
 `capacity_type: spot` makes it a Spot node group.
- An extra node group uses the default group's operating system (`eks_ami_type`, Bottlerocket by
 default), with the arm64 or NVIDIA image where the instance type needs one. The plan refuses a pool
 with no matching image, such as a GPU pool on FIPS Bottlerocket.
- An `arm64` pool needs a Graviton type, such as `m7g.large`; an `amd64` pool an x86 type.
- **Size.** A node group starts with `desired_size` nodes and stays there: nothing scales it, and a
 later change to `desired_size` does not resize it. For capacity that follows demand, use Karpenter.
- **Isolation.** Every node group has the default group's controls: IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1, the
 same private subnets and security group, an encrypted gp3 root volume, and the same IAM policies.

records.title: AWS template
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not let Karpenter's default pool launch arm64 instances.
- It does not autoscale extra managed node groups.
- It does not count Karpenter's instances in plan-time cost guards.

records.title: Azure template
records.text: Azure template. What the Azure OpenTofu template builds — AKS, Azure Database, Azure Managed Redis, Cosmos DB, the Application Gateway and the rest — and the logging, parameter, encryption and node pool settings you can change.

records.title: Azure template
records.text:
The Azure template (`infra/templates/project/azure/`) builds an AKS cluster and the Azure services
your design declares, in your subscription. Controllers in the cluster use workload identities, with
no client secrets.

 AKS["AKS and its node pools"]
 VNet --> AGW["Application Gateway v2 (opt-in)"]
 WAF["WAF policy"] --> AGW
 AGW --> AGIC AKS
 VNet --> Data["Azure Database, Managed Redis, Cosmos DB, Service Bus, Storage, ACR, Key Vault"]
`} />

records.title: Azure template
records.heading: What it builds
records.text:
File Resources 
 --- --- 
 `aks.tf` AKS cluster, default node pool, Microsoft Entra ID integration 
 `nodepools.tf` The node labels, taints and extra node pools 
 `vnet.tf` Virtual network, subnets, network security group, NAT gateway 
 `azure-db.tf` Azure Database for PostgreSQL or MySQL (Flexible Server) 
 `azure-cache-redis.tf` Azure Managed Redis 
 `cosmos-db.tf` Cosmos DB account, database and container 
 `service-bus.tf` Service Bus namespace, queues and topics 
 `storage-account.tf` Storage account and blob containers 
 `acr.tf` Azure Container Registry 
 `azure-dns.tf` Azure DNS zone 
 `key-vault.tf` Key Vault with Azure RBAC, the provisioner's Key Vault Secrets Officer role, and secrets 
 `azure-waf.tf` WAF policy: OWASP 3.2 and your custom rules 
 `application-gateway.tf` Application Gateway v2, its public IP, and the ingress controller's workload identity 

These files call modules under `modules/` for AKS, the database, Redis, Cosmos DB, ACR, storage,
Service Bus, DNS, the WAF, Key Vault and the virtual network.

records.title: Azure template
records.heading: Ingress through an Application Gateway
records.text:
Azure has no load balancer per Ingress. Instead, the template can build one Application Gateway v2,
and the Application Gateway Ingress Controller turns each `Ingress` with
`ingressClassName: azure-application-gateway` into rules on it. A WAF policy attaches to a gateway,
so turning the WAF on also builds a gateway (WAF_v2 tier) and binds the policy to it.

The gateway bills per hour while it exists. It is built only when you turn the WAF on or set
`azure_application_gateway_enabled: true`, and it needs the template to create the virtual network.
Without it, use the Traefik add-on.

records.title: Azure template
records.heading: Logs
records.text:
A Log Analytics workspace bills per GB ingested, so each logging setting adds cost.

- **Control plane.** On the cluster, `aks_log_retention_days` (30 to 730) creates a workspace with that
 retention, turns on Container Insights, and sends the `kube-apiserver` and `kube-audit-admin` logs
 to it.
- **Database.** On the database, `azure_db_log_exports` lists the categories to send:
 `PostgreSQLLogs`, `PostgreSQLFlexSessions`, `PostgreSQLFlexQueryStoreRuntime`,
 `PostgreSQLFlexQueryStoreWaitStats`, `PostgreSQLFlexTableStats` and `PostgreSQLFlexDatabaseXacts`
 for PostgreSQL; `MySqlSlowLogs` and `MySqlAuditLogs` for MySQL. Some stay empty until a server
 parameter is on: `audit_log_enabled` for MySQL audit logs, Query Store
 (`pg_qs.query_capture_mode`) and wait sampling for the Query Store categories.
- **Cache.** On the cache, `azure_cache_log_categories: ["ConnectionEvents"]`.

Database and cache logs go to the cluster's workspace, or to the workspace in
`azure_db_log_workspace_id` or `azure_cache_log_workspace_id`. The plan fails if they have nowhere to
go, or if a category belongs to the other engine.

records.title: Azure template
records.heading: Database server parameters
records.text:
On the database, `azure_db_database_flags` sets Flexible Server parameters as strings, for example
`{ "max_connections": "200" }`. The template refuses `require_secure_transport`,
`ssl_min_protocol_version` and `tls_version`, which could weaken TLS below 1.2.

 
 Other parameters can also weaken the server and are accepted, such as `password_encryption: md5`
 or changes to `pgaudit.log`. Review them as security changes. A static parameter restarts the
 server.

records.title: Azure template
records.heading: Storage encryption with your own key
records.text:
On a bucket, `cmek_enabled: true` encrypts the project's storage account with a key in the project's
Key Vault. Azure encrypts a whole account with one key, so every container uses it. A managed identity
reaches the key with only the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role, on that key.
`key_vault_purge_protection_enabled` must stay `true`.

records.title: Azure template
records.heading: Node pools
records.text:
The template always makes the default pool, a pool per extra VM size in `aks_instance_types`
(`pool1`, `pool2` and so on), and a `spot` pool when `aks_spot_enabled` is `true`. The autoscaler
scales each between its bounds; `aks_node_desired_size` and `aks_spot_node_min_size` set only the
starting counts.

The [node pool keys](/reference/node-pools) build these on
AKS:

- `node_labels` reach every pool. `node_taints` reach the named extra pools only.
- Each entry in `extra_node_pools` is a user node pool with its own VM size and bounds, keyed by name.
 A name that collides with the temporary name AKS uses when rebuilding another pool is refused.
- **Spot.** `capacity_type: spot` uses the cluster's Spot settings: `aks_spot_eviction_policy`
 (`Delete`) and `aks_spot_max_price` (`-1`, up to the on-demand price).
- **arm64.** An arm64 pool needs an Arm VM size: one with `p` after the vCPU count, such as
 `Standard_D4ps_v5`. The plan refuses a mismatch.
- **Isolation.** A named pool has the default pool's subnet, disk type and size, and pod limit.

 
 Changing a pool's `name` or `capacity_type` replaces it. Changing its `instance_type` replaces every
 node without draining it first: pods

records.title: Azure template
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not build an Application Gateway unless you turn on the WAF or the gateway.
- It does not refuse every risky server parameter, only the TLS ones.
- It does not encrypt one container with a different key from the rest of the account.

records.title: GCP template
records.text: GCP template. What the GCP OpenTofu template builds — GKE, Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Firestore and the rest — and the node pool, Query Insights and bucket encryption settings you can change.

records.title: GCP template
records.text:
The GCP template (`infra/templates/project/gcp/`) builds a GKE cluster and the Google Cloud services
your design declares, in your project. Pods reach Google Cloud through GKE Workload Identity, with no
key files.

 GKE["GKE: Standard with node pools, or Autopilot"]
 GKE --> WI["Workload Identity service accounts"]
 Net --> Data["Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Firestore, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, Artifact Registry"]
 Edge["Cloud DNS, Cloud Armor"] --> GKE
`} />

records.title: GCP template
records.heading: What it builds
records.text:
File Resources 
 --- --- 
 `gke.tf` GKE cluster with Workload Identity and its default node pool, or an Autopilot cluster 
 `nodepools.tf` The node labels, taints and extra node pools 
 `networking.tf` VPC network, subnets, Cloud NAT and Cloud Router, firewall rules, private services access 
 `cloud-sql.tf` Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL or MySQL, with backups and optional regional high availability 
 `memorystore.tf` Memorystore for Redis 
 `memorystore-valkey.tf` Memorystore for Valkey 
 `firestore.tf` Firestore database and indexes 
 `pubsub.tf` Pub/Sub topics and subscriptions 
 `cloud-storage.tf` Cloud Storage buckets, and the Cloud KMS key for buckets that use your own key 
 `artifact-registry.tf` Artifact Registry repositories 
 `cloud-dns.tf` Cloud DNS managed zone 
 `secret-manager.tf` Secret Manager secrets 
 `cloud-armor.tf` Cloud Armor security policy 

These files call modules under `modules/` for GKE, Cloud SQL, both Memorystore products, Firestore,
Artifact Registry, Cloud Storage, Cloud Armor, Cloud DNS, Pub/Sub, Secret Manager and the VPC network.

GKE Autopilot (`enable_autopilot`) leaves node management to Google.

records.title: GCP template
records.heading: Node pools
records.text:
The template always makes one default pool, sized by `gke_node_min_size`, `gke_node_max_size` and
`gke_node_desired_size`. The [node pool keys](/reference/node-pools)
build these on GKE:

- `node_labels` reach every pool. The template's own labels (`environment`, `service`, `managed-by`
 and classification tags) cannot be reused as keys. `node_taints` reach the extra pools only.
- Each entry in `extra_node_pools` is a node pool named ` - `, shortened with a hash
 past GKE's 40-character limit. Pools are keyed by name, so removing one leaves the others.
- **Size.** The cluster autoscaler keeps a pool between `min_size` and `max_size` across its zones. A
 zonal cluster's pool starts with `desired_size` nodes (or `min_size`). A regional cluster's pool
 spans three zones and starts with a multiple of three: `desired_size` rounded up, kept within the
 bounds where a multiple of three fits, otherwise up to two nodes over `max_size` until the
 autoscaler removes them. After creation the autoscaler owns the count.
- **Spot.** `capacity_type: spot` uses Spot VMs, which Google can reclaim at any time.
- **arm64.** An arm64 pool needs an Arm machine family: `t2a`, `c4a`, `n4a` or `a4x`. The p

records.title: GCP template
records.heading: Cloud SQL Query Insights
records.text:
On a database, `cloud_sql_query_insights_enabled: true` turns on Query Insights. Two more keys, both
needing it, add detail: `cloud_sql_query_insights_record_application_tags` and
`cloud_sql_query_insights_record_client_address`. To turn it off, set it to `false`: removing the key
leaves the instance as it is. Database logs already go to Cloud Logging; change what is logged with
`cloud_sql_database_flags`.

records.title: GCP template
records.heading: Bucket encryption with your own key
records.text:
On a bucket, `cmek_enabled: true` encrypts it with a Cloud KMS key, `gcs-buckets`, in the project's
key ring. The Cloud Storage service agent gets `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` on that key
only. The bucket must be in the project's region, and the Cloud KMS API must be on. Objects already in
a bucket keep their encryption; only new objects use the key.

 
 Disabling or destroying the key makes the objects written under it unreadable. If you turn
 `cmek_enabled` off on every bucket, the template removes the key and Cloud KMS destroys its versions
 after 30 days. Cloud KMS never deletes a key name, so you then cannot turn `cmek_enabled` on again
 in that project: creating `gcs-buckets` again fails with `409 AlreadyExists`. Keep it on for at
 least one bucket to keep the option.

records.title: GCP template
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not manage node pools on Autopilot.
- It does not turn Query Insights off when you remove the key.
- It does not offer cache logging: the Google provider has no logging setting for Memorystore.

records.title: Hetzner template
records.text: Hetzner template. What the Hetzner OpenTofu template builds — Talos Linux servers, the private network and firewall — why the worker count is fixed, how extra worker pools get their subnets, and what Hetzner refuses.

records.title: Hetzner template
records.text:
The Hetzner template (`infra/templates/project/hetzner/`) builds a Kubernetes cluster on Hetzner Cloud
servers that run Talos Linux. Hetzner has no managed Kubernetes, so the template creates the servers,
private network and firewall itself, and Talos turns them into a cluster.

 CP["1 control-plane server"]
 Net --> W["Default workers"]
 Net --> P["Extra worker pools, one /24 subnet each"]
 Talos["Talos machine secrets and configs"] --> CP
 Talos --> W
 Talos --> P
 CP --> K["Cilium, Hetzner cloud controller, volume driver"]
`} />

records.title: Hetzner template
records.heading: What it builds
records.text:
The template has no modules: each file builds one part.

 File Resources 
 --- --- 
 `servers.tf` The control-plane server, default workers, and the servers of each extra pool 
 `talos.tf` Talos machine secrets, a machine configuration per role and pool, the bootstrap and the admin kubeconfig 
 `image.tf` A Talos disk snapshot per CPU architecture the cluster uses 
 `network.tf` The private network (or yours), the node subnet, public IPv4 addresses and the firewall 
 `cilium.tf`, `csi.tf` Cilium, the Hetzner cloud controller manager and volume driver, rendered for the runner to apply 
 `dns.tf` A Hetzner DNS zone, when Cloud DNS is on 
 `buckets.tf` Hetzner Object Storage buckets 

 Servers Count Type 
 --- --- --- 
 Control plane 1 The worker server type 
 Default workers `worker_count` (default 1) `worker_server_type` (default `cpx22`) 
 An extra pool The pool's `desired_size`, or `min_size` The pool's `instance_type` 

Every server is on the private network, behind the firewall, with a public IPv4 and IPv6 address,
which Talos uses to configure it. All servers join with the same machine secrets, so a server can only
join its own cluster. `cax` types are arm64; `cx`, `cpx` and `c

records.title: Hetzner template
records.heading: The worker count is fixed
records.text:
The template installs no cluster autoscaler. An autoscaler that creates servers would need the Talos
worker configuration, which holds the cluster's join secrets, inside the cluster, and would use a
token that can create and delete every server in the Hetzner project. Alethia keeps the join secrets
out of the cluster until it can keep them safe.

To change the number of workers:

1. Set the count: the cluster's **Desired** (or **Min**) node count for default workers, at least 1;
 `desired_size` (or `min_size`) for a pool.
2. Plan. The plan adds servers at the end of the pool, or removes those with the highest index.
3. If it removes servers, drain their nodes first with `kubectl drain `: the apply deletes them
 without moving pods.
4. Apply.

Plan for peak load. For short-lived extra capacity, add a pool and set its size to `0` afterwards.

records.title: Hetzner template
records.heading: Worker pools, labels and taints
records.text:
The [node pool keys](/reference/node-pools) work as on
every cloud. Servers are named ` - - - `. A pool's servers use its
`arch` image, the default workers' firewall and network, and their own `/24` subnet.

provider_config:
 extra_node_pools:
 - name: db
 instance_type: ccx23
 min_size: 2
 max_size: 2
 taints:
 - { key: dedicated, value: db, effect: NoSchedule }
 - name: arm
 instance_type: cax21
 arch: arm64
 min_size: 3
 max_size: 3

Labels are set in the Talos machine configuration, so a changed label reaches running nodes on the
next apply. `node_labels` do not reach the control plane. Taints are set when a node registers, and
Kubernetes does not let a node change its own taints afterwards.

 
 A taint change reaches only servers that join after it. To retaint a whole pool, set its size to `0`
 and apply, then set it back and apply again.

records.title: Hetzner template
records.heading: How a pool gets its subnet
records.text:
The `/24` subnets of the cluster network are numbered from `0`, the subnet of the control plane and
default workers. A free `/24` is numbered `1` or higher and outside the pod and service ranges; the
default `10.0.0.0/16` has 95. The plan gives each pool, in order:

1. the number in `node_pool_subnet_index` for that pool, if set;
2. the number recorded for the pool when it was created;
3. the `/24` its servers already use;
4. for a new pool, the free `/24` its name hashes to, or the lowest free one.

So pools never share a `/24`, and a pool keeps its subnet when others are added, removed or
reordered. The record is a label on the cluster's firewall, `subnet.alethia.io/ = `,
outside the OpenTofu state.

 
 Do not edit the `subnet.alethia.io/` labels, and set `node_pool_subnet_index` only for a pool you are
 adding. Moving a pool's subnet replaces its servers. Changing the network range, `pod_cidr` or
 `service_cidr` can move pools too: change those before you add pools.
 

A cluster created before the record existed keeps each pool's current `/24` on its first plan; apply
once before adding pools. With your own network (`provision_network: false`), the plan cannot see its
existing s

records.title: Hetzner template
records.heading: What Hetzner refuses
records.text:
Beyond the rules every cloud applies, the plan refuses:

- `capacity_type: spot`. Hetzner has no interruptible servers.
- An `instance_type` that is not a Hetzner type (`cx`, `cpx`, `ccx` or `cax` and a size).
- An `arch` that does not match the type: `cax` needs `arm64`.
- A pool that does not fit: no free `/24` left, or a `node_pool_subnet_index` that is `0`, outside the
 network, in the pod or service range, already taken, or names no pool.

records.title: Hetzner template
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not autoscale workers.
- It does not offer Spot.
- It does not update the taints of registered nodes.
- It does not change resources when you set none of the pool keys; the first plan after an upgrade
 shows only the new output `nodepool_contract_render`.

records.text: Infrastructure templates. The OpenTofu templates a runner provisions from — one per cloud, plus the self-deployed runner template and the ArgoCD manifests — and how a design reaches them.

records.title: Infrastructure templates
records.text:
A runner provisions from OpenTofu templates that ship inside its image, one per cloud. Each template
is plain OpenTofu: a design reaches it only as variables, and its state goes through the control
plane.

 Vars["terraform.tfvars.json"]
 Vars --> T["infra/templates/project/ "]
 T --> Plan["tofu plan and apply"]
 Plan --> Out["Outputs"]
 Out --> Argo["infra/templates/argocd"]
`} />

records.title: Infrastructure templates
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
Template Path What it builds 
 --- --- --- 
 [AWS](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates/aws) `infra/templates/project/aws/` EKS with Karpenter, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, SQS and SNS, S3, ECR, WAF and the network. 
 [GCP](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates/gcp) `infra/templates/project/gcp/` GKE (Standard or Autopilot), Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Firestore, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, Artifact Registry, Cloud Armor and the network. 
 [Azure](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates/azure) `infra/templates/project/azure/` AKS, Azure Database, Azure Managed Redis, Cosmos DB, Service Bus, Storage, ACR, Key Vault, the WAF and Application Gateway, and the network. 
 [Hetzner](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates/hetzner) `infra/templates/project/hetzner/` A Talos Kubernetes cluster on Hetzner servers, its network, firewall, DNS zone and object storage buckets. 
 Runner `infra/templates/runner/aws/` A self-deployed runner on ECS Fargate. See [Job execution](/concepts/runner/job-execution#runner-lifecycle). 
 ArgoCD `infra/templates/argocd/` The platform Applications installed after the apply. See [GitOps and ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd). 

Each per-cloud runner image c

records.title: Infrastructure templates
records.heading: Settings you can change
records.text:
Most templates accept settings beyond the canvas form, as keys in a component's `provider_config`. In
the console, open the component on the canvas and set them on its template settings card. Settings
are off by default: a project that sets none gets the same infrastructure as before the setting
existed. The cloud pages list them.

The node pool keys `node_labels`, `node_taints` and `extra_node_pools` are the same on every cloud;
their rules are in [Node labels, taints and extra pools](/reference/node-pools).
Every cloud taints arm64 pools with `alethia.io/arch=arm64:NoSchedule`, because the images Alethia
builds are amd64 only, and keeps the default pool untainted for Alethia's add-ons.

records.title: Infrastructure templates
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not template the `.tf` files. Values reach them only through variables.
- It does not download providers at job time.
- It does not let you edit the template for one project. To provision from your own code, use
 [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).

records.title: Job execution
records.text: Job execution. What a runner does for each job type — plan, deploy and destroy, cluster probes and image builds, scans and audits, kubeconfig mints and runner lifecycle jobs — and what happens when a step fails.

records.title: Job execution
records.text:
Every job is claimed the same way and gets the same per-job credential; the job type decides what the
runner then runs. This page describes the work for each type. What each type is for, from the
console's side, is in [Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types).

 Proc["PROCESSING"]
 Proc --> Cred["Per-job credential"]
 Cred --> Type{"Job type"}
 Type --> Tofu["PLAN, DEPLOY, DESTROY, DETECT_DRIFT: OpenTofu"]
 Type --> K8s["PROBE_CLUSTER, BUILD, MINT_KUBECONFIG: the cluster"]
 Type --> Scan["IAC_SCAN, CHART_SCAN, AUDIT, ANALYZE_REPO: read and check"]
 Type --> Run["DEPLOY_RUNNER, UPDATE_RUNNER, DESTROY_RUNNER"]
 Tofu --> Done["SUCCESS or FAILED, with results"]
 K8s --> Done
 Scan --> Done
 Run --> Done
`} />

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Job types
records.text:
Job type What the runner does 
 --- --- 
 `PLAN` Plans, checks the plan with [Elench](/concepts/elench), prices it, and saves the plan file. 
 `DEPLOY` Checks the reviewed plan, applies it behind the Elench gate, and sets up the cluster. 
 `DESTROY` Destroys every resource in the environment's state. 
 `DETECT_DRIFT` Runs a refresh-only plan. See [Drift detection](/concepts/drift). 
 `PROBE_CLUSTER` Checks that the cluster's API server answers. Read-only. 
 `BUILD` Builds your repository's container images inside your cluster. 
 `MINT_KUBECONFIG` Mints a short-lived cluster credential sealed to your key. See [Cluster access](/concepts/cluster-access). 
 `IAC_SCAN` Clones a [bring-your-own module](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac), pins its commit and runs the safety gate. 
 `CHART_SCAN` Renders a [bring-your-own chart](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts) and checks its manifests, always in the sandbox. 
 `AUDIT` Checks a plan or manifests you supply with the Elench controls. Provisions nothing. 
 `ANALYZE_REPO` Reads a source repository, without running it, and reports its services. 
 `DEPLOY_RUNNER`, `UPDATE_RUNNER`, `DESTROY_RUNNER` Manage a self-deployed runner. 
 `STATE_SURGERY` Break

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Plan
records.text:
1. Write the snapshot as OpenTofu variables and initialize against the [state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state).
2. Run `tofu plan -out=plan.tfplan`, then `tofu show -json` for the plan JSON.
3. Evaluate the plan JSON with Elench. On a plan the report is advisory: it is shown in the Plan tab.
4. Price the plan with Infracost, if a key is configured. See [Cost estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation).
5. Save the plan file with the control plane for the deploy.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Deploy
records.text:
1. Check the plan this deploy names: the plan job succeeded, the configuration has not changed, and the
 saved plan file's SHA-256 matches. Any mismatch refuses the job.
2. Run Elench on the plan. A failing hard control that no authorized
 [override](/guides/jobs/verify-override) waives fails the job before any resource changes. An
 evidence [receipt](/concepts/elench/receipts) is sealed for the apply.
3. Run `tofu apply plan.tfplan`. State is written back as each resource settles.
4. Read the outputs, write a kubeconfig that mints tokens in the runner process, and check that the
 cluster answers. A successful apply with an unreachable cluster is reported as not ready.
5. Install ArgoCD and the platform services. See [GitOps and ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).
6. Report the cluster details, outputs with secrets removed, the Elench report and receipt, and timings.

The control plane then writes the cluster, database and cache endpoints onto the environment and sets
it `ACTIVE`. A component marked existing, such as a network you reuse, is read with a data source
instead of created.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Destroy
records.text:
The runner initializes against the state proxy and runs `tofu destroy -auto-approve`; you confirmed in
the console or CLI. The state object stays, empty, and the environment becomes `DESTROYED`. If a
destroy fails partway, the state shows what is gone, and a retry removes only the rest.

 
 Destroy deletes data. Database contents, cache contents and secret values are gone.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Probe
records.text:
The runner reads the environment's outputs from state with a backend-only workspace, so it runs no
provider and clones no module. It builds a kubeconfig and calls the API server's `/readyz` with a
30-second limit. The cluster is reachable only when the answer is `ok`; then it also reads the
Kubernetes version and node readiness. An unreachable cluster is a successful probe with
`reachable: false`, not a failed job.

The control plane probes on a schedule (production every 10 minutes, staging every hour, development
every 6 hours) every environment it believes holds a cluster, and on demand from the canvas **Run**
menu. When a reachable cluster becomes unreachable, it raises one alert.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Build

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Runner lifecycle
records.text:
These jobs manage a self-deployed runner. `DEPLOY_RUNNER` applies the runner template (on AWS, an ECS
Fargate service with its IAM roles, log group and security groups) and registers the runner.
`UPDATE_RUNNER` rolls it to the latest image. `DESTROY_RUNNER` destroys it and removes its
registration. Managed runners need no job: they register themselves.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: When a step fails
records.text:
The runner writes the error to the log, marks the job `FAILED`, keeps the partial state, clears the
credentials, and claims the next job. A retry continues from the state.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not apply a plan other than the one the deploy names.
- It does not run your Dockerfile on the runner.
- It does not treat an unreachable cluster as a failed probe.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.text: Warm-pool scaling. How the managed runner fleet sizes itself — a warm pool of Hetzner VMs per cloud, raised by queue depth and lowered once it has been idle, by a scaler inside the control plane.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.text:
The managed fleet keeps a warm pool of runners for each cloud, one runner by default, so most jobs
start without waiting for a VM to boot. A scaler inside the control plane adds VMs when jobs queue
up and destroys idle ones when the queue clears.

 wake Tick
 Timer["Every 60 s"] --> Tick["Scaler pass (leader only)"]
 Tick --> Plan["Plan: health, then count, placement, version"]
 Plan --> Act["Create, drain or destroy VMs"]
 Act --> Ledger["Fleet action ledger"]
 Act --> VM["Hetzner VM boots the runner image"]
 VM --> bootstrap token Reg["Runner registers"]
 Reg --> Claim["Claims jobs"]
`} />

This page is for operators of the managed fleet. To run it, see
[Managed provisioning](/self-host/managed-provisioning).

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: The loop
records.text:
The scaler runs every 60 seconds, and also at once whenever a job is queued, so a new job does not
wait for the next tick. Within one control plane process only one pass runs at a time. Across
replicas, only the replica that holds the fleet leader lease acts; a crashed leader is replaced when
its lease expires.

Each pass compares the pool's target with the VMs that exist and fixes, in order: unhealthy VMs, the
count, the spread over locations, and the runner version.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Pools
records.text:
A pool is one row per cloud, edited in the console. The scaler reads the enabled pools on every pass,
so a change applies without a redeploy.

 Setting Default Meaning 
 --- --- --- 
 Warm minimum `1` Runners kept ready with an empty queue. `0` lets the pool scale to zero, at the cost of a cold start. 
 Maximum `10` Ceiling on healthy runners. 
 Buffer `1` Spare runners above demand. 
 Slots per runner `1` Jobs one runner runs at once. 
 Surge `1` Extra runners allowed during a version rollout. 
 Scale-down grace `5` ticks Passes the pool must be over target before idle runners are destroyed. 
 Locations `fsn1` Hetzner locations to spread across. 
 Minimum per location `0` Healthy runners to keep in each location.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Target size
records.text:
demand = max(inFlightJobs, ceil(queuedJobs / slotsPerRunner))
target = clamp(max(warmMin, demand + buffer), 0, max)

Both job counts are for the pool's cloud. Scale-up fills locations below their minimum first, then
the least-loaded one.

**Scale-down** waits until the pool has been over target for the grace period, then destroys idle
runners down to the target: never a busy one, and never below a location's minimum. A runner that
may hold a job is **drained** first: it stops claiming, finishes its job, and is destroyed once idle.
Drain is used for version rollouts and for a pool you pause or delete. A VM that never registers is
removed.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: VMs
records.text:
The provider is chosen with `FLEET_PROVIDER`. `hcloud` creates Hetzner VMs; the default, `manual`,
only logs what it would do. A VM is an `ubuntu-24.04` server, ARM `cax21` first and x86 `cpx31` as
the fallback (`HCLOUD_SERVER_TYPES` and `HCLOUD_IMAGE` change them). Its cloud-init runs one
container: `ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner- : `.

A VM holds no long-lived credential. It boots with a bootstrap token minted for that one VM, short
lived and swept when unused. The runner exchanges it for its own runner ID and token, then claims
jobs. Cloud credentials are minted per job and state goes through the state proxy.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: The ledger
records.text:
Each create, drain or destroy is recorded with its reason (`scale-up-demand`, `min-per-location`,
`rollout-surge`, `rollout-drain`, `scale-down-idle`, `reap-dead`, `reap-drained` or `teardown`), the
queue depth and the pool size at that moment.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Cold start and cost
records.text:
A cold start happens only when demand passes the warm pool, or for a pool with a warm minimum of `0`.
The job stays queued while the VM boots, pulls the image, registers and claims.

You pay for the VM-hours of the warm pool and of the VMs above it while a backlog lasts. Managed
runner time is billed by provisioned hours: a session opens when a runner comes online and closes when
it is destroyed.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not run a separate scaling service. The scaler is part of the control plane.
- It does not destroy a busy runner.
- It does not put a shared secret on fleet VMs.
- It does not scale self-operated runners. Those are yours to size.

records.title: Security
records.text: Security. The keyless model — Alethia's own OIDC issuer, how AWS, GCP and Azure trust it and what Alethia may do in each, Hetzner's token, key rotation, execution isolation and tenant isolation.

records.title: Security
records.text:
Alethia stores no static cloud credential for AWS, GCP or Azure. The control plane is its own OIDC
issuer: it signs short-lived assertions, and each cloud exchanges one for a session of about an hour
on a role, service account or managed identity that you create and can delete at any time.

 >C: publishes JWKS at /api/oidc/jwks
 R->>A: request an assertion for one cloud
 A-->>R: RS256 assertion, 10 min or less, fixed subject and audience
 R->>C: exchange the assertion
 C->>C: check issuer, subject, audience, signature
 C-->>R: session of about 1 hour
`} />

records.title: Security
records.heading: The issuer
records.text:
The issuer lives at `${APP_URL}/api/oidc` and publishes its public keys and an OIDC discovery
document. Each assertion it signs lasts 10 minutes or less, has the fixed subject `alethia-connector`,
and names one cloud as its audience: `sts.amazonaws.com`, `alethia-gcp-wif` or
`api://AzureADTokenExchange`. The audience stops an assertion for one cloud being replayed at another.

The only long-lived secret is the issuer's signing key, `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`, held by the
control plane. To revoke Alethia's access, delete the role, the federation provider or the managed
identity in your account. How a runner uses the assertion during a job is in
[Cloud credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Security
records.heading: Per cloud
records.text:
AWS GCP Azure 
 --- --- --- --- 
 You create An IAM OIDC provider for the issuer, and `AlethiaProvisionerRole`, whose trust policy allows only `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` from that provider for the fixed audience and subject A Workload Identity Pool with an OIDC provider for the issuer, and a service account bound with `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` A user-assigned managed identity with a federated credential for the issuer, in your subscription. No app registration 
 Alethia stores The role ARN The project ID and federation configuration The tenant, subscription and client IDs 
 Permissions Five scoped policies instead of `AdministratorAccess` 11 predefined and 5 custom roles instead of `roles/editor` A custom "Alethia Provisioner" role instead of `Contributor` 

There is no ExternalId and no trust in an Alethia AWS account: the subject and audience pin replaces
it. No access key, service account key or client secret exists.

records.title: Security
records.heading: What Alethia may do in your cloud
records.text:
The trust controls who may use the role. The permissions control what it may do.

- **AWS.** Four data-plane policies list the specific EC2, EKS, RDS and other actions the templates
 use. An IAM policy lets the templates create the roles they need, explicitly denies attaching
 `AdministratorAccess`, `PowerUserAccess` or `IAMFullAccess`, limits `PassRole` to the provisioned
 services, and denies `organizations:*`, `account:*` and billing. Reads stay `Describe*`, `Get*` and
 `List*`. See [Connect AWS](/guides/connectors/aws).
- **GCP.** Predefined admin roles for services whose Google-maintained role is already narrow, such as
 GKE, networking, Cloud SQL and DNS. Five custom roles replace admin roles that included data access:
 bucket management without object data, Firestore management without entity data, Pub/Sub management
 without publish or consume, add-on service account management, and a project metadata reader. IAM
 bindings are scoped to resources, so the provisioner needs no project `setIamPolicy`.
 `cloudkms.admin` creates the key for Kubernetes Secrets encryption but cannot use it. See
 [Connect GCP](/guides/connectors/gcp).
- **Azure.** The custom role lists only the act

records.title: Security
records.heading: Hetzner
records.text:
Hetzner has no federation, so it is not keyless. It uses one API token, scoped to a whole Hetzner
project. You choose to store it encrypted in Alethia, or to keep it only in your own runner so it never
enters Alethia's database. See [Cloud credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials#hetzner).

records.title: Security
records.heading: Key rotation
records.text:
The signing key rotates without downtime. During the overlap, the published key set holds the old and
the new key, and each assertion's `kid` header selects one. New assertions use the new key; the old
one is retired once every cloud has refreshed its copy of the key set. See
[Rotating the issuer signing key](/self-host/managed-cloud-connectors#rotate-the-issuer-signing-key).

records.title: Security
records.heading: Execution isolation
records.text:
Keyless credentials control who can reach a cloud. [Isolated execution](/concepts/isolated-execution)
controls what provisioning code can do once it runs. Alethia's own templates run in the runner. Your
OpenTofu or Helm runs, on the managed fleet, in a per-job container with no platform secrets, no cloud
metadata, and egress only to allowed domains. One job's state token reaches only its own state, and
cloud credentials are minted per job.

records.title: Security
records.heading: Signing in
records.text:
People sign in to the console with OAuth or an email code, and to the CLI with a device grant or a
service-account token. Runners use a per-runner token stored only as a hash. See
[Authentication](/concepts/authentication).

records.title: Security
records.heading: Row-level security
records.text:
Every table that belongs to an organization has a Postgres row-level security policy on its
organization ID. Each request sets the active organization, so even a query that forgets to filter
returns only that organization's rows. Role and permission decisions are made above it, by the
[access control](/concepts/access-control) layer.

records.title: Security
records.heading: Git tokens
records.text:
OAuth tokens for GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are kept on your sign-in account. Alethia checks a
token's expiry before use and refreshes it through the provider. A job gets the token when it needs
it, never in its snapshot.

records.title: Security
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not store a cloud key for AWS, GCP or Azure.
- It does not give the connector account admin rights in any cloud.
- It does not make Hetzner keyless.
- It does not let one job read another job's state.

records.title: OpenTofu state
records.text: OpenTofu state. Where Alethia keeps OpenTofu state, how a runner reads and writes it through the control plane without a storage key, and how state makes retries safe.

records.title: OpenTofu state
records.text:
OpenTofu records the resources it manages in a state file. Alethia keeps one state file per
environment in S3-compatible object storage, and every runner reaches it only through the control
plane's state proxy, so no runner holds a storage credential.

 >P: GET or POST state, lock, unlock (per-job token)
 P->>P: check the token, derive the state key from the job
 P->>S: read or write the environment's state object
 S-->>P: state
 P-->>R: state
`} />

records.title: OpenTofu state
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
For each job, the runner writes an OpenTofu `http` backend that points at the control plane:

address = "{console_url}/api/jobs/{job_id}/state"
lock_address = "{console_url}/api/jobs/{job_id}/state/lock"
unlock_address = "{console_url}/api/jobs/{job_id}/state/lock"

The runner authenticates with a token minted for that job. It passes the token to `tofu` in the
`TF_HTTP_PASSWORD` environment variable and never writes it to the work directory. The control plane
derives the state object's key from the job, so one job's token reaches only its own environment's
state.

The state key is `{project}-{environment}-{region}/tofu.tfstate`. Each environment, not only each
project, has its own state, which is why `staging` and `production` are isolated. With
[Fabrics](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement), state is per Fabric.

The storage behind the proxy is any S3-compatible service: SeaweedFS by default, or Garage, MinIO,
AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2. Its endpoint and credentials are set on the control plane only. See
[Self-host configuration](/self-host/configuration).

records.title: OpenTofu state
records.heading: Locking
records.text:
`tofu` takes a lock through the proxy before it writes. The lock is fenced: a runner whose lock was
taken over cannot overwrite the state written by the new holder.

records.title: OpenTofu state
records.heading: State and retries
records.text:
OpenTofu writes state after each resource it creates, changes or deletes. If a run stops partway, the
state holds everything done so far. The next run reads it and plans only what remains, so nothing is
created twice.

A destroy removes every resource in the state. The state object stays, empty.

records.title: OpenTofu state
records.heading: Plan files
records.text:
A plan job saves its binary plan file with the control plane, in a separate bucket. A deploy downloads
that file and applies it, after checking its SHA-256 against the plan you reviewed. See
[Provisioning pipeline](/concepts/provisioning-pipeline#6-apply).

records.title: OpenTofu state
records.heading: What it does not do
records.text:
- It does not give a runner a storage key. This is what lets untrusted
 [bring-your-own code](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac) run against state safely.
- It does not use the backend your own module declares. Alethia overrides it with the proxy.
- It does not share state between environments.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.text: How Alethia compares. The plain differences between Alethia and Porter, Qovery and Spacelift, including where each of them is the better choice.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.text:
Alethia is a control plane you can host yourself. It designs Kubernetes clusters and the services
around them, provisions them with OpenTofu into your cloud account, and delivers applications with
ArgoCD. This page states how that differs from three tools people compare it with, and where each
of them is the better choice. Product details of other vendors change: check their own
documentation before you decide.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.heading: At a glance
records.text:
Alethia Porter Qovery Spacelift 
 --- --- --- --- --- 
 What it is Control plane that provisions clusters and services and delivers apps with GitOps Platform that builds and deploys apps onto a cluster in your cloud Platform that provisions Kubernetes in your cloud and deploys apps onto it Orchestrator that runs the infrastructure code you write 
 Who runs the control plane You (open source), or Alethia Labs Porter Qovery Spacelift, or you on its self-hosted offering 
 Who writes the infrastructure code Alethia's templates, or your own (bring-your-own IaC) The platform The platform You 
 App delivery ArgoCD, from your Git repository The platform's own pipeline The platform's own pipeline Not an app platform 
 Source code AGPL-3.0, except `ee/` Proprietary Proprietary Proprietary

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.heading: How Alethia signs in to your cloud
records.text:
On AWS, GCP and Azure, Alethia stores no cloud key: your account trusts the instance's OIDC issuer,
and each job gets a short-lived credential. On Hetzner, DigitalOcean and Civo, which have no such
federation, Alethia stores your API token encrypted. See [Security](/concepts/security).

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.heading: Porter
records.text:
Choose Porter when you want to push a repository and get a running app with logs, metrics,
autoscaling and preview environments, and a hosted control plane suits you. Its app experience and
day-2 operations are more mature than Alethia's.

Choose Alethia when the control plane must run on your own infrastructure, when you want standard
ArgoCD rather than a platform pipeline, or when you need databases, caches, queues and DNS designed
with the cluster. If you stop using Alethia, the cluster, the OpenTofu code and the GitOps setup keep
working.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.heading: Qovery
records.text:
Qovery is the closest in shape: it also provisions Kubernetes in your account and deploys onto it.
Choose Qovery for its mature app platform and its range of clouds and bring-your-own clusters.

Choose Alethia when you must host the control plane yourself under an open-source licence, when you
want ArgoCD as the delivery layer, or when you want the managed data services in the same design as
the cluster.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.heading: Spacelift
records.text:
Spacelift runs plan and apply for infrastructure code you already have, across many tools
(Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, CloudFormation, Ansible and more), with policy as code and drift
detection. Choose it for a large, existing infrastructure-as-code estate.

Choose Alethia when you want a working cluster and its services without writing the code first, and
GitOps delivery on top. Alethia also runs your own OpenTofu modules (see
[bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac)) and detects drift (see [Drift](/concepts/drift)),
but it is not a general orchestrator for every infrastructure tool.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.heading: Where Alethia is behind
records.text:
- It is a young product, with a smaller community and fewer integrations than all three.
- Day-2 application operations (logs, metrics, rollbacks) are thinner than Porter's and Qovery's.
- Its own templates cover AWS, GCP, Azure and Hetzner.

records.title: Editions
records.text: Editions. Alethia's two editions — the open-source Community edition and the licensed Enterprise edition — and where the line between them is.

records.title: Editions
records.text:
Alethia is open-core. Both editions are built from the same code:

- Community is open source under AGPL-3.0, and free. It is the complete
 product for one person or one shared account, with no licence key.
- Enterprise adds what many people in one organization need:
 multi-member organizations, teams, SSO, custom roles, the access portal, Activity export, and the
 optional OpenFGA engine. It needs a licence.

You can self-host either edition. Where Alethia runs and which edition it runs are separate choices.
On the hosted service, each organization's plan decides what it can use.

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Where the line is
records.text:
Everything you need to design, deploy and govern infrastructure is in Community, including the
permission model itself: built-in roles, per-resource grants, deny rules, Row-Level Security between
tenants, and the Activity log. Enterprise adds the machinery for organizations of people: inviting
and grouping them, signing them in with SSO, writing custom roles, and deciding access at scale.

The open-source code never depends on the Enterprise package and runs without it. See
[the open-core architecture](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/authorization.md).

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Pages in this section
records.text:

records.title: Licensing
records.text: Licensing. How an Enterprise licence turns on entitlements in a self-hosted Alethia, how it is checked, and what happens when it ends.

records.title: Licensing
records.text:
An Enterprise licence turns on a fixed set of entitlements. The product
reads those entitlements; nothing else in the code asks whether the instance is licensed. To install
a licence, see [Enterprise setup](/self-host/enterprise-setup).

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Entitlements
records.text:
Entitlement Turns on 
 --- --- 
 `organizations` Multi-member organizations, members, invitations, the organization switcher 
 `teams` Teams, and grants to a team 
 `sso` SSO sign-in over OIDC and SAML 
 `customRoles` The custom-role editor and the access portal 
 `activityExport` CSV export of the Activity log. Viewing it is free. 
 `alerting` Alert policies, channels and the delivery log 
 `advancedAlerting` Alert rules on security events from the Activity log 
 `agentPolicy` Agent policy: a different approver, and the OAuth client allow-list 
 `byoRunners` Bring-your-own runners on the hosted service. A self-hosted operator always has them. 
 `managedPools` Managed runner pools on the hosted service. A self-hosted operator always has them. 

A licence also carries scheduling quotas: concurrent jobs, priority, included runner minutes and
Activity retention.

Without a licence every entitlement is off, and the console is Community: one personal
organization, the four built-in roles, and an Activity log you can browse but not export.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: How the licence is checked
records.text:
The licence is a signed token that Alethia Labs issues, set as `ALETHIA_LICENSE_KEY`. The console
checks it offline against public keys built into the published image, and sends nothing to Alethia
Labs. A licence that is missing, malformed, expired past its grace period, or signed by another key
grants nothing. The console still starts, as Community.

`ALETHIA_EDITION` decides whether the Enterprise package loads: `community` never loads it,
`enterprise` (the published image's setting) requires it, and `auto` loads it when present. The
open-source code never imports the package directly, so a build without it is a complete Community
product. See [the open-core architecture](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/authorization.md).

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: When a licence ends
records.text:
A licence keeps granting for its grace period after the end date: 30 days unless the licence states
another period. Then the instance goes back to Community. No data is deleted, and members keep their
data, but Enterprise-only operations stop until a valid licence is installed. No restart is needed.

 
 Running Enterprise in production needs a commercial licence. The `ee/` directory is source-visible
 under its own licence, not AGPL. Running Community never needs one.
