records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Assign values
records.text:
Open the resource and use its classification picker:

 Resource Where 
 --- --- 
 Projects Project → **Settings → General** 
 Environments A project's **Environments** 
 Clusters **Clusters** 
 Cloud identities and connector credentials **Connectors** → the account in the detail sheet 
 Runners **Runners** 
 Members, Roles **Settings → Members**, **Settings → Roles** 
 Alert policies, alert channels **Alerts → Policies**, **Alerts → Channels** 
 Support cases The case's detail 

Alert deliveries and runner usage sessions cannot be classified: they are records, not things you
manage. From the CLI, see [Classification commands](/reference/cli/classification).

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: What classification does not do
records.text:
Classification does not enforce anything. No permission check, policy, provisioning step or
verify gate reads the labels. They describe your resources; they do not control them.

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The resource shows the value as a chip. On **Settings → Classification**, each value shows how many
resources carry it. Select the count to see which kinds of resource. Each dimension shows its
coverage, and unused values are marked, so you can delete or reuse them.

records.title: Classify resources
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Organizations](/guides/access/organizations)
- [Custom roles](/guides/access/custom-roles)

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.text: Find and open a cluster. Find a cluster in the clusters table, read its status, open its record, and get its endpoint, ArgoCD link and a kubeconfig.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.text: Find a cluster that Alethia deployed, check its health, and get what you need to reach it.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- At least one environment has deployed. A cluster appears when an environment's first deploy
 succeeds, and stays until the environment is destroyed.
- Your role can view clusters.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Open Clusters
records.text:
Select **Clusters** in the sidebar for every cluster in the organization, or **Clusters** inside a
project for that project's clusters. Each row is one environment's cluster.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Narrow the list
records.text:
Use the filter bar: **Search** (environment, project or cluster name), **Cloud**, **Region**, and
the status chips **Needs attention**, **In progress**, **Healthy** and **Unverified**. **Reset**
clears them. The filters and page number are in the page URL, so you can share the view. The list
updates by itself when a cluster changes.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Open the record
records.text: Select a row. The cluster's record opens in a side panel, and its URL opens the same record.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Read the table
records.text:
Column What it shows 
 --- --- 
 **Environment** The environment, with the cluster's name in the cloud under it 
 **Project** The project. Hidden on a project's own page. 
 **Status** See [Statuses](#statuses). A second line says what failed, such as **Last run failed** or **Deleted outside Alethia**, and links to the newest run. 
 **Cloud** Cloud, region and Kubernetes version 
 **Components** Healthy components out of all, such as `3 / 4 healthy`: the control plane, databases and caches 
 **Last observed** When Alethia last saw the control plane, or **Never**

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Statuses
records.text:
The status comes from the control plane, the databases and caches, and the environment's current run.

 Status Meaning Filter 
 --- --- --- 
 **Active** Every component is healthy. Healthy 
 **Queued**, **Deploying**, **Destroying** A run is in progress. In progress 
 **Reconciling** A component is changing. A changing control plane shows its own state, such as **Updating**. In progress 
 **Degraded** A database or cache failed. Needs attention 
 **Unreachable** A probe could not reach the control plane. Needs attention 
 **Missing** A drift scan or probe found the cluster deleted outside Alethia. Needs attention 
 **Unverified** Nothing confirmed the control plane recently. Unverified 

A cluster whose last run failed is under **Needs attention**, even when it is **Active**.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Use the record
records.text:
- **Status**: the result, the healthy components, when and how the control plane was last seen (a
 probe or the last deploy), and how long a current run has taken. **Details** shows what the cloud
 answered to a failed probe.
- **Components**: the control plane (EKS, GKE, AKS, or `k8s` on Hetzner), each database and cache,
 and the DNS domain, each with its status and an endpoint to copy.
- **Cluster access**: the API endpoint, the kubeconfig commands and the download. Shown only when
 the cluster has an API endpoint.
- **ArgoCD**: the ArgoCD address, a button that opens it, and the command that reads the admin
 password.

At the bottom, **Open project**, **Open Architecture** and **View last run** take you to the project,
the environment on the canvas, and the newest run.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Resolve a missing cluster
records.text:
For a **Missing** cluster with no run in progress, the record offers three choices. Nothing changes
until you pick one.

- **Redeploy** or **Tear down** opens the environment on the canvas, where you deploy or destroy it.
- **Mark as destroyed** records the environment and cluster as destroyed. It calls no cloud and starts
 no job, so remove leftover resources in the cloud account yourself. The history stays, and you can
 deploy again later.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Get a kubeconfig
records.text:
**Cluster access** lists each way the cluster supports:

- `alethia cluster kubeconfig `: a runner mints a short-lived kubeconfig, so you need
 no cloud login. Works on AWS, GCP, Azure and Hetzner. See [Get a kubeconfig](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).
- The cloud's own command, under **Or, with access to the cloud account**: runs under your own cloud
 login. AWS, GCP and Azure only.
- **Download kubeconfig (1h, read-only)**: a static, read-only file that expires after an hour. Only
 people with `cluster:access_readonly` see it.

The cloud commands, filled in from the cluster's last successful deploy:

 
 
 aws eks update-kubeconfig --name {cluster-name} --region {region}
 
 
 gcloud container clusters get-credentials {cluster-name} --region {region} --project {gcp-project-id}
 
 A zonal cluster uses `--zone {zone}` instead of `--region {region}`.
 
 
 az aks get-credentials --resource-group {resource-group} --name {cluster-name}
 
 

When a value the cloud command needs was not recorded, only the `alethia` command is shown. When
there is no command at all, a note says why. `alethia cluster get` prints the same commands. See
[Accessing a cluster with kubectl](/reference/cli/clusters#acc

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Download a kubeconfig
records.text:
Select **Download kubeconfig (1h, read-only)**. The record shows **A runner is minting it.**, and
after 20 seconds **Still waiting for a runner to mint it.** with a link to the runners; with no runner
online, it cannot finish. The browser then saves the file. **Cancel**, or closing the record, stops the wait, and a kubeconfig finished
after that expires unread. Details, including private endpoints, are in
[Get a kubeconfig](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig#get-a-kubeconfig-from-the-console).

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: What every cluster has
records.text:
ArgoCD installs ArgoCD itself, External DNS, the External Secrets Operator, Metrics Server and a
storage class (GP3 EBS, Persistent Disk or Managed Disk). On AWS it also installs the AWS Load
Balancer Controller and Karpenter. See [GitOps with ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).

The names, endpoints and ArgoCD address come from the OpenTofu outputs of the last successful deploy.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The record shows the cluster's status and components, and `kubectl` with the kubeconfig lists the
cluster's nodes.

records.title: Find and open a cluster
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Get a kubeconfig](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig)
- [Cluster commands](/reference/cli/clusters)
- [Troubleshoot cluster access](/troubleshooting/cluster-access)

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.text: Connect an AWS account. Connect an AWS account with a keyless IAM role that trusts the Alethia OIDC issuer, from AWS CloudShell, a Terraform module, or the CLI.

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.text:
Connect an AWS account so that Alethia can provision into it. Alethia stores only a role ARN. It
signs in with a short-lived token, never with an access key.

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You can create IAM roles, policies and identity providers in the AWS account.
- Your Alethia role can manage connections (`manage_identities`).
- An AWS account can have one IAM OIDC provider for each issuer URL. If you connected this account
 before, the setup reuses the existing provider.

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
The **AWS CLI / CloudShell** and **Terraform / IaC** tabs create the same resources.

 
 
 

 ### Open the connect sheet
 In the console, open **Connectors**, select **Amazon Web Services**, then select **Connect**.

 ### Run the setup in AWS CloudShell
 Select **Open CloudShell** and paste the command from the sheet. The `aws` CLI in CloudShell is
 already signed in. To run it on your own machine, select **Download script**. A self-hosted
 console passes its own issuer URL as the script's first argument.

 ### Paste the role ARN it prints
 Paste the ARN that the script prints into **IAM Role ARN**, then select **Connect**. You can
 paste the whole output: the field keeps only the ARN.

 
 
 
 

 ### Open the connect sheet
 In the console, open **Connectors**, select **Amazon Web Services**, select **Connect**, then
 choose **Terraform / IaC**.

 ### Apply the module
 Select **Download module** and apply it with `tofu apply` or `terraform apply`. It needs no
 variables. A self-hosted console sets `issuer_url` to its own issuer.

 ### Paste the role_arn output
 Paste the `role_arn` output into **IAM Role ARN**, then select **Connect**.

 
 
 

To connect from a terminal, run `alethi

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.heading: What the setup creates
records.text:
Resource Purpose 
 --- --- 
 An IAM OIDC provider for the Alethia issuer The trust root for Alethia in your account. 
 `AlethiaProvisionerRole` Trusts only `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` from that provider, for audience `sts.amazonaws.com` and subject `alethia-connector`. No external ID. 
 Five policies: `AlethiaProvisionerRole-ComputeNet`, `-ComputeScale`, `-Data`, `-Edge` and `-IAM` Name the exact actions the templates use, instead of `AdministratorAccess`.

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.heading: IAM role permissions
records.text:
The role can manage EC2 and VPC networking, EKS, RDS (Aurora), ElastiCache, Route 53, ACM,
Secrets Manager, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, ECR, S3, KMS, CloudWatch Logs, Kinesis Firehose, EventBridge,
Application Auto Scaling, and the IAM roles of the in-cluster controllers. A project uses only the
services it needs.

The `-IAM` policy denies attaching `AdministratorAccess`, `PowerUserAccess` or `IAMFullAccess` to
anything. It limits `iam:PassRole` to the provisioned services, and denies `organizations:*`,
`account:*` and billing actions. So the role cannot give itself admin rights. The full scope is in
[Security](/concepts/security#per-cloud).

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
When you select **Connect**, the console checks the connection at once. No runner is involved. It
assumes the role, calls `sts:GetCallerIdentity`, and runs a few read calls. The account then shows
one of these states:

 State Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Connected** Alethia can assume the role and has the permissions it checks for. 
 **Limited permissions** Alethia can assume the role, but some permissions are missing. They are listed. 
 **Verification failed** AWS refused the assume. The reason is shown. 

To fix a failed check, see [Troubleshoot: connect a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect#aws).

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.heading: Stop Alethia's access
records.text:
Delete `AlethiaProvisionerRole`, and its OIDC provider if nothing else uses it. To also remove the
account from Alethia, see
[Disconnect an account](/guides/connectors/managing-connections#disconnect-an-account).

records.title: Connect an AWS account
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Manage connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections): add a second account, re-verify, rename, disconnect.
- [Connection health and inventory](/concepts/connection-health): how Alethia re-checks the connection and lists your resources.
- [Security](/concepts/security): the keyless model for every cloud.

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.text: Connect an Azure subscription. Connect an Azure subscription with a user-assigned managed identity that trusts the Alethia OIDC issuer. No client secret and no app registration.

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.text:
Connect an Azure subscription so that Alethia can provision into it. You create a managed identity
in your own subscription. Alethia signs in as that identity with a short-lived token, so there is
no client secret.

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You can create managed identities, custom roles and role assignments in the subscription. You do
 not need directory-admin rights, and no app registration is made.
- Your Alethia role can manage connections (`manage_identities`).
- You know the subscription ID (Azure Portal → **Subscriptions**).

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
The **Azure CLI** and **Terraform / IaC** tabs create the same resources.

 
 
 

 ### Open the connect sheet
 In the console, open **Connectors**, select **Microsoft Azure**, then select **Connect**. Enter
 the **Subscription ID** and choose **Azure CLI**.

 ### Run the setup in Azure Cloud Shell
 Select **Open Cloud Shell** and paste the command from the sheet. It already names your
 subscription.

 ### Enter the IDs it prints
 Enter the **Tenant ID** and **Client ID**, then select **Connect**.

 
 
 
 

 ### Open the connect sheet
 In the console, open **Connectors**, select **Microsoft Azure**, then select **Connect**. Enter
 the **Subscription ID** and choose **Terraform / IaC**.

 ### Apply the module
 Download the module from the sheet and apply it with `tofu apply` or `terraform apply`.

 ### Enter the tenant_id and client_id outputs
 Enter them in **Tenant ID** and **Client ID**, then select **Connect**.

 
 
 

To connect from a terminal, run `alethia connector azure --subscription `. To submit an identity
you already made, add `--tenant-id` and `--client-id`. See
[`alethia connector azure`](/reference/cli/connector#alethia-connector-azure).

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.heading: What the setup creates
records.text:
Resource Detail 
 --- --- 
 User-assigned managed identity A plain ARM resource in your subscription. 
 Federated identity credential Trusts the Alethia issuer for subject `alethia-connector` and audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. 
 **Alethia Provisioner** custom role Lists only the actions the project templates need, instead of `Contributor`.

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.heading: Assign the least-privilege role
records.text:
The setup assigns the **Alethia Provisioner** role to the identity. The role covers resource
groups, AKS, virtual networks, PostgreSQL Flexible Server, Redis Cache, DNS zones, Container
Registry, Key Vault, Storage, Service Bus, Cosmos DB, WAF policies, and the managed identities of
in-cluster workloads.

Its one escalation-grade permission, `roleAssignments/write`, has an ABAC condition. It can assign
only the **DNS Zone Contributor** role, so the identity cannot make itself Owner. Details are in
[Security](/concepts/security#per-cloud).

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
When you select **Connect**, the console signs in as the managed identity and runs an ARM read
call. No runner is involved. The account then shows **Connected**, **Limited permissions** (missing
permissions are listed), or **Verification failed**. To fix a failed check, see
[Troubleshoot: connect a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect).

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.heading: Stop Alethia's access
records.text:
Delete the managed identity or its role assignment. Alethia stores only the tenant ID, the
subscription ID and the identity's client ID, which are all public identifiers.

records.title: Connect an Azure subscription
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Manage connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections): add a second subscription, re-verify, rename, disconnect.
- [Connection health and inventory](/concepts/connection-health): how Alethia re-checks the connection and lists your resources.
- [Security](/concepts/security): the keyless model for every cloud.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.text: Connect a private chart repository. Connect a private Helm or OCI chart source so that Alethia can scan the charts it holds and ArgoCD can pull them.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.text:
Connect a private chart source so that Alethia can scan your Helm charts and ArgoCD can pull them.
Public charts, including every add-on in the marketplace, need no connector.

A chart repository credential is not a container registry credential. A
[container registry](/guides/design-project/container-registry) credential lets your workloads pull
images. A chart repository credential lets Alethia and ArgoCD read charts. One does not do the job
of the other.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your role can manage connections (`manage_identities`).
- You have a username and a token that can read the charts.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Providers
records.text:
Provider Registry host Credential 
 --- --- --- 
 HTTPS Helm Repository The full repository URL, which you give Username, password or token 
 GitHub Container Registry (OCI Helm) `ghcr.io` Username, password or token 
 Docker Hub (OCI Helm) `registry-1.docker.io` Username, access token 
 GitLab Container Registry (OCI Helm) `registry.gitlab.com`, or your own host Username, password or token 
 Scaleway Container Registry (OCI Helm) Your Scaleway host, for example `rg.fr-par.scw.cloud` Secret key 
 Generic OCI Registry (Helm) Your host, for example Harbor or JFrog Username, password or token 

Amazon ECR and ECR Public are listed as **Coming soon**. An ECR token expires after 12 hours, so
there is no stable password to store.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Connect the provider
records.text:
Open **Connectors**, find the provider under **Chart Repos**, select **Connect**, and enter the
credential.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Add a chart repository to the environment
records.text:
On the canvas, select **Add → DevOps → Chart repository**, and pick the connected provider. Each
environment has its own, so staging and production can read from different registries.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Give the host
records.text:
GitHub Container Registry and Docker Hub need nothing more. For a self-hosted or generic registry,
give the bare host, such as `registry.acme.io`, with no scheme and no path. For an HTTPS Helm
repository, give the full `https://` URL.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Attach the private chart
records.text:
Select **Add → Bring your own Helm chart**, choose **OCI registry**, and give the full reference with
the chart name, such as `oci://ghcr.io/acme/payments`, and a version (`*` for the latest). The dialog
tells you whether a chart repository on the environment covers that host.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Deploy
records.text: Before it syncs any chart, the runner writes an ArgoCD repository credential for the repository.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: How Alethia matches a chart to a credential
records.text:
Alethia picks the credential from the chart's host, and takes the most specific match:

- An OCI chart matches by URL prefix. A credential for `oci://ghcr.io` covers
 `oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/payments`.
- An HTTPS chart repository must match exactly.

ArgoCD uses the same rule. So one credential serves both the
[safety scan](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts#read-the-safety-scan) when you attach a chart
and ArgoCD's pull at deploy time. A chart whose host matches nothing is read without a credential:
that works for a public chart and fails with an authentication error for a private one.

The token is the only secret. The repository URL and host are stored as configuration and appear in
the project's configuration snapshot. The token reaches the runner when it claims the job, and is
never written into the configuration, the job record or the job logs.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Registries on a private network
records.text:
By default, the runner refuses to pull a chart from a private or link-local address, so that a chart
URL cannot reach internal services or the cloud metadata service. If your registry is on an internal
network, such as a self-hosted Harbor on RFC 1918 addresses, set
`ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1` on the runner. See
[Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated#environment-variables). Loopback and
link-local addresses stay blocked.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The chart dialog says the environment's chart repository covers the chart's host, and the safety
scan finishes without an authentication error.

records.title: Connect a private chart repository
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Bring your own Helm charts](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts)
- [Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool](/guides/connectors/pluggable)

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.text: Read secrets from another cloud account. Let a cluster read secrets from a cloud secret manager in another AWS account, GCP project or Azure subscription, through a read-only grant and no stored key.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.text:
Let a cluster read secrets from a secret manager in another account, project or subscription. The
owner of the secrets creates a read-only grant for the cluster's identity. Alethia stores only
references to that grant, never a key.

 
These three connectors are listed as **Coming soon** in the connector catalog, so you cannot connect
them yet. This page describes how they work.
 

 Connector Reads from What you enter 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS Secrets Manager (cross-account) Secrets Manager in another AWS account Target Role ARN, target account ID, region, and optionally External ID 
 GCP Secret Manager (cross-project) Secret Manager in another GCP project Target project ID 
 Azure Key Vault (cross-subscription) Key Vault in another subscription of the same tenant Target subscription ID, vault URL

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The cluster runs the [External Secrets Operator](/guides/design-project/secrets), which signs in
 with the cluster's workload identity: IRSA on AWS, Workload Identity on GCP and Azure.
- You can create IAM grants in the account that owns the secrets.
- You have the Alethia repository. The grant modules are in `infra/connector/ /secrets-xacct/`,
 each with a README.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: Create the grant in the secrets account
records.text:
Apply the module for your cloud in the account that owns the secrets:

 Cloud Module It grants 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS `infra/connector/aws/secrets-xacct` A read-only role that trusts the cluster's external-secrets identity, with `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on the secret ARNs you name. There is no wildcard: the module refuses to apply without a list. 
 GCP `infra/connector/gcp/secrets-xacct` `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on each secret you name, for the cluster's external-secrets service account. 
 Azure `infra/connector/azure/secrets-xacct` The **Key Vault Secrets User** role on the vault, for the cluster's workload identity. 

On AWS, you can also set `external_id` on the module. Then enter the same value in the connector's
**External ID** field. AWS refuses the read when the two differ. GCP and Azure bind the grant to one
identity instead, so they have no such field.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: Enter the references in the connector
records.text:
Open **Connectors**, select the connector under **Secrets**, and enter the values from the first
table.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: Deploy
records.text:
Alethia adds a second `ClusterSecretStore` that reads from the other account, next to the cluster's
own store.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: Keep the grant working when you rebuild a cluster
records.text:
Each grant names the cluster's external-secrets identity. On AWS that identity has a stable name, so
a rebuild keeps working. On GCP, a re-created service account is a new identity, even with the same
name. On Azure, a re-created managed identity gets a new object ID. So on those two clouds, a
rebuilt cluster cannot read until you apply the grant again.

To avoid this, create the identity yourself once, grant it access, and set these template variables:

 Cloud Variables 
 --- --- 
 GCP `external_secrets_service_account_email` 
 Azure `external_secrets_identity_name`, `external_secrets_identity_resource_group` 

The template then uses your identity and never creates, changes or deletes it. Leave them unset to
let the template own the identity.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: What is not supported
records.text:
- **Hetzner** has no cloud secret manager. Use the
 [HashiCorp Vault connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) instead.
- **Azure across tenants.** A managed identity cannot be used in another tenant. A vault in another
 tenant needs an app registration and a federated credential there, which this connector does not
 make.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
An `ExternalSecret` that names a secret in the other account syncs, and its Kubernetes Secret has
the value.

records.title: Read secrets from another cloud account
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Secrets](/guides/design-project/secrets): choose a secrets provider for a project.
- [Security](/concepts/security): the keyless model.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.text: Connect a GCP project. Connect a Google Cloud project with Workload Identity Federation, from Cloud Shell, a Terraform module, or the CLI. No service account key is made.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.text:
Connect a Google Cloud project so that Alethia can provision into it. Your project's Workload
Identity Pool trusts the Alethia OIDC issuer, so no service account key is ever made.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You can enable APIs, create service accounts and Workload Identity Pools, and grant IAM roles in
 the project.
- Your Alethia role can manage connections (`manage_identities`).
- You know the project ID.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
The **gcloud CLI** and **Terraform** tabs create the same resources.

 
 
 

 ### Open the connect sheet
 In the console, open **Connectors**, select **Google Cloud**, then select **Connect**. Enter the
 **Project ID** and choose **gcloud CLI**.

 ### Run the setup in Cloud Shell
 Select **Open Cloud Shell** and paste the command from the sheet. It already names your project.
 To run it with a local `gcloud`, select **Download script**.

 ### Enter the project number it prints
 Enter the number in **Project number**, then select **Connect**.

 
 
 
 

 ### Open the connect sheet
 In the console, open **Connectors**, select **Google Cloud**, then select **Connect**. Enter the
 **Project ID** and choose **Terraform**.

 ### Apply the module
 Select **Download module** and apply it with your `gcloud` login. Set `project_id`. The other
 variables have defaults.

 ### Enter the project_number output
 Enter it in **Project number**, then select **Connect**.

 
 
 

Alethia builds the credential configuration from the project ID and number. For a custom setup,
select **Paste a credential config instead** and paste a full `external_account` configuration, for
example the module's `credenti

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: What the setup creates
records.text:
Resource Value 
 --- --- 
 Workload Identity Pool and OIDC provider `alethia-pool`, `alethia-oidc-provider`. Issuer `https://alethialabs.io/api/oidc`, audience `alethia-gcp-wif`, subject `alethia-connector`. 
 Provisioner service account `alethia-provisioner`, which the pool may impersonate. 
 Application database account `alethia-appdb`, for [password-free Cloud SQL](#password-free-cloud-sql). 
 external-dns account `alethia-external-dns`. It can list zone names only; record writes are granted per zone at deploy time. 

The project number is needed because the token exchange names the pool by number, and a number
cannot be looked up before Alethia is signed in.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Service account permissions
records.text:
The provisioner gets predefined admin roles for GKE, Compute networking and security, Service
Networking, Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Cloud DNS, Artifact Registry, Secret Manager and Cloud KMS, plus
`iam.serviceAccountUser`. It never gets `roles/editor`.

Six custom roles replace the predefined roles that also read data. They manage Cloud Storage
buckets without object access, Firestore databases without entity access, Pub/Sub topics without
publish or consume, add-on service accounts, project metadata, and DNS-zone IAM.

`cloudkms.admin` lets the provisioner create the key that encrypts Kubernetes Secrets. It cannot
use the key, so it cannot read a Secret. IAM grants are scoped to one zone, one secret, or one
service account, so the provisioner does not need project `setIamPolicy`. Details are in
[Security](/concepts/security#per-cloud).

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Optional APIs you enable yourself
records.text:
Alethia does not hold `serviceusage.services.enable`, because it would let the provisioner turn on
any API, including billable ones. It can only check whether an API is on.

 Feature API Enable with 
 --- --- --- 
 Container registry → **Vulnerability scanning** `containerscanning.googleapis.com` `gcloud services enable containerscanning.googleapis.com --project ` 

If you turn on scanning without the API, the deploy stops before it changes anything and names the
API. Enable it and deploy again. With scanning off, repositories are created with scanning
disabled and need nothing.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Password-free Cloud SQL
records.text:
To let your apps reach Cloud SQL with an IAM token instead of a password, set this value on the
project in Alethia:

cloud_sql_app_service_account_email = alethia-appdb@ .iam.gserviceaccount.com

The script prints it at the end, and the module outputs it as `cloud_sql_app_service_account_email`.
If you leave it unset, apps use password authentication, and turning on IAM auth shows a warning.

`alethia-appdb` has `roles/cloudsql.client` and `roles/cloudsql.instanceUser`. Google grants these
only on the whole project, and that needs `setIamPolicy`, which the provisioner does not hold. So
you make this grant once, at setup.

 
Every environment in the project shares `alethia-appdb`. An app in one environment can log in to
another environment's Cloud SQL instance; its SQL grants still limit what it can do. To isolate
environments by identity, use separate Google Cloud projects. On AWS and Azure, Alethia creates
one database identity per environment instead.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
When you select **Connect**, the console exchanges a token through your pool and runs a Compute
read call. No runner is involved. The account then shows **Connected**, **Limited permissions**
(missing permissions are listed), or **Verification failed**. To fix a failed check, see
[Troubleshoot: connect a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect#gcp).

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Stop Alethia's access
records.text:
Delete the Workload Identity Pool, or remove the service account binding. Alethia stores only the
project ID, the project number and the configuration built from them.

records.title: Connect a GCP project
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Manage connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections): add a second project, re-verify, rename, disconnect.
- [Connection health and inventory](/concepts/connection-health): how Alethia re-checks the connection and lists your resources.
- [Security](/concepts/security): the keyless model for every cloud.

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.text: Connect a Git provider. Connect GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket over OAuth so that Alethia can list your repositories and ArgoCD can deploy from them.

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.text:
Connect a Git provider so that Alethia can list your repositories and ArgoCD can watch them. All
three providers connect over OAuth, and Alethia refreshes the token for you.

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have an account on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket that can read the repositories you deploy.
- This console has an OAuth app for the provider. If it does not, the card reads
 **Not enabled on this instance**. A self-hosted console sets this up in
 [Configuration](/self-host/configuration).

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Open **Connectors** and find the provider under **Source**.
2. Select **Connect**.
3. On the provider's page, approve access. GitHub asks for the `repo` scope.

The provider sends you back to **Connectors**.

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.heading: What the token is used for
records.text:
Use Detail 
 --- --- 
 Repository lists The project form and the canvas list repositories from the provider. 
 GitOps ArgoCD reads your repositories with the token and syncs changes. 
 Templates Alethia can read infrastructure templates from your repositories. 

When the access token expires, Alethia uses the stored refresh token to get a new one the next time
it needs the provider. If that fails, the card reads **Needs reconnection**: select **Reconnect**.

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The card reads **Connected**, and the repository picker in a project lists your repositories.

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.heading: Disconnect a Git provider
records.text:
Select **Manage** on the card, then **Disconnect**. Alethia deletes the stored tokens.

 
Every project that deploys from this provider loses repository access. ArgoCD shows its sync as
failed until you connect the provider again.

records.title: Connect a Git provider
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Repositories](/guides/design-project/repositories): pick the repositories a project deploys.
- [GitOps with ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd): how ArgoCD uses the repository.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.text: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project. Connect a Hetzner Cloud project with a scoped, encrypted, revocable API token. Alethia provisions a self-managed Talos Linux Kubernetes cluster on it.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.text:
Connect a Hetzner Cloud project so that Alethia can provision into it. Hetzner Cloud has no OIDC
provider and no role-assumption API, so Hetzner is the one supported cloud that is not keyless: it
connects with an API token that is scoped to one project, encrypted at rest, and revocable at any
time.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have a Hetzner Cloud project for Alethia. A token reaches everything in its project, so use a
 project that does not already hold infrastructure you value.
- Your Alethia role can manage connections (`manage_identities`).

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: What Alethia provisions on Hetzner
records.text:
Hetzner Cloud has no managed Kubernetes and no managed data services. Alethia provisions a
self-managed [Talos Linux](https://www.talos.dev/) Kubernetes cluster on Hetzner servers (ARM `CAX`,
or x86 `CX`, `CPX` and `CCX`), with Cilium networking and the Hetzner CSI driver for volumes.
Databases, caches and queues run in the cluster through ArgoCD: CloudNativePG for PostgreSQL, Valkey
for caches, and RabbitMQ for queues.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Create a project-scoped API token
records.text:
In the [Hetzner Cloud Console](https://console.hetzner.cloud/), open the project, then
**Security → API Tokens → Generate API token**. Give it **Read & Write** permission, because
provisioning creates servers, networks and volumes.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Paste the token
records.text:
In Alethia, open **Connectors**, select **Hetzner Cloud**, then select **Connect**. Paste the token
into **API Token**.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Add Object Storage keys (optional)
records.text:
To provision storage buckets, open **Object Storage keys (optional)** and paste an S3 access key
and secret key. Hetzner has no API that makes these keys: generate them in the Hetzner Console
under S3 credentials. Give both keys or neither.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Connect
records.text:
Select **Connect**.

 

To connect from a terminal, run `alethia connector hetzner --token-stdin` and pipe the token in. A
`--token` flag also works, but it lands in your shell history. Add `--s3-access-key` and
`--s3-secret-key` for buckets. See [Connector commands](/reference/cli/connector).

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: With a self-operated runner
records.text:
A runner you operate can read the token from `HCLOUD_TOKEN` in its own environment, so that
Alethia does not store a token. See [Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated).

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: How the token is kept
records.text:
The console encrypts the token with AES-256-GCM before it stores it, and never returns it. The
console decrypts it to check the connection, and when a runner claims a job, to hand it to that
runner. It is never written into a project's configuration snapshot.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
When you select **Connect**, the console calls the Hetzner Cloud API
(`GET /v1/locations`) with the token. No runner is involved.

 Result State 
 --- --- 
 `200` **Connected**. Alethia also syncs the project's locations, which placement uses. 
 `401` or `403` **Verification failed**: the token is wrong or was revoked. 

To fix a failed check, see [Troubleshoot: connect a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect#hetzner).

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Stop Alethia's access
records.text: Delete the token in the Hetzner Cloud Console. Alethia's access ends at once.

records.title: Connect a Hetzner Cloud project
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Manage connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections): re-verify, rename, disconnect.
- [Connection health and inventory](/concepts/connection-health): how Alethia re-checks the connection.
- [Security](/concepts/security): how Alethia handles credentials.

records.title: Connectors
records.text: Connectors. Connect the cloud accounts, Git providers and third-party tools that your projects provision into and read from.

records.title: Connectors
records.text:
Connect the accounts that Alethia needs before your first deploy: one cloud account and one Git
provider. Other connectors are optional. They let a project use a tool you already run instead of
the cloud's own service.

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your role can manage connections (`manage_identities`). Connections belong to the organization,
 and every member sees them.

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Choose what to connect
records.text:
Group on the Connectors page Providers How it signs in Guide 
 --- --- --- --- 
 **Clouds** AWS, GCP, Azure Keyless: a short-lived token from the Alethia OIDC issuer. Alethia stores no key. [AWS](/guides/connectors/aws), [GCP](/guides/connectors/gcp), [Azure](/guides/connectors/azure) 
 **Clouds** Hetzner A project-scoped API token, encrypted at rest and revocable. [Hetzner](/guides/connectors/hetzner) 
 **Source** GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket OAuth [Git providers](/guides/connectors/git-providers) 
 **Registries**, **Secrets**, **Observability**, **DNS** Docker Hub, HashiCorp Vault, Datadog, Cloudflare and others API key or token, encrypted at rest [Pluggable connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable) 
 **Chart Repos** Private Helm and OCI chart sources Username and token, encrypted at rest [Chart repositories](/guides/connectors/chart-repositories) 
 **Secrets** A cloud secret manager in another account A read-only grant in that account [Cross-account secret managers](/guides/connectors/cross-account-secret-managers)

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Open **Connectors**.
2. Find the provider. Filter by group or status, or search by name.
3. Select **Connect** on its card, and follow the provider's guide.

Each cloud account you connect becomes a **cloud identity**: the account that projects provision
into. A provider can hold several accounts. See
[Manage connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections).

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The card shows its state:

 State Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Connected** The credential works. 
 **Limited permissions** A cloud account signs in, but some permissions are missing. 
 **Verification failed** A cloud account cannot sign in. 
 **Needs reconnection** A Git token expired and could not be refreshed. Select **Reconnect**. 
 **Not connected** Nothing is stored. 
 **Coming soon** The provider is listed but cannot be connected yet. 
 **Not enabled on this instance** This console lacks the setup that the provider needs.

records.title: Connectors
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Connection health and inventory](/concepts/connection-health): how cloud connections are checked and what is listed.
- [Connectors](/concepts/connectors): how the catalog and credential storage work.
- [Troubleshoot: connect a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect)

records.title: Manage connections
records.text: Manage connections. Add a second account to a cloud, re-verify a connection, rename an account, or disconnect one, from the connector's detail sheet.

records.title: Manage connections
records.text:
Change a cloud connection after you made it: add another account, check it again, rename it, or
remove it. To connect a cloud for the first time, see [Connectors](/guides/connectors).

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your role can manage connections (`manage_identities`). Without it, you see the same controls,
 disabled, with the reason.
- Connections belong to the organization. Every member sees them.

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Open the detail sheet
records.text:
1. Open **Connectors**.
2. Select **Manage** on the provider's card.

The sheet lists every account you connected to that provider, including one that failed to
verify, with its state and three buttons: **Re-verify**, **Rename** and **Disconnect**. These
actions run in the console. No runner or job is involved.

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Add another account
records.text:
Connect a second AWS account, GCP project or Azure subscription to the same provider.

1. In the detail sheet, select **Add another account**.
2. Complete the provider's connect flow: [AWS](/guides/connectors/aws), [GCP](/guides/connectors/gcp),
 [Azure](/guides/connectors/azure) or [Hetzner](/guides/connectors/hetzner).

The new account gets its own row. It does not replace the existing one. If this console no longer
offers new connections for the cloud, the button is missing and the sheet says why. Existing
accounts keep their buttons.

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Re-verify a connection
records.text:
Check an account again with its stored configuration, for example after you changed its role or
policy in the cloud.

1. In the detail sheet, find the account.
2. Select **Re-verify**.

The account shows **Verifying…**, then one of these states:

 State Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Connected** Alethia can sign in and has the permissions it checks for. 
 **Limited permissions** Alethia can sign in, but some permissions are missing. They are listed. 
 **Verification failed** Alethia cannot sign in. The reason is shown.

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Rename an account
records.text:
Replace a default name such as `AWS Account (123456789012)` with one people recognize.

1. In the detail sheet, find the account.
2. Select **Rename**, type the name, and select **Save name**.

The name changes nothing else.

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Disconnect an account
records.text:
Remove Alethia's access to one account. Other accounts on the same provider are not changed.

1. In the detail sheet, find the account.
2. Select **Disconnect**.
3. The dialog lists the projects that use the account. Type the account's name to confirm.

Disconnecting:

- deletes the account's stored credentials,
- unlinks every project that used the account, so those projects cannot provision until you pick
 another account,
- deletes the account's [asset inventory](/concepts/connection-health#asset-inventory).

The trust you created in the cloud stays. To end access on the cloud side too, delete the role,
pool, managed identity or token there.

To disconnect a Git provider or a pluggable connector, select **Disconnect** at the bottom of its
sheet. From the CLI, run `alethia connector remove `.

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The account's row shows its new state or name, or is gone from the sheet. `alethia connector list`
prints the same list.

records.title: Manage connections
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Connection health and inventory](/concepts/connection-health): when Alethia checks a connection on its own.
- [Troubleshoot: connect a cloud](/troubleshooting/connect): fix **Limited permissions** and **Verification failed**.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.text: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool. Connect Cloudflare, HashiCorp Vault, Docker Hub, Datadog and other tools with an API key, so a project uses them instead of the cloud's own service.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.text:
Connect a tool you already run, so that a project uses it instead of the cloud's own service. For
example, Cloudflare instead of Route 53, or Vault instead of AWS Secrets Manager. These connectors
sign in with an API key or token.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your role can manage connections (`manage_identities`).
- You have an API credential for the tool, with the permission listed below.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: Connect the provider
records.text: Open **Connectors**, find the provider, and select **Connect**.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: Enter the credential
records.text:
Fill in the fields from the table. Alethia encrypts secret fields with AES-256-GCM. It stores
non-secret fields, such as a Vault address or a username, as they are.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: Check the credential
records.text:
Alethia calls the provider's API to check the credential, for example Cloudflare's token check or
a Docker Hub sign-in. A credential that fails the check is still saved, so you can fix it and try
again.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: Use it in a project
records.text:
On the canvas, pick the provider for the component:
[DNS](/guides/design-project/dns), [Secrets](/guides/design-project/secrets),
[Container registry](/guides/design-project/container-registry) or
[Observability](/guides/design-project/observability).

 

When the project deploys, the runner adds the provider's module to the plan and leaves out the
cloud's own resource for that component. Observability has no cloud default, so it only adds.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: How the credential reaches the runner
records.text:
Secret fields are never written into a project's configuration snapshot. The console decrypts them
only when a runner claims a job that needs them, and hands them to that runner. A self-hosted
console sets the encryption key in `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY`; see
[Configuration](/self-host/configuration).

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The card reads **Connected**, and the provider appears as a choice in the component on the canvas.

records.title: Connect a DNS, secrets, registry or observability tool
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Connectors](/concepts/connectors): how the catalog and credential storage work.
- [Manage connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections)

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.text: Find your way around the console. Use the organization overview, the sidebar and a project's pages to reach your projects, jobs, usage and alerts.

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.text:
Find a project, a job or your usage from the organization overview, and move between a project's
pages.

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You are signed in and a member of the organization. Each card and list shows only what your role
 can see, and says so when it hides something.

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.heading: Use the overview
records.text:
The overview is the organization's home page. Select **Overview** in the sidebar to return to it.

 Part What it shows 
 --- --- 
 **Usage** card Runner minutes this billing period, jobs running now against your plan's limit, included AI usage for the current 5-hour session and the week, projects, and seats. **Manage** or **Upgrade** opens billing. 
 **Alerts** card The latest alert deliveries. On a plan without alerting, it says that alerting needs the Pro plan. 
 **Recent jobs** card The latest jobs. Select one to open it. 
 **Projects** Every project as a card or a row, with its cloud and region. 

To find a project:

1. Type in **Search projects…**, or filter by cloud or by **Repository**.
2. Sort by activity or by name.
3. Select the project to open its canvas.

The project's menu (**⋯**) opens its **Architecture**, **Jobs** or **Settings**, copies it with
**Duplicate to another cloud…**, or adds it to your favourites. Use **Create** to start a project,
connect a cloud account or invite a member.

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.heading: Use the sidebar
records.text:
The sidebar has three groups:

1. **Overview**, **Clusters**, **Jobs**, **Evidence**
2. **Connectors**, **Alerts**, and **Runners** when your organization runs its own runners
3. **Usage**, **Support**, **Settings**

Inside a project, the sidebar shows the project's own pages instead:

 Page Use it to 
 --- --- 
 **Architecture** Design the project on the canvas, and plan and deploy it. See [Design a project](/guides/design-project). 
 **Environments** See each environment and its state. 
 **Jobs** See the project's jobs. See [Find a job](/guides/jobs). 
 **Clusters** See the project's clusters. See [Clusters](/guides/clusters). 
 **Usage** See what the project uses. 
 **Settings** Change the project's name, access and preview settings, and read its activity.

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.heading: Copy a project to another cloud
records.text:
1. In the project's menu, select **Duplicate to another cloud…**.
2. Pick a cloud account on another cloud, a region and a name.
3. Confirm.

Every service is translated to its native equivalent on the other cloud. Settings that do not map
directly, such as instance types, WAF rules or DNS zones, are shown as warnings. You need a
connected account on another cloud. See [Multi-cloud conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The page you wanted is open, and the breadcrumb above the content names it.

records.title: Find your way around the console
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [The console](/get-started/the-console): a first tour.
- [Plan and deploy from the console](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply)

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.text: Bring your own Helm chart. Attach your own Helm chart from Git or an OCI registry, read its safety scan, and bind the workloads it deploys to your databases, caches, queues and secrets.

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.text:
Deploy a Helm chart you already have. Alethia scans it, draws each workload it deploys, and lets you
bind those workloads to the infrastructure on your canvas. It never rewrites the chart: the chart
deploys unchanged, as one ArgoCD Application. What the chart may create, how it syncs and how to
remove it are in [Bring-your-own charts](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts).

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your operator turned on bring-your-own charts for your instance. The capability is opt-in, and is
 limited to charts you own on your own cluster.
- For a chart in Git, its [Git provider is connected](/guides/connectors/git-providers).
- For a chart in a private OCI registry, the registry is connected as a
 [chart repository](/guides/connectors/chart-repositories) on the environment. Alethia uses that
 credential to scan the chart and ArgoCD uses it to pull. A public chart needs nothing. A registry
 on an internal network also needs
 [`ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE`](/guides/runners/self-operated#environment-variables) on
 the runner.
- Charts in Amazon ECR cannot be scanned yet. GitHub Container Registry, GitLab, Docker Hub,
 Scaleway and other OCI registries work.

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.heading: Attach the chart
records.text:
1. On the canvas, press **⌘K** and choose **Bring your own Helm chart** in the **Sources** group.
2. On **Source**, choose **Git repository** or **OCI registry**.
3. Describe where the chart is:

 Source Steps 
 --- --- 
 Git **Repository**, then **Chart path** (such as `charts/payments`), then **Ref**: a branch, tag or commit 
 OCI **Registry**: the `oci:// / / ` reference, such as `oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/payments`. Then **Ref**: the chart version, or `*` for the latest release. 

4. On **Review**, set the namespace and your values, as schema-checked fields or raw
 `values.yaml`. Leave the namespace empty to get `byo- `, such as `byo-payments`.
5. Select **Attach chart**.

The namespace must be your own. The form refuses `default`, `kube-system` and any other `kube-`
name, `argocd`, and the namespaces of the platform's controllers and add-ons, such as
`cert-manager`, `external-secrets-operator`, `ingress-nginx` and `monitoring`.

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.heading: Read the safety scan
records.text:
Attaching starts a scan. The runner fetches the chart, then renders it with `helm template` in a
sandbox with no network and no secrets, and the [Elench](/concepts/elench) engine
checks the manifests. It looks for privileged containers, host access, wildcard RBAC, missing
resource limits and mutable image tags.

1. Select the chart's card.
2. Read the verify report in the inspector.

The registry credential is used only to fetch, outside the sandbox, so the chart never sees it.

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.heading: Bind a workload to your infrastructure
records.text:
From the same render, Alethia draws each workload the chart deploys as a dashed card under the
chart. Each card shows the workload's kind (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, CronJob or Job),
image, ports, environment variable names, resources and replicas. Values are never captured, so a
secret in the chart's manifests is never read into Alethia. The cards refresh on every scan, and
never deploy anything themselves.

1. Select a workload card.
2. Connect it to a database, cache, queue or secret, the same way as a
 [service](/guides/design-project/services).
3. Check the **value-path** each binding writes to, such as `postgresql.auth.existingSecret`.
 Alethia suggests it from the chart's conventions. Correct it if your chart differs.

Endpoints and ports are written into the chart's values as plain values. Credentials are written as
a reference to a Kubernetes Secret that the cluster provisions, never as a value in your chart or in
Git. A chart with no way to accept an existing Secret is flagged rather than given a credential.

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.heading: Override replicas and environment
records.text:
In the same inspector, you can set:

- **Replicas**, to override the rendered count.
- **Environment**, to add or override environment variables.

Like bindings, overrides are written into the chart's values at the inferred or corrected value-paths
(`replicaCount`, `image.tag`, `*.existingSecret`). Your corrections win over the inferred paths and
survive a new scan.

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, the chart's ArgoCD Application is **Synced** and **Healthy**, in the namespace you
chose:

kubectl get pods -n byo-payments

If the **Deploy** tab warns that the chart was skipped or moved, see
[Troubleshoot design and GitOps](/troubleshooting/design-project#a-chart-is-skipped-because-of-its-namespace).

records.title: Bring your own Helm chart
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Bring-your-own charts](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts): what a chart may create, sync and removal.
- [Use a starter template](/guides/design-project/starter-templates): a chart that meets the contract.
- [Connect an apps repository](/guides/design-project/repositories): for charts that install CRDs.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.text: Bring your own IaC. Provision an environment from your own OpenTofu root module instead of the built-in template, behind a static safety scan.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.text:
Point an environment at your own OpenTofu root module in Git. Alethia then scans, plans and applies
your module instead of its built-in template. The module replaces the template for that
environment. Why the safety gate exists, the variable and cluster-output contracts, and who may run
a module are in [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your operator set `ALETHIA_BYO_IAC_ENABLED=true` for your instance. Without it, attaching,
 scanning and provisioning a module are refused.
- The module's [Git provider is connected](/guides/connectors/git-providers). If none is, the
 repository step offers to connect one.
- The environment has no deployed or in-progress template infrastructure. Destroy it first.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Write a minimal module

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Platform context from Alethia. Declare only what you use.
records.text:
variable "alethia_project" { type = string }
variable "alethia_environment" { type = string }

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Your own variables must not start with alethia_.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Attach the module
records.text:
1. On the canvas, press **⌘K** and choose **Bring your own IaC** in the **Sources** group.
2. On **Repository**, choose the repository.
3. On **Path & ref**, set the root-module path (empty for the repository root) and, optionally, a
 branch, tag or commit (empty for `HEAD`).
4. On **Variables**, add any tfvars the module needs, or none to use its defaults:

 Field Rule 
 --- --- 
 **Name** Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter or underscore. Unique. 
 **Type** `string`, `number` or `bool` 
 **Value** Must parse as the type 

 These are stored as plain tfvars, so never put a secret here.
5. On **Review**, check the summary and select **Attach source**.

A safety scan starts on its own.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Read the safety scan
records.text:
The module appears as an **External IaC** card with its repository, ref, path, the commit the scan
pinned, and a scan status. Select the status to open **IaC safety scan**. It runs the
[static safety gate](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac#the-safety-gate) and `tofu validate` on the
pinned commit, and shows:

- A verdict: **No blocking issues found**, or **Issues found — resolve before deploying**.
- The `tofu validate` result and a count per severity. An `error` blocks the deploy; a `warning`
 does not.
- Each finding, worst first, with a rule ID, `file:line` and a message.
- The providers and modules it found.

After you push a fix, select **Rescan**. Only a clean scan pins a commit for deploys. A failed scan
clears the pin, so nothing deploys until a clean scan, and what deploys is exactly the commit
scanned.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Plan and deploy
records.text:
While the module is attached, the environment's plan, deploy and destroy run your module. Its
resources appear as read-only cards, and the **Add** picker is disabled, because the module is the
source of truth. Each deploy's **Plan** tab carries the same verify verdict as a template deploy.
The **External IaC** card shows **DEPLOYED** or **NOT DEPLOYED**, and the commit the last deploy
applied.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Detach the module
records.text:
To go back to the built-in template, open the **External IaC** card and select **✕**. You can
detach only a module that has never deployed. Otherwise, destroy the environment first.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After a deploy, the **External IaC** card reads **DEPLOYED**, and the applied commit matches the
pinned one. For the minimal module, the plan output shows `pet` and `greeting`.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac): the safety gate and the module contract.
- [Read the canvas](/concepts/canvas#bring-your-own-iac-modules): how module resources are drawn.
- [Bring your own Helm chart](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts): attach one chart instead.

records.title: Add a cache
records.text: Add a cache. Add a Redis or Valkey cache to an environment and size it by node type or by memory.

records.title: Add a cache
records.text: Add an in-memory cache to the environment. You can add as many as you need.

records.title: Add a cache
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - You have a project open on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas).

records.title: Add a cache
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **Cache** in the **Data** group.
2. Choose the engine. The first cache is named `primary`.

 Cloud Engines 
 --- --- 
 AWS Redis (ElastiCache), Valkey (ElastiCache Serverless) 
 GCP Redis or Valkey (Memorystore) 
 Azure Redis (Azure Managed Redis) 
 Hetzner Valkey, in your cluster 

3. Size the cache in one of two ways:
 - Choose a **Node type**. Each option shows its memory and an approximate monthly price per node.
 - Or set **Memory** in GB (0.5–512). Alethia picks the nearest tier on the project's cloud, so
 the setting survives a move to another cloud.
4. Set **Nodes** (1–6, default 1). On Azure this field is unavailable, because Azure Managed Redis
 is sized by its tier: use **Memory** instead.
5. Optional: turn on **Multi-AZ** to replicate across availability zones, so a replica takes over
 if the primary fails. This adds replica nodes to the cost.
6. Optional: add **Allowed CIDR blocks**, extra networks that can reach the cache. The cluster
 always can. This field is unavailable on Azure, which has no firewall rule for Managed Redis.
7. Optional: under **Advanced**, pin an **Engine version**.

On Hetzner, set **Storage**, the volume per Valkey node i

records.heading: Node types
records.text:
Cloud Types (memory) Default 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS `cache.t3.micro` (0.5 GB), `cache.t3.small` (1.37 GB), `cache.t3.medium` (3.09 GB), `cache.r6g.large` (13.07 GB), `cache.r6g.xlarge` (26.32 GB) `cache.t3.medium` 
 GCP `M1` (1 GB), `M2` (4 GB), `M3` (10 GB), `M4` (35 GB) `M1` 
 Azure `Balanced_B0` (0.5 GB), `Balanced_B1` (1 GB), `Balanced_B3` (3 GB), `Balanced_B5` (6 GB), `Balanced_B10` (12 GB), `Balanced_B20` (24 GB) `Balanced_B1` 
 Hetzner 1, 2 or 4 GiB 1 GiB

records.title: Add a cache
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, open the cache's **Status** tab. **Endpoints** shows the primary endpoint, and a
reader endpoint when Multi-AZ is on. Redis and Valkey listen on port 6379.

records.title: Configure the cluster
records.text: Configure the cluster. Set the Kubernetes version, node size, node count, capacity type, disk and cluster admins for an environment's cluster.

records.title: Configure the cluster
records.text:
Size the Kubernetes cluster that the environment runs on. To add more node pools, labels or
taints, see [Add node pools](/guides/design-project/node-pools).

records.title: Configure the cluster
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - You have a project open on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas).

records.title: Configure the cluster
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select the environment's name at the start of the toolbar. The cluster settings are on
 **Settings**.
2. Choose the **Kubernetes version**. The default is 1.35. On Hetzner the field is read-only: Talos
 installs Kubernetes 1.35.6.
3. Size the nodes in one of two ways:
 - Choose an **Instance type**. Each option shows its vCPU and memory.
 - Or set **vCPU per node** (1–96) and **Memory per node** (1–768 GB). The runner picks the
 nearest instance type on the project's cloud. This setting works on every cloud, so it
 survives a move to another cloud.
4. Set **Min nodes**, **Desired nodes** and **Max nodes**. Each is 1–100, and min ≤ desired ≤ max.
 The defaults are 2, 2 and 5.
5. Choose **Capacity**: **On-demand** (the default) or **Spot**. Spot nodes cost less, but the cloud
 can take one back at short notice. On Azure, Spot adds a separate Spot pool and the system pool
 stays on-demand. Spot is not available on Hetzner or on a GKE Autopilot cluster.
6. Optional: set **Node disk**, the worker root volume in GB. Leave it empty for the cloud's default.
 Hetzner has no such field, because the disk comes with the server type.
7. Optional: under **Security**, add **Cluster admins**. T

records.title: Configure the cluster
records.heading: Versions and instance types
records.text:
The version and instance type lists come from your cloud account when Alethia can read them. When
it cannot, the lists are these:

 Hetzner 1.35 `cpx22` `cax11`, `cax21`, `cax31`, `cx23`, `cx33`, `cpx22`, `cpx32` 

On GCP, a deploy onto `e2-medium` or `n1-standard-1` is refused before it spends anything. GKE

The disk floor and default per cloud:

The maximum is 2,000 GB.

Run a plan from the review view. It shows the cluster and node group to create, and its cost. After
the deploy, [get a kubeconfig](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig) and run `kubectl get nodes`: you see the

records.title: Add a container registry
records.text: Add a container registry. Create private image repositories in your cloud's registry or in Docker Hub, with immutable tags and vulnerability scanning.

records.title: Add a container registry
records.text:
Create a private repository for your container images. You can add as many as you need, for
example one each for `api`, `frontend` and `worker`.

records.title: Add a container registry
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- To use Docker Hub instead of your cloud's registry, connect it as a
 [pluggable connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable), with a username and an access token.

records.title: Add a container registry
records.heading: Add a repository
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **Container registry** in the **DevOps** group.
2. Enter a name, such as `api`.
3. Turn on **Immutable tags** to stop a pushed tag from being overwritten. Use it in production, so
 a tag such as `v1.2.3` always points to the same image.
4. Turn on **Vulnerability scanning** to scan each pushed image for known CVEs.

records.title: Add a container registry
records.heading: Choose the registry
records.text:
One environment pushes and pulls through one registry.

1. Select the environment's name at the start of the toolbar.
2. On **Settings**, under **Container registry**, choose **Cloud native** or Docker Hub. For Docker
 Hub, you can set a namespace or organization; it defaults to the username.

 Registry What Alethia creates 
 --- --- 
 AWS ECR repositories 
 GCP Artifact Registry repositories 
 Azure ACR repositories 
 Hetzner A Harbor registry in your cluster, with a scoped robot account for pulls 
 Docker Hub No repository. Alethia adds an `imagePullSecret` so workloads can pull from Docker Hub. **Immutable tags** and **Vulnerability scanning** are not shown. 

On AWS, GCP and Azure, nodes pull from the project's registry with their own cloud identity, so no
pull secret is needed.

records.title: Add a container registry
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, open the registry's **Status** tab. **Endpoints** shows the repository URL, such
as `123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/api`. Push an image to it:

docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/api:v1.0.0

records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Add a service](/guides/design-project/services): deploy an image from the registry.
- [Pluggable connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable)

records.title: See what an environment costs
records.text: See what an environment costs. Read an environment's monthly cost, each resource's cost, and what a plan changes, from the last Infracost estimate.

records.title: See what an environment costs
records.text:
See the monthly cost of an environment and of each resource. Every figure comes from the last plan:
the runner prices each plan with Infracost. How the estimate is made is in
[Cost estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation).

records.title: See what an environment costs
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The environment has been planned at least once. Until then, nothing is priced, and Alethia shows
 no figure rather than `$0.00`.

records.title: See what an environment costs
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Run a plan: select **Review plan** on the changes bar, then **Run plan**. The review view shows
 **Cost after this plan** as a monthly total.
2. For the environment's total from the last plan, open the **⋯** menu in the toolbar and read
 **Cost, from the last plan**.
3. For one resource, read the monthly cost on its card, or open it and read the **Cost** section of
 its **Status** tab. It lists the cost per OpenTofu address, most expensive first. A resource
 never priced says **Not priced yet**.

records.title: See what an environment costs
records.heading: What the figure leaves out
records.text:
- It is as fresh as the last plan. After a design change, plan again.
- Infracost prices what is in the OpenTofu plan. Usage-based resources (NoSQL tables, queues,
 topics, bucket storage) and data transfer are not estimated.
- A plan whose cost breakdown is missing or broken shows as not priced, never as a wrong number.

records.title: See what an environment costs
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After a plan, the **⋯** menu shows **Cost, from the last plan**, and each priced card shows its
monthly cost.

records.title: Add a database
records.text: Add a database. Add a managed PostgreSQL or MySQL database to an environment, set its capacity, backups and version, and read its credentials.

records.title: Add a database
records.text: Add a relational database to the environment. You can add as many as you need.

records.title: Add a database
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - You have a project open on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas).

records.title: Add a database
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **Database** in the **Data** group.
2. Choose **PostgreSQL** or **MySQL**. On Hetzner, only PostgreSQL is offered. The first database
 is named `primary`.
3. Under **General**, check the **Port**. The default is 5432.
4. Under **Capacity**, set **Min capacity** and **Max capacity**. The database scales between them:

 Cloud Service Unit Range Default 
 --- --- --- --- --- 
 AWS Aurora Serverless v2 ACU (about 2 GiB of memory each) 0.5–128 0.5–4 
 GCP Cloud SQL vCPU 1–96 1–4 
 Azure Azure Database Flexible Server vCores 1–64 2–4 

 On Hetzner the database runs in your cluster on CloudNativePG. Set **Storage**, the volume per
 PostgreSQL instance in GiB, and **Instances**, one primary plus replicas (1–5), under
 **In-cluster sizing** instead.
5. Under **Security**:
 - Turn on **IAM authentication** so that services connect with short-lived cloud tokens instead
 of a password. See [Use keyless database auth](/guides/design-project/keyless-database-auth).
 It is unavailable on Hetzner, and the switch says why.
 - Set **Backup retention** in days (0–35). `0` turns automated backups off. Point-in-time restore
 covers this window.
6. Optional: under **Advanced**, p

records.title: Add a database
records.heading: Engine versions
records.text:
The lists come from your cloud account when Alethia can read them. When it cannot:

 Cloud PostgreSQL MySQL 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS 14–18, default 16 8.0 and 8.4, default 8.0 
 GCP 14–18, default 15 5.7, 8.0 and 8.4, default 8.0 
 Azure 14–18, default 16 5.7, 8.0.21 and 8.4, default 8.0.21 
 Hetzner 16 Not offered

records.title: Add a database
records.heading: Read the credentials
records.text:
Alethia generates the database's password at deploy. A service gets it through a
[binding](/guides/design-project/services), as a Kubernetes Secret that the External Secrets
Operator keeps in sync, so you never copy it.

records.title: Add a database
records.heading: Read the extra database user on AWS
records.text:
On AWS, Alethia also creates a second database user, `demouser`, on the database `demodb`. It
generates the password and stores the user name, password and database name in AWS Secrets
Manager. After the deploy, the database records that secret's ARN as `extra_secret_ref`. Read the
credentials from the secret.

You cannot change this user on the canvas or in `provider_config`, because the template variable
`rds_extra_credentials` holds the password too, and Alethia does not store a credential in a
component's configuration.

A project saved earlier can still hold an `rds_extra_credentials` value. Alethia keeps applying it
and never shows it. To remove it:

1. Open the database's **Advanced** group.
2. Choose **Remove the stored value**.
3. Deploy. The secret is rewritten with the default user, database and a new password.
4. Update the services that read the old credentials.

records.title: Add a database
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, open the database's **Status** tab. **Endpoints** shows the hostname, with a copy
button.

records.heading: Related
