records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.text: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF. Give an environment a DNS zone, a managed TLS certificate and an in-cluster Let's Encrypt issuer, and put a web application firewall in front of it.

records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.text:
Manage the environment's domain, get TLS certificates, and protect it with a web application
firewall (WAF).

records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You own the domain. To use a zone you already have, it is in the project's cloud account, or in
 a connected [Cloudflare connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable).

records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **DNS** in the **Networking** group. The environment has one DNS card.
2. Leave **Enabled** on.
3. Choose the **DNS provider**: the cluster cloud's own DNS (Route 53, Cloud DNS or Azure DNS), or
 **Cloudflare**. For Cloudflare, also set the zone ID and whether records are proxied. Alethia
 reads the Cloudflare credential at deploy and never stores it in the project.
4. Enter the **Domain name**, such as `example.com`.
5. Optional: in **Existing zone ID**, enter a zone you already own. Leave it empty to create a zone.

 Cloud Zone ID looks like 
 --- --- 
 AWS A public Route 53 hosted zone: `Z1234567890ABC` 
 GCP A Cloud DNS managed zone: `projects/…/managedZones/…` 
 Azure An Azure DNS zone: `example.com` 

6. Turn on **Managed TLS certificate** to get a certificate for the domain.
7. Turn on **Web application firewall (WAF)** to protect the load balancer.

The certificate and the WAF apply to the cloud's own DNS only, not to Cloudflare.

records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.heading: Certificates
records.text:
Cloud Issued by Validation 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) DNS, through Route 53 
 GCP cert-manager in your cluster, from Let's Encrypt ACME DNS01, through Cloud DNS 
 Azure cert-manager in your cluster, from Let's Encrypt ACME DNS01, through Azure DNS 
 Hetzner Nothing. Bring your own certificate. — 

Certificates renew before they expire. On AWS the certificate stays in ACM, because an Application
Load Balancer can only use a certificate from ACM or IAM.

On AWS, GCP and Azure the same switch installs cert-manager and creates a `ClusterIssuer` named
`letsencrypt-prod`. Reference it from an Ingress to get a Let's Encrypt certificate for any host in
your zone:

metadata:
 annotations:
 cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod

The issuer solves DNS01 challenges, so it works before you have a public ingress and can issue
wildcard certificates. It writes challenge records with the same cloud identity as `external-dns`,
so there is no API key to supply.

records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.heading: WAF
records.text:
Cloud WAF 
 --- --- 
 AWS AWS WAFv2 on the load balancer, with AWS managed rule groups. A CloudFront WAF is available only through `provider_config` (`cloudfront_waf`), for your own distribution. 
 GCP Cloud Armor at the load balancer 
 Azure Azure WAF 
 Hetzner None. Hetzner sells no WAF. 

On Hetzner the canvas still shows both switches, but they create nothing.

records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, look up the domain:

dig +short NS example.com

The name servers are your cloud's (or Cloudflare's). With a certificate, `https://` on a host in the
zone answers with a valid certificate.

records.title: Configure DNS, certificates and a WAF
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Pluggable connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable): connect Cloudflare.
- [Multi-cloud conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion): duplicating a project onto another cloud clears the zone ID and domain.
- [See the cost](/guides/design-project/cost)

records.title: Enforce chart admission
records.text: Enforce chart admission. Move the namespaces of an environment's bring-your-own charts from warn to enforce, so Pod Security baseline and the admission policy refuse instead of only reporting.

records.title: Enforce chart admission
records.text:
Turn on refusal in every bring-your-own chart namespace of one environment. For what the two modes do,
see [Chart namespace admission](/concepts/chart-admission).

records.title: Enforce chart admission
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The environment has at least one [bring-your-own chart](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts).
- Its latest deploy produced a complete admission report. If it did not, deploy again first.
- Each chart's warnings on the **Deploy** tab are fixed. A warning names the chart, the object and the
 field that `enforce` would refuse.

records.title: Enforce chart admission
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Open **Environments**. On the environment's card, next to **BYO admission**, select **Change**.
2. Read the report. It lists each bring-your-own namespace, its current mode, and what refusal would
 refuse there, from the latest deploy. An object kind the deploy could not check is marked **Could
 not be checked**.
3. Turn on **Refuse in every BYO namespace**, confirm that you read the report, and save. The card
 shows **Redeploy to apply**.
4. Start a new deploy of the environment.

records.title: Enforce chart admission
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The **Deploy** tab shows each namespace that changed, for example `warn → enforce`, and the card no
longer shows **Redeploy to apply**.

Objects that already run keep running until they are replaced. From then on, Pod Security enforces
`baseline` and the admission policy refuses.

records.title: Enforce chart admission
records.heading: Things to know
records.text:
- **The setting takes effect on the next new deploy.** A re-run, an approval-gated deploy planned
 before the change, and a promotion of an earlier plan keep the old value.
- **The report covers only what ran at that deploy.** A `CronJob` between runs, a workload scaled to
 zero, and a chart attached after that deploy are not in it.
- **To undo it,** turn the setting off and deploy again. The namespaces the setting moved, marked
 `alethia.io/byo-admission-source=environment-setting`, go back to `warn`. A namespace that was
 already in `enforce`, such as one made for a new chart, stays in `enforce`.
- **A label you set with `kubectl` is kept.** If the setting had moved that namespace, also remove the
 `alethia.io/byo-admission-source` label, or turning the setting off returns it to `warn`.
- **It needs a runner that supports it.** An older runner deploys as before, and the **Deploy** tab
 shows the mode each namespace really has.
- Each change of the setting is recorded in the project's audit log.

records.heading: Related
records.text:

records.title: Use keyless database auth
records.text: Use keyless database auth. Connect a service to a PostgreSQL or MySQL database with short-lived cloud IAM tokens instead of a password.

records.title: Use keyless database auth
records.text:
Connect a service to its database with its own cloud identity and a short-lived token, so no
database password sits in the cluster. How it works on each cloud is in
[Keyless database auth](/concepts/keyless-database-auth).

records.title: Use keyless database auth
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The project runs on AWS, GCP or Azure. Hetzner runs PostgreSQL in your cluster, with no cloud
 identity to mint tokens, so there the database keeps a generated password.
- The database engine is PostgreSQL or MySQL.
- Your runner has `ALETHIA_KEYLESS_DB_AUTH_ENABLED=true`. Without it, the binding uses the password
 path.
- Your runner runs a published image. It schedules its own image as a sidecar and as a setup Job.
 Set `ALETHIA_RUNNER_IMAGE` only to use a private mirror. A runner built from source has no
 published image, so keyless deploys fail there.

records.title: Use keyless database auth
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select the database card. Under **Security**, turn on **IAM authentication**.
2. Connect the service to the database: drag from the service's handle to the database card.
3. In the service's **Connections** tab, map these values to environment variables. Do not map
 `password`: there is none.

 Value Resolves to 
 --- --- 
 `endpoint` `127.0.0.1`: a proxy in the service's pod 
 `port` 5432 for PostgreSQL, 3306 for MySQL 
 `username` The service's cloud login, filled in from the deploy 

4. Configure your application to connect to that host, port and user with no password. You do not
 change any other code.
5. Review the plan and deploy.

You do not mark the binding as keyless. It follows the database: with **IAM authentication** on,
the binding is keyless; with it off, the binding uses a generated password. To switch, change the
setting on the database and deploy again.

records.title: Use keyless database auth
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
- The deployment's **Deploy** tab lists no omitted binding. If Alethia cannot wire a keyless
 binding, for example because an identity is missing, it leaves the binding out and names the
 reason there.
- Your service's pod has a second container: the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on GCP, or
 `alethia db-authproxy` on AWS and Azure.
- No Kubernetes Secret holds a password for this database.
- The application connects. A failed login means the database user and the cloud identity do not
 match: see [Troubleshoot design and GitOps](/troubleshooting/design-project#a-keyless-binding-is-omitted-at-deploy).

records.title: Use keyless database auth
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Keyless database auth](/concepts/keyless-database-auth): the proxy, the database role and the setup Job on each cloud.
- [Add a database](/guides/design-project/databases)
- [Security](/concepts/security)

records.title: Add queues and topics
records.text: Add queues and topics. Add message queues, with ordered delivery if you need it, and publish/subscribe topics with their subscriptions.

records.title: Add queues and topics
records.text:
Add queues for point-to-point messages and topics for publish/subscribe. You can add as many of
each as you need.

records.title: Add queues and topics
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have a project open on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas).
- If you want ordered delivery, your publisher can set an ordering key on every message.

records.title: Add queues and topics
records.heading: Add a queue
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **Queue** in the **Messaging** group.
2. Set **Visibility timeout (s)**, how long a message stays hidden after a consumer reads it
 (0–43,200, default 30).
3. Set **Message retention**, how long an unconsumed message is kept (1–14 days, default 4).
4. Decide on **Ordered (FIFO) delivery** now. Changing it later destroys the queue and every
 message in it, because each cloud fixes it when the queue is created.

On Hetzner, a queue is a RabbitMQ server in your cluster. Set its **Storage** in GiB (1–256); the
other fields are not shown.

 Cloud Queue With ordered delivery 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS SQS A FIFO queue. The name gains `.fifo`, which counts toward the 80-character limit. Deduplication is by content. The dead-letter queue is FIFO too. 
 GCP A pull subscription on Pub/Sub Message ordering on the subscription. All messages for one key must be published from one region. 
 Azure Service Bus queue Sessions. They need the Standard or Premium tier: a Basic project is blocked before it deploys.

records.title: Add queues and topics
records.heading: What ordered delivery means
records.text:
Messages with the same ordering key arrive in the order the service received them. Messages with
different keys have no order between them and are still processed in parallel. A queue whose
messages carry no key is unordered, even with the setting on.

 Cloud The key Cost 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS `MessageGroupId` A higher price per request, and at most 300 messages a second (3,000 batched) 
 GCP `orderingKey` At most 1 MB/s per key, and higher latency. A redelivered message makes every later message for its key arrive again. Order is lost in a dead-letter topic. 
 Azure `SessionId` One receiver holds a session at a time. A message moved back from the dead-letter queue loses its place. 

On Azure, your consumer must also accept sessions. After you turn sessions on, a client that sends
or receives plain messages stops working.

records.title: Add queues and topics
records.heading: Add a topic
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **Topic** in the **Messaging** group.
2. Under **Subscriptions**, add each subscriber: a **Protocol** (**HTTPS**, **Queue**, **Email** or
 **Function**) and its **Endpoint**.

 Cloud Topic 
 --- --- 
 AWS SNS 
 GCP Pub/Sub topic 
 Azure Service Bus topic 
 Hetzner NATS in your cluster 

On Hetzner, Alethia creates the topic but not its subscriptions: a NATS subscriber is a client that
connects, so your application subscribes itself.

Messaging is priced per message, so a plan cannot estimate its cost from the design.

records.title: Add queues and topics
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, the queue's card shows its delivery mode and visibility timeout, and the topic's
card shows its subscription count. Their **Status** tabs show the endpoints.

records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Add a service](/guides/design-project/services): connect a service to a queue.
- [Troubleshoot design and GitOps](/troubleshooting/design-project#azure-refuses-an-ordered-queue)

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.text: Migrate from ingress-nginx. Move an environment from the deprecated Ingress NGINX add-on to the Traefik add-on, and from Ingress objects to Gateway API routes.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.text:
Replace the deprecated **Ingress NGINX** add-on with **Traefik**, then, when you are ready, move
from Ingress objects to Gateway API routes. The Kubernetes project retired ingress-nginx: its last
release is 4.15.1, and it gets no more security fixes.

From 2027-02-09, Ingress NGINX accepts no new installs from the console or the CLI. An environment
that already has it keeps it: it still deploys, you can still change its settings, and Alethia never
removes it for you.

The migration has two stages:

1. **Swap the controller.** Traefik serves your existing Ingress objects unchanged.
2. **Move to Gateway API.** Rewrite each Ingress as an `HTTPRoute`. This stage is optional.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You can run `kubectl` against the cluster. See [Get a kubeconfig](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).
- `jq` is installed, for the annotation review.
- For Stage 2, [ingress2gateway](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/ingress2gateway) is installed.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Stage 1: swap the controller
records.text:
Traefik's NGINX provider reads Ingress objects with `ingressClassName: nginx` and their
`nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/*` annotations. The add-on setting **Serve NGINX-class Ingresses**
turns it on; it is off by default. Both controllers can run at once, each behind its own load
balancer, and you move traffic by moving DNS.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Review your annotations
records.text:
List the annotations your Ingress objects use:

kubectl get ingress --all-namespaces -o json \
 jq -r '.items[].metadata.annotations // {} keys[]' \
 grep '^nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/' sort uniq -c

Compare the list with the [annotation reference](/reference/ingress-nginx-annotations). Traefik
ignores an annotation it does not support and still serves the route. Three are access controls:
`denylist-source-range`, the ModSecurity and OWASP rule annotations, and `auth-tls-match-cn`. For
each, add a Traefik middleware first, or keep that Ingress on Ingress NGINX by leaving the setting
off: it applies to every NGINX-class Ingress at once.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Enable Traefik
records.text:
1. On the canvas, select **Add** and choose **Traefik**.
2. Turn on **Serve NGINX-class Ingresses** once the review is done. From then on, every NGINX-class
 Ingress answers on Traefik's load balancer, even before you move DNS.
3. Select **Enable add-on**, then deploy.

From the CLI:

alethia addon enable traefik --project my-project --set ingressNginx=true

The setting needs an IngressClass named `nginx` with `spec.controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx`, which
the Ingress NGINX add-on creates. On an environment that never ran it, create the class yourself, or
leave the setting off and use `ingressClassName: traefik`.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Check that Traefik serves your routes
records.text:
Get Traefik's address, then send a request for one of your hosts to it without changing DNS:

kubectl -n traefik get service -l app.kubernetes.io/name=traefik
curl --resolve app.example.com:443: https://app.example.com/

Repeat for each host. Check each behaviour an annotation controls: redirects, rewrites,
authentication and allowlists.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Move DNS
records.text:
Point each host at Traefik's address. If external-dns manages your records, both controllers write
their address to the Ingress status and compete for the record until you remove Ingress NGINX, so
do the next steps in a quiet period.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Keep the nginx IngressClass
records.text:
Removing the Ingress NGINX add-on deletes the `nginx` IngressClass, and Traefik then stops serving
your Ingresses. Tell ArgoCD to keep it:

kubectl annotate ingressclass nginx argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options=Delete=false --overwrite

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Remove Ingress NGINX
records.text:
Open **Ingress NGINX** on the canvas, select **Remove**, then deploy. The controller and its load
balancer go. Your Ingress objects and the `nginx` IngressClass stay.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Install the Gateway API CRDs
records.text:
Neither the Traefik chart nor an Alethia cluster includes them. Install the standard channel before
the next step, or the add-on cannot sync:

kubectl apply --server-side \
 -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.6.3/standard-install.yaml

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Turn on Gateway API in Traefik
records.text:
Open **Traefik** on the canvas, turn on **Gateway API**, save, and deploy. Traefik creates a
`traefik` GatewayClass and a `traefik-gateway` Gateway in the `traefik` namespace, with one HTTP
listener on port 8000. For HTTPS, add a listener with `certificateRefs` under `gateway.listeners` in
the add-on's raw Helm values.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Convert each Ingress
records.text:
Write a first draft of the routes:

ingress2gateway print --providers ingress-nginx --all-namespaces > routes.yaml

Review it before you apply it: the tool does not convert authentication, cookie affinity, rate
limits or snippets. Point each route's `parentRefs` at `traefik-gateway` in the `traefik` namespace.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Remove the Ingress
records.text:
When the route serves the host, delete the Ingress. When no NGINX-class Ingress is left, turn off
**Serve NGINX-class Ingresses**.

records.title: Migrate from ingress-nginx
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
kubectl get ingressclass nginx
kubectl get httproute --all-namespaces

After Stage 1, the `nginx` class still exists and every host answers through Traefik. After
Stage 2, each host has an `HTTPRoute` and no NGINX-class Ingress is left.

records.title: Configure the network
records.text: Configure the network. Create a new VPC or VNet for an environment, or deploy into a network that already exists in your cloud account.

records.title: Configure the network
records.text: Give the environment a new network, or attach it to one that already exists in your account.

records.title: Configure the network
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The project's cloud account is connected. To use an existing network, it must be in the
 project's region and show in the account's [asset inventory](/concepts/connection-health).

records.title: Configure the network
records.heading: Open the network settings
records.text:
1. On the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas), select the environment's name at the start
 of the toolbar.
2. On **Settings**, find **Network (VPC)**.

records.title: Configure the network
records.heading: Create a new network
records.text:
1. Leave **Provision a new network** on.
2. Set **CIDR block**. The default is `10.0.0.0/16`. Each cloud carves subnets out of this range, so
 it must be at least this wide:

 Cloud Widest prefix allowed 
 --- --- 
 AWS, Azure `/18` 
 Hetzner `/22` 
 GCP Any valid IPv4 CIDR 

3. Choose the NAT gateway. **Single NAT gateway** is on by default: one shared NAT, which costs
 less. Turn it off for one NAT per availability zone. On AWS, one NAT costs about $35 a month and
 three cost about $105.
4. Optional: add **Allowed CIDR blocks**, the extra networks that can reach resources in this
 network.

 Cloud What Alethia creates 
 --- --- 
 AWS A VPC with public and private subnets across availability zones, an internet gateway, NAT gateways and route tables 
 GCP A VPC network with custom-mode subnets in the region, and Cloud NAT with a Cloud Router 
 Azure A VNet with subnets for nodes and services, a NAT gateway and network security groups

records.title: Configure the network
records.heading: Use an existing network
records.text:
On AWS, GCP and Azure you can deploy into a network you already have:

1. Turn off **Provision a new network**.
2. Choose the network under **Existing network**. The list comes from the asset inventory, which
 updates itself.

At deploy, the runner does not create a network. The template reads yours and puts the cluster in
it:

 Cloud What the template uses 
 --- --- 
 AWS The VPC's subnets, split into public and private 
 GCP The VPC network's subnetwork in the project's region, with its secondary ranges for pods and services 
 Azure One of the VNet's subnets, for AKS 

The network is the only resource you can reuse this way, because the cluster attaches into it. A
database, cache or bucket that already exists is not something to provision: give your service its
endpoint and credentials instead.

records.title: Configure the network
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
Run a plan from the review view. It lists the network resources to create. With an existing
network, it creates none.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.text: Use the inspector. Rename a resource, change its settings, connect a service, read its status and cost, and duplicate, delete or destroy, from the panel beside the canvas.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.text:
Change a resource from the inspector, the panel docked on the right of the
[canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas). The board stays usable while it is open.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - Open a project's **Architecture** view.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Open and close the inspector
records.text:
1. Select a card. With the keyboard, move to it with **Tab** and press **Enter**.
2. To close the inspector, select an empty area of the board, select **✕**, or press **Esc**.

Every subject has the same layout. From the top: **Back**, when you came from another subject. Then
the icon, kind, name and a summary. Then one suggested action, a status badge, the tabs, messages,
and the body.

 You select The inspector shows 
 --- --- 
 A resource **Settings** and **Status**, and **Connections** for a service 
 The secrets vault Its secrets, with a filter. A row opens that secret 
 An add-on Its configuration and how it is installed 
 A bring-your-own chart Its safety scan 
 A chart workload What the chart describes, and its connections 
 A bring-your-own IaC card The read-only list of its resources 
 The environment **Settings**, **Sources**, **Status** and **Activity** 
 Several cards **Duplicate** or **Remove**, as one undo step 

There is no **Save** button. Each edit goes into the design at once, and the changes bar counts it.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Rename a resource
records.text:
1. Select the name in the identity row.
2. Type the new name.

You can rename the project and any resource you can add more than one of. Names are lowercased as
you type, to match cloud naming rules.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Change settings
records.text:
1. Open the **Settings** tab.
2. Select a group to open it. A collapsed group shows a summary of its values.
3. Edit a field. The change applies when you leave the field, or when you close the inspector or
 select another card.

A group with a value that would stop the deploy opens by itself, and the problem shows under the
field. A group for one cloud carries a badge, such as `AWS only`. Groups for other clouds are not
shown. The inspector remembers which groups you open for each kind.

The cloud account is not set here. It is chosen once, when the project is created.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Connect a service
records.text:
1. Select a service and open **Connections**.
2. Add the database, cache, queue or secret it uses, and choose what it gets from each one.

A connection you draw on the board opens this tab too.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Read status, endpoints and cost
records.text:
The **Status** tab is read-only:

 Section Shows 
 --- --- 
 **State** The state and the reason for it 
 **Endpoints** What the deploy produced, such as a database hostname, each with a copy button. Shown after a deploy. 
 **Drift** Each OpenTofu address that drifted 
 **Cost** The monthly cost from the last plan, per OpenTofu address. **Not priced yet** until a plan runs.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Duplicate or delete a resource
records.text:
1. Open **Settings** and scroll to **Danger zone**.
2. Select **Duplicate** to copy the resource, or **Delete** to remove it. Press **⌘Z** to undo.

You can also select a card and press **Delete**, or right-click it and choose **Remove**. The
project, add-ons and bring-your-own charts have no **Danger zone**.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Destroy an environment
records.text:
1. Select the environment's name in the toolbar, or choose **Environment settings** from the **⋯**
 menu.
2. On **Settings**, select **Destroy**.
3. Confirm with **Destroy environment**.

This queues a job that removes the environment's cloud infrastructure. You cannot undo it.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The changes bar counts your edit as a pending change. After you deploy, **Status** shows the new
state and endpoints.

records.title: Use the inspector
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Use the canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas)
- [Read the canvas](/concepts/canvas): what each state means.
- [Troubleshoot a destroy](/troubleshooting/destroy): when a destroy does not finish.

records.title: Add node pools, labels and taints
records.text: Add node pools, labels and taints. Label every node, add node pools beside the default pool, taint them, and run a workload on a chosen pool or on arm64.

records.title: Add node pools, labels and taints
records.text:
Label your nodes, add node pools beside the default pool, and schedule workloads onto them. The
same keys work on AWS, GCP, Azure and Hetzner, so the configuration survives a move to another
cloud. Every field and rule is in the [node pools reference](/reference/node-pools).

records.title: Add node pools, labels and taints
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You can edit the project from the CLI, with `alethia apply` or `alethia project component add`.
 The canvas has no fields for these keys.
- On GCP, the cluster is not an Autopilot cluster (`gke_enable_autopilot: true`). Autopilot makes its
 own nodes, so it refuses all three keys.

records.title: Add node pools, labels and taints
records.heading: Add the keys
records.text:
Three keys in the cluster's `provider_config` do the work:

 Key What it does 
 --- --- 
 `node_labels` Labels the nodes of every pool, the default pool included 
 `node_taints` Taints the nodes of the extra pools only. The default pool runs Alethia's add-ons, so it is never tainted. 
 `extra_node_pools` Adds node pools beside the default pool 

1. Add the keys under the cluster in `alethia.yaml`. This example labels every node and adds a pool
 of four arm64 nodes for batch jobs:

 environments:
 - name: prod
 components:
 cluster:
 provider_config:
 node_labels:
 team: payments
 node_taints:
 - key: dedicated
 value: batch
 effect: NoSchedule
 extra_node_pools:
 - name: batch
 instance_type: m7g.large
 arch: arm64
 min_size: 4
 max_size: 4
 labels:
 workload: batch
 
2. Send it:

 alethia apply
 
 Or set one key from the CLI, as JSON:

 alethia project component add --project boutique --kind cluster \
 --set 'provider_config={"node_labels":{"team":"payments"}}'
 
 [Setting template knobs](/reference/cli/project#setting-template-knobs) explains how a write
 merges and how to remove a key.

3. Plan and deploy the environment.

The server checks only that each key exists in the cloud

records.title: Add node pools, labels and taints
records.heading: Run a workload on a pool
records.text:
Every node of an extra pool carries the label `alethia.io/pool: `. Select the pool with it,
and tolerate every taint on the pool. For the `batch` pool above:

spec:
 nodeSelector:
 alethia.io/pool: batch
 kubernetes.io/arch: arm64
 tolerations:
 - key: dedicated
 value: batch
 effect: NoSchedule
 - key: alethia.io/arch
 value: arm64
 effect: NoSchedule
 - key: kubernetes.io/arch
 value: arm64
 effect: NoSchedule

The last toleration is for GKE, which taints its own arm64 nodes. It does no harm on other clouds.

records.title: Add node pools, labels and taints
records.heading: Run a workload on arm64
records.text:
Alethia taints every arm64 pool with `alethia.io/arch=arm64:NoSchedule`, so an amd64 image does not
land there and fail with `exec format error`. The images Alethia builds are amd64 only. To run on
arm64:

1. Build a multi-arch image, or an arm64 image.
2. Add a toleration for `alethia.io/arch` with value `arm64` and effect `NoSchedule`.
3. Add the node selector `kubernetes.io/arch: arm64`.

records.title: Add node pools, labels and taints
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
kubectl get nodes -L alethia.io/pool,team

The new pool's nodes show its name, and every node shows the `team` label. A pod with the selector
and tolerations above runs on a `batch` node.

records.title: Add a NoSQL table
records.text: Add a NoSQL table. Add a DynamoDB, Firestore or Cosmos DB table to an environment, with its keys, capacity mode, backups and replicas.

records.title: Add a NoSQL table
records.text: Add a NoSQL table to the environment. You can add as many as you need.

records.title: Add a NoSQL table
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - You have a project open on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas).

records.title: Add a NoSQL table
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **NoSQL table** in the **Data** group.
2. Under **Schema**, set the **Partition key** (default `id`) and its **Key type**.
3. Optional: set a **Sort key** and its **Sort key type**. With the partition key it forms a
 composite key. GCP and Hetzner do not offer a sort key.
4. Under **Capacity**, choose the **Capacity mode**. Only AWS offers more than one.
5. Leave **Point-in-time recovery** on (the default) for continuous backups that you can restore to
 any second in the retention window. It is unavailable on Hetzner, which backs up on a schedule.
6. Optional: under **Replication**, add **Global replica regions**, such as `us-east-1`. Only AWS and
 Azure support them.

 Cloud Service Key types Capacity modes 
 --- --- --- --- 
 AWS DynamoDB String, Number, Binary On-Demand, Provisioned 
 GCP Firestore String, Number Native Mode 
 Azure Cosmos DB String, Number Serverless 
 Hetzner ScyllaDB in your cluster, with its DynamoDB-compatible API — — 

On Azure, replicas apply to the whole Cosmos DB account: it uses every table's list together. The
first replica moves the account from serverless to provisioned billing. On a project that is already
deployed, this rep

records.title: Add a NoSQL table
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, the table's card shows a solid dot and its partition key, capacity mode and
point-in-time recovery setting. Its **Status** tab shows the endpoint.

records.heading: Related
records.text:

records.title: Turn on observability
records.text: Turn on observability. Send an environment's cluster metrics, logs and traces to Datadog or Grafana Cloud.

records.title: Turn on observability
records.text:
Send the cluster's metrics, logs and traces to Datadog or Grafana Cloud. Observability has no
cloud default: you always pick a provider and connect its credential.

records.title: Turn on observability
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Connect [Datadog or Grafana Cloud](/guides/connectors/pluggable). Datadog needs an API key and an
 application key. Grafana Cloud needs an instance ID and an API token. Alethia encrypts the
 credential and passes it to the runner at deploy; it is never stored in the project.
- Install the [CLI](/get-started/install-the-cli). The canvas has no observability card yet, so you
 turn it on from the CLI.

records.title: Turn on observability
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Add the observability component with your provider. For Datadog, set the site (`datadoghq.com`
 by default, or `datadoghq.eu`, `us3.datadoghq.com`, `us5.datadoghq.com`, `ap1.datadoghq.com`):

 alethia project component add --project my-project --kind observability \
 --set enabled=true --set provider=datadog \
 --set 'provider_config={"site":"datadoghq.eu"}'
 
 For Grafana Cloud, the remote-write URL is required:

 alethia project component add --project my-project --kind observability \
 --set enabled=true --set provider=grafana \
 --set 'provider_config={"remote_write_url":"https://prometheus-prod-01.grafana.net/api/prom/push"}'
 
2. Plan and deploy the environment.

 Provider Alethia installs 
 --- --- 
 Datadog The Datadog agent, with Helm 
 Grafana Cloud The Grafana Agent, writing metrics to your remote-write URL 

For a metrics stack inside the cluster instead, add the **kube-prometheus-stack**
[add-on](/reference/cli/addons). It installs Prometheus, Grafana and Alertmanager.

records.title: Turn on observability
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
alethia project component list --project my-project --kind observability

The component shows as enabled. A few minutes after the deploy, the cluster's metrics appear in
Datadog or Grafana Cloud.

records.title: Set the project basics
records.text: Set the project basics. Set a project's name, its default environment's stage, and its region on the Project card.

records.title: Set the project basics
records.text: Set the project's name, the stage of its default environment, and its region.

records.title: Set the project basics
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have a project open on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas). The cloud account
 was chosen when you created the project.

records.title: Set the project basics
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select the **Project** card. The inspector opens with two groups, **General** and **Placement**.
2. Under **General**, set **Project name**. Use up to 100 characters, with at least one letter or
 number. Alethia derives a URL-safe identifier from it, which it also uses to name cloud
 resources and the OpenTofu state.
3. Under **General**, choose **Environment**:

 Stage Use it for 
 --- --- 
 **Development** Short-lived, low-cost defaults 
 **Staging** A copy of production for testing 
 **Production** Live traffic, with durable sizing 

4. Under **Placement**, choose the **Region**. The list shows your cloud's regions, grouped by
 geography.

The stage belongs to the environment, not to the project. A project can have several environments,
each with its own stage and its own OpenTofu state.

Alethia runs OpenTofu 1.11.4. You cannot choose another version on the canvas.

records.title: Set the project basics
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The **Project** card shows the region and the stage. The changes bar counts the edit as a pending
change.

records.title: Set the project basics
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Configure the network](/guides/design-project/network)
- [OpenTofu state](/concepts/terraform-state)

records.title: Connect an apps repository
records.text: Connect an apps repository. Name the Git repository that ArgoCD syncs your application manifests from, lay it out, and choose an overlay path.

records.title: Connect an apps repository
records.text:
Name the Git repository that ArgoCD syncs your manifests from. It is optional: without one, the
environment still gets ArgoCD, but ArgoCD runs none of your applications. How the sync behaves, what
Alethia commits back, and what your manifests may create are in
[The apps repository](/concepts/apps-repository).

records.title: Connect an apps repository
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Connect the repository's [Git provider](/guides/connectors/git-providers): GitHub, GitLab or
 Bitbucket. A public `https://` repository also works without a connection. An `ssh://` or
 `git@host:path` repository always needs one.
- To run [marketplace add-ons in GitOps mode](/concepts/apps-repository#which-git-providers-support-gitops-mode),
 the repository is on GitHub.

records.title: Connect an apps repository
records.heading: Lay out the repository
records.text:
ArgoCD syncs one directory of your repository's default branch: the repository root, or the
overlay path you set.

 Path What it holds 
 --- --- 
 The synced directory Your manifests, directly in it: ArgoCD does not read subdirectories of a plain directory. A Kustomize or Helm source there reads its own subdirectories. 
 `addons/` The add-ons you run in GitOps mode. Alethia creates it. Create it empty to avoid an ArgoCD error before then. 
 `overlays/ /` Optional. With no overlay path set, each one becomes its own Application, `apps- `. 

To start from a working layout, copy the
[apps starter template](/guides/design-project/starter-templates).

records.title: Connect an apps repository
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. On the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas), select **Add**, then **Repository** in the
 **DevOps** group.
2. Choose the **ArgoCD apps repository**.
3. Optional: set **Overlay path**, the directory this environment syncs, such as `overlays/dev`.
 Leave it empty to sync the repository root.
4. Review the plan and deploy.

Use an overlay path when several environments share one repository: `overlays/dev` for development,
`overlays/prod` for production. Setting one turns overlay discovery off for this environment, so it
does not also take over the directories other environments deliver.

The path must:

 Rule Accepted Refused 
 --- --- --- 
 Be empty or `.` for the root, or relative to the root `overlays/dev` `/overlays/dev` 
 Be normalized `overlays/dev` `../shared`, `overlays//dev`, `overlays/dev/` 
 Have segments that start with a letter or digit, then letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-` `env-1.2_a` `overlays/$env` 
 Be at most 512 characters 

A path that breaks a rule is refused, never corrected.

 
Anyone who can push to the default branch can change what runs: a commit there deploys without an
Alethia deploy or an approval. Protect the branch if that is not what you want

records.title: Connect an apps repository
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, the `apps` Application in ArgoCD is **Synced** and **Healthy**, and your
resources exist:

kubectl get applications -n argocd

If the deploy succeeded but the cluster is empty, see
[Troubleshoot design and GitOps](/troubleshooting/design-project#the-deploy-succeeded-but-the-cluster-is-empty).

records.title: Add secrets
records.text: Add secrets. Create secrets in your cloud's secret store or in a connected store such as HashiCorp Vault, generate their values or set your own, and read them in the cluster.

records.title: Add secrets
records.text:
Create secrets for your services. Alethia creates each one in the environment's secret store and
syncs it into the cluster with the External Secrets Operator.

records.title: Add secrets
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- To keep secrets outside your cloud, connect a secrets store, such as HashiCorp Vault, as a
 [pluggable connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable).

records.title: Add secrets
records.heading: Add a secret
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **Secret** in the **Security** group. All secrets on the board collect in
 one card, the vault. Open it to add, find or remove a secret.
2. Enter a name. Use letters, digits and hyphens.
3. Choose how the value is made:
 - Leave **Auto-generate value** on, and set **Length** (8–128) and
 **Include special characters**. Alethia generates the value when it creates the secret.
 - Or turn **Auto-generate value** off to set the value yourself after the deploy.

records.title: Add secrets
records.heading: Choose where secrets are stored
records.text:
One environment reads all its secrets through one store.

1. Select the environment's name at the start of the toolbar.
2. On **Settings**, under **Secrets**, choose **Cluster native** (the cloud's secret manager) or a
 connected store. For HashiCorp Vault, set the KV mount path (default `secret`) and KV version
 (`1` or `2`, default `2`).

 Cloud Cluster native store 
 --- --- 
 AWS AWS Secrets Manager 
 GCP Secret Manager 
 Azure Key Vault 
 Hetzner A Vault that Alethia runs in your cluster 

On Hetzner, Hetzner sells no key management service, so the Vault's unseal key is a Kubernetes
Secret in the same cluster. It adds an audit log, leases and revocation, but no protection against
someone with cluster-admin access.

records.title: Add secrets
records.heading: Set a secret's value
records.text:
Alethia does not accept a secret's value in the project's settings, because it would be stored in
plain text. Write it in the store instead:

1. Turn **Auto-generate value** off and deploy. On AWS, the secret is created with the placeholder
 value `editme`.
2. Write the real value into the store. On AWS:

 aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
 --secret-id \
 --secret-string ' '
 
 With a connected store, write the value there.

A project saved earlier can still hold a value in the AWS template's `value` variable. Alethia keeps
applying it and never shows it. To remove it, open the secret's **Advanced** group and choose
**Remove the stored value**.

records.title: Add secrets
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, check that the External Secrets Operator synced the secret:

kubectl get externalsecrets --all-namespaces

Each secret shows `SecretSynced`. A service bound to it reads the value from a Kubernetes Secret.

records.title: Add a service
records.text: Add a service. Run your own code on the cluster, built from a repository or deployed from an image, with ports, environment variables, bindings, resources and a health check.

records.title: Add a service
records.text:
Add a service to run your own code on the environment's cluster. Alethia builds it from a
repository, or deploys an image you already pushed, and turns it into Kubernetes manifests at
deploy.

records.title: Add a service
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - To build from a repository, connect its [Git provider](/guides/connectors/git-providers).

records.title: Add a service
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. On the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas), select **Add**, then **Service** in the
 **Workloads** group. The inspector opens on the new card.
2. Under **Identity**, enter a **Name**, unique in the environment, and choose a **Type**:

 Type Use it for 
 --- --- 
 **Deployment** (default) Long-running, load-balanced workloads 
 **Job** A task that runs once to completion 
 **CronJob** A task that runs on a schedule 
 **StatefulSet** A workload that needs a stable identity and storage 

3. Under **Source**, choose where the image comes from:
 - **Repository**: enter the **Repository URL** and, optionally, the **Path** to build from.
 Under **Build**, you can set the **Dockerfile** path and the build **Context**. Alethia builds
 and pushes the image without a stored key.
 - **Prebuilt image**: enter the **Image**, such as `ghcr.io/org/api:1.4.0`. It deploys as-is.
4. Under **Networking**, add each **Container port** (1–65535), with an optional **Protocol**
 (`TCP` or `UDP`) and **Name**.
5. Under **Environment**, add plain **Variables** as name and value pairs. Do not put credentials
 here: use a binding.
6. Under **Bindings**, connect the service to a database, cache, queu

records.title: Add a service
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After a deploy, the service card shows a solid dot. Check the workload:

kubectl get deployments --all-namespaces grep 

The ready count matches **Replicas**.

records.title: Use a starter template
records.text: Use a starter template. Copy one of three public template repositories to start an apps repository, a bring-your-own Helm chart, or an AI retrieval stack.

records.title: Use a starter template
records.text:
Start from one of Alethia's three public template repositories instead of an empty repository.
Each one holds only paths that Alethia reads.

records.title: Use a starter template
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - You have a GitHub account, and its [Git provider is connected](/guides/connectors/git-providers).

records.title: Use a starter template
records.heading: Choose a template
records.text:
Repository What it is Attach it as 
 --- --- --- 
 [alethia-starter-apps](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-apps) An apps repository that ArgoCD syncs [Apps repository](/guides/design-project/repositories) 
 [alethia-starter-chart](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-chart) A Helm chart with a Deployment, a Service and a ConfigMap [Bring-your-own chart](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) 
 [alethia-starter-ai](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-ai) A retrieval-augmented generation stack Both 

All three are Apache-2.0. Each has a `TEMPLATE_VERSION` file and a `CHANGELOG.md`. A change to a
chart's `values.schema.json` is a major version, because your values are written against it.

When you create a project with **Start from a template**, the **Template** choice points you to a
starter. **Standard** points to alethia-starter-apps, **AI Workloads** to alethia-starter-ai, and
**Custom** to none. The choice does not change the cluster: all three make the same node pool, with
no GPU.

Where code goes decides what it may create. An apps repository may create cluster-scoped resources,
such as CustomResourceDefinitions. A bring-your-o

records.title: Use a starter template
records.heading: Use the apps template
records.text:
1. On the repository page, select **Use this template** to make your own copy.
2. Add a **Repository** card and set **ArgoCD apps repository** to your copy. Leave
 **Overlay path** empty.
3. Deploy.

 Path Purpose 
 --- --- 
 `kustomization.yaml` The root manifest. Without it, the root Application manages nothing. 
 `namespace.yaml` The namespace the root delivers into 
 `base/` The application, defined once 
 `overlays/dev/`, `overlays/staging/` Discovered as `apps-dev` and `apps-staging` 
 `addons/` Keeps the `addons` Application out of ComparisonError

records.title: Use a starter template
records.heading: Use the chart template
records.text:
1. Select **Use this template** to make your own copy.
2. Run `hack/check-byo-contract.sh` against your chart before you attach it. It fails if a change
 breaks the bring-your-own contract. Its list of kinds differs slightly from Alethia's: it accepts
 `Endpoints` and `NetworkPolicy`, which Alethia refuses, and refuses `DaemonSet`, which Alethia
 accepts.
3. On the canvas, press **⌘K** and choose **Bring your own Helm chart**.
4. Choose your repository, set **Chart path** to `chart`, and set **Ref** to `HEAD` or a tag.
5. Deploy.

records.title: Use a starter template
records.heading: Use the AI template
records.text:
The stack holds a vector database, a CPU embedding server, CPU inference, model serving and job
queueing. It splits across both places:

 Component Goes in Why 
 --- --- --- 
 KServe, Kueue, the GPU operator `addons/` in the apps repository They install CustomResourceDefinitions 
 Qdrant, embeddings, inference, the RAG application `chart/`, as a bring-your-own chart Only Deployments, Services and PersistentVolumeClaims 

1. Copy the repository, then attach it as an apps repository and its `chart/` directory as a
 bring-your-own chart.
2. Make sure cert-manager is installed, because KServe needs it for its admission webhook:

 You created the project Do this 
 --- --- 
 From **AI Workloads** Nothing. Alethia installs cert-manager on every cloud, with no domain needed. 
 Any other way On the DNS card, set **Domain name** and turn on **Managed TLS certificate**. This works on AWS, GCP and Azure. 

 Do not add cert-manager to `addons/`: a second copy fights the platform's copy.
3. Deploy.

The template is CPU-only. A GPU node pool is the costliest thing to provision by accident, so you
add one yourself: see the repository's `gpu/` directory.

On Hetzner, the cluster the template was la

records.title: Use a starter template
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
In ArgoCD, the root Application and each discovered overlay (`apps-dev`, `apps-staging`) are
**Synced** and **Healthy**. A chart shows a passed safety scan on its card.

records.title: Add a bucket
records.text: Add a bucket. Add an object storage bucket to an environment, with versioning, encryption, public access and CORS origins, on any cloud.

records.title: Add a bucket
records.text:
Add a bucket for files and assets. You can add as many as you need, and each name is unique in
the environment.

records.title: Add a bucket
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - You have a project open on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas).

records.title: Add a bucket
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Select **Add**, then **Bucket** in the **Storage** group.
2. Enter a name (default `assets`). It must be 3–63 characters of lowercase letters, digits and
 hyphens, and start and end with a letter or digit. These are the strictest cloud rules, so the
 name works on every cloud. The field lowercases what you type and drops other characters.
3. Under **General**:
 - Turn on **Versioning** to keep every version of an object.
 - Leave **Encryption at rest** on (the default) for server-side encryption with the cloud's keys.
4. Under **Access**:
 - Leave **Public access** off to keep the bucket private. Turn it on to allow reads without
 authentication, for static assets.
 - Optional: add **CORS origins**, separated by commas, such as `https://app.example.com`. They
 can read and write objects (`GET`, `PUT`, `POST`) from a browser.

The bucket uses the project's cloud account and region unless you place it on another connected
account.

 Cloud Service 
 --- --- 
 AWS S3 
 GCP Cloud Storage 
 Azure Blob Storage 
 Hetzner Hetzner Object Storage

records.title: Add a bucket
records.heading: Differences between clouds
records.text:
**Hetzner** always encrypts at rest, so **Encryption at rest** is not shown. **CORS origins** is not
shown either, because the provider does not apply CORS there.

**Azure** keeps every bucket of a project in one storage account, and some settings belong to the
account:

- **Versioning** on any bucket turns it on for every bucket in the project.
- **CORS origins** form one rule for the account, made of every bucket's origins. An origin allowed
 on one bucket can call every bucket. `*` allows every origin on every bucket. The rule holds at
 most 64 distinct origins.
- Each origin is `*`, or a scheme, a host and an optional port, such as `http://localhost:3000`. A
 path, a trailing slash, or a scheme other than `http` or `https` fails the plan.
- **Public access** is set per bucket. The account allows public containers only while at least
 one bucket asks for it.

**GCP**: **Public access** lets the bucket accept public grants and gives everyone read access.
Uniform bucket-level access stays on for every bucket. An organization policy
`constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` blocks public grants: under it, the deploy refuses a
public bucket and says why.

records.title: Add a bucket
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The bucket's card shows its access (`public` or `private`), versioning (`on` or `off`) and the
number of CORS origins. After the deploy, its **Status** tab shows the endpoint.

records.title: Use the canvas
records.text: Use the canvas. Find your way around the Architecture canvas, add and connect resources, and review and deploy the plan.

records.title: Use the canvas
records.text:
Design one environment on the **Architecture** canvas, then plan and deploy it. What the cards,
rules and status dots mean is in [Read the canvas](/concepts/canvas).

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You have a project. The cloud account is chosen when you create the project, and you cannot
 change it on the canvas.
- To deploy, a runner is online for your organization. See [Runners](/guides/runners).

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Find your way around
records.text:
One environment is one Kubernetes cluster inside one network. The board stands for both, so
neither is a card.

 [ environment Select Hand Add Connect Undo Redo Tidy Fit Run Sources ⌘K ? ⋯ ]

 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐
 │ the cards │ │ the inspector │
 │ │ │ (or the review │
 │ [ Pending changes · 3 Discard Review plan ] │ │ view) │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘

 Area What it does 
 --- --- 
 **Toolbar**, top centre Starts with the environment's name: select it to size the cluster and the network. Then the select and hand tools, **Add**, **Connect**, **Undo**, **Redo**, **Tidy layout**, **Fit view**, the **Run** menu (plan, audit, detect drift, probe the cluster), **Sources**, the command palette, the shortcut list and the **⋯** menu. A disabled tool's tooltip says why. On a narrow window some tools move into the **⋯** menu and the command palette. 
 **Inspector**, right Opens when you select a card. See [Use the inspector](/guides/design-project/node-inspector). 
 **Changes bar**, bottom centre Shows **Pending changes** with a count, **Not deployed yet**, **Saved, not deployed

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Start an empty board
records.text:
An empty board offers three ways to start:

- **Start from a template** sizes the cluster from a starter template. It changes the cluster, not
 the cards.
- **Add the first piece yourself** opens the **Add** picker.
- **Bring your own** attaches a [Helm chart](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) or a
 [bring-your-own IaC module](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-iac).

A link to the board can carry a starting point (`?seed=…`). The board applies it once and removes
it from the address.

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Add a resource
records.text:
1. Select **Add** in the toolbar, or press **A**. You can also press **⌘K** and type a service name,
 such as `postgres`, `redis` or `s3`.
2. Pick the resource. For a database or a cache, pick the engine.

The card appears on the board and the inspector opens on it. The picker lists only what your
project's cloud can run. A resource already on the board that can exist once is disabled, and a
resource that is not available yet shows **Soon**.

On Hetzner, databases, caches, queues, topics, NoSQL tables, the registry and secrets run inside
your cluster, and their cards say so (for example `Runs as · CloudNativePG`).

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Connect a service to what it uses
records.text:
A service connects to a database, a cache, a queue or a secret. At deploy, Alethia gives the
service that resource's endpoint and credentials without a stored key.

1. Drag from the handle at the bottom of the service card.
2. Release on the card you want to connect to. While you drag, the card under the pointer says
 whether you can connect to it.
3. In the inspector's **Connections** tab, choose what the service gets from the resource.

If you release on empty board, a menu offers what the service can connect to, including a new
resource placed where you let go. Without a pointer, select the service and press **C**.

To remove a connection, select the line and press **Delete**, or select **Remove connection**.

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Review and deploy
records.text:
1. Select **Review plan** on the changes bar, or press **⌘S**.
2. Check the design changes at the top of the review view.
3. Select **Run plan**. This saves the design and shows what would change in the cloud.
4. Select **Deploy**. It applies exactly that plan, and is enabled only for a current plan you
 reviewed. When it is disabled, the view says why.

If you open a card while the review is open, the review steps aside until you close the card.

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Keyboard
records.text:
Press **Tab** to move between cards and lines. Letter keys do nothing while you type in a field.
On Windows and Linux, read **Ctrl** for **⌘**.

 Key Does 
 --- --- 
 **Enter** Opens the focused card. On a line, opens the service it starts from. 
 Arrow keys Move the selected cards. **Shift** makes a larger step. 
 **Delete** or **Backspace** Removes the selection. 
 **C** Connects the selected service. 
 **A** Opens the **Add** picker. 
 **V** / **H** Select tool / hand tool. Hold **Space** to pan. 
 **⇧L** / **⇧1** Tidy layout / fit view. 
 **⌘Z** / **⇧⌘Z** Undo / redo. 
 **⌘D** Duplicates the selection. 
 **⌘S** Opens the review view. 
 **⌘K** Opens the command palette. 
 **⌘I** Asks the AI assistant. 
 **Esc** Closes the inspector. 
 **?** Lists every key.

records.title: Use the canvas
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
After the deploy, the changes bar reads **Up to date** and each card shows a solid dot. A card
with a hollow-centre dot failed: open it and read **Status**.

records.heading: Related
records.text:

- [Use the inspector](/guides/design-project/node-inspector)
- [Troubleshoot design and GitOps](/troubleshooting/design-project)

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.text: Run a warm pool of runners. On a self-hosted console, configure a warm pool of managed runners for a cloud, so the fleet controller keeps capacity sized to demand.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.text:
Keep ready runners waiting for jobs, within a spend ceiling, on one version. A **warm pool** states
the target for one cloud's managed runners. The **fleet controller** reads every pool every 60
seconds and provisions, drains or replaces runners to match. A change to a pool takes effect on the
next tick, with no redeploy.

Pools are for managed runners, which the controller creates and removes for you. To add a runner you
operate yourself, use **Add Runner** on the [Runners](/guides/runners) page.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You run your own console. The **Pools** panel is not shown on the hosted service.
- You are an owner or admin. Others see the panel read-only, and **Add pool** is disabled with the
 reason.
- `FLEET_PROVIDER=hcloud` is set, so that runners are real Hetzner servers. Without it, a pool is
 advisory: the controller logs what it would do and creates nothing, and the panel says so.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Add a pool
records.text:
There is one pool per cloud. A cloud that has a pool is disabled in the picker, and a pool's cloud
cannot change later.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Open the wizard
records.text:
On the **Runners** page, find **Pools** in the left column and select **Add pool**. The wizard has
five steps: **Cloud**, **Placement**, **Capacity**, **Version** and **Review**.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Choose the cloud
records.text:
Pick the **Cloud provider**. A **Display name (optional)** names the pool card. It defaults to the
cloud's name.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Set placement
records.text:
Enter **Locations** as region codes separated by commas, such as `fsn1,nbg1` on Hetzner. The
controller spreads runners across them, so one bad region does not take the pool down. Set a
**Minimum per location** to keep that many runners in each, or `0` for none.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Set capacity
records.text:
Field Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Warm minimum** Runners kept ready at all times, even with no jobs queued. 
 **Maximum** The most runners the pool ever runs, however long the queue. 
 **Idle buffer** Spare runners kept above demand, so a new job rarely waits for a boot. `0` matches demand exactly. 
 **Slots / runner** Jobs one runner runs at once. More slots share one server's CPU and memory. 

The maximum must be at least the warm minimum, and the idle buffer cannot exceed the maximum. If
the minimum per location times the number of locations exceeds the maximum, the wizard warns you.
A preview says what the numbers mean, including the most jobs at once (maximum × slots).

Under **Advanced scaling**:

 Field Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Rollout surge** Extra runners allowed above the maximum during a version change, so capacity does not drop. 
 **Scale-down grace** Idle 60-second ticks before a runner is removed. More ticks stop the pool from shrinking and growing on spiky demand.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Choose the version source
records.text:
- **Channel** follows a release stream, usually `stable`. Each tick, the controller picks the newest
 release on it.
- **Pinned** holds one version until you change it.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Create the pool
records.text:
Check the summary and select **Create pool**. The controller starts at once.

 

New runners always start at the target version. When the version changes, the controller replaces
runners one step per tick. It drains an old runner only when it can start a new one first, so online
capacity never drops below the warm minimum.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Edit, pause or delete a pool
records.text:
Open **Pool actions** (**⋮**) on the pool card:

 Action What happens 
 --- --- 
 **Edit** Opens the wizard on the pool. Everything but the cloud can change. 
 **Pause** Drains every runner to zero and closes each runner's usage session, so nothing keeps billing. **Resume** rebuilds the warm minimum over the next few ticks. 
 **Delete** Drains and removes the pool's runners on the next tick, then the pool. It cannot be undone. 

Pause and delete drain a busy runner first: it stops taking new jobs and finishes the one it runs.
No running job is dropped.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
The pool card shows:

- **Warm capacity**: online runners against the target, as a meter of online, busy and missing
 runners, with how many are below the floor, busy or draining.
- **Rollout**: the share of runners on the target version, with progress during a change.
- **Versions** and **Locations**: where the runners are, flagged when one is on another version or a
 location has an offline runner.
- **Healthy**, or **Degraded** when the pool is below its warm minimum or a runner is offline. A
 paused pool is dimmed and marked **Paused**.
- For managers, this month's provisioned hours, estimated cost and use.

records.title: Run a warm pool of runners
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Runners](/guides/runners)
- [Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated)

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.text: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster. Get a short-lived kubeconfig for a cluster that Alethia deployed, from the CLI or the console, without a login to the cloud account.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.text:
Get a kubeconfig that lets `kubectl` reach your cluster for a limited time. You do not need a login
to the cloud account. How this works, and how to revoke it, is in
[Cluster access](/concepts/cluster-access).

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- The `alethia` CLI is installed and you are signed in. See [Install the CLI](/get-started/install-the-cli).
- The cluster runs on AWS, GCP, Azure or Hetzner, and its environment has had at least one
 successful deploy.
- The environment has a `dedicated` placement. An environment on a shared cluster (`namespace` or
 `vcluster`) cannot get a kubeconfig. See [Fabrics & Placement](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement).
- A runner is online for your organization. See [Runners](/guides/runners).
- Your role is owner, admin or operator. Only owners and admins can get admin access.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Run the command
records.text:
alethia cluster kubeconfig

The CLI lists your clusters and asks which one you want. To skip the question, name the project,
the cluster, or the cluster ID:

alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Wait for the runner
records.text:
A runner in your organization makes the credential. On an idle runner this takes a few seconds. The
CLI waits up to 10 minutes.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Use the context
records.text:
The CLI adds the context `alethia- - ` to your kubeconfig, makes it the current
context, and prints a command to try:

kubectl --context alethia-api-backend-production get namespaces

 
 

The CLI writes to the first file in `$KUBECONFIG`, or to `~/.kube/config`. It replaces an older
context with the same name and leaves your other contexts alone. To write a separate file, add
`--output api-backend.kubeconfig`.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Get a kubeconfig from the console
records.text:
1. Open **Clusters** and select the cluster's row.
2. Under **Cluster access**, select **Download kubeconfig (1h, read-only)**.
3. Wait while the record shows **A runner is minting it.** Your browser then saves
 `alethia- - .kubeconfig`.

The console file is always read-only, lasts 1 hour, and holds the credential itself. Anyone who has
the file can use it until it expires, so treat it as a password. For anything else, use the CLI.
The download needs Chrome 133, Firefox 130 or Safari 17 or later, over HTTPS.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Choose the options
records.text:
You want Add What changes 
 --- --- --- 
 Full control of the cluster `--admin` The cloud's own admin credential instead of read-only. Owners and admins only, and never a service token. 
 A longer or shorter lifetime `--ttl 4h` From `15m` to `8h`; the default is `1h`. An admin credential lasts at most what the cloud allows, about an hour. 
 A file that needs only `kubectl` `--static` The file holds the credential. Without it, the file calls `alethia cluster token` each time it needs a new one. Hetzner is always static. 
 A separate file `--output ` Writes that file instead of merging into your kubeconfig. `--output -` prints to stdout. 

Read-only access lets you run `kubectl get`, `describe`, `logs` and `events`. It cannot read
Secrets or custom resources, run `exec` or `port-forward`, or change anything. The full list of
resources is in [Cluster access](/concepts/cluster-access#what-read-only-allows).

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Use it in CI or on another machine
records.text:
A static file works on any machine with `kubectl` until it expires:

alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --static --output - > api-backend.kubeconfig

An exec kubeconfig needs the `alethia` CLI and a session on the machine that runs `kubectl`. In
CI, set `ALETHIA_TOKEN` to a service token. See
[Running in CI](/reference/cli/authentication#running-in-ci). A service token gets read-only access
only.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: If the cluster's endpoint is private
records.text:
The CLI and the console say so when they hand you the kubeconfig. The credential is valid, but
`kubectl` must reach the endpoint: connect through a VPN or a bastion host first. Alethia does not
proxy traffic to the cluster.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text:
kubectl --context alethia-api-backend-production get nodes

You see the cluster's nodes. If you see `Unauthorized`, a refusal, or the CLI times out, see
[Troubleshoot cluster access](/troubleshooting/cluster-access).

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Cluster access](/concepts/cluster-access): how the credential is made, how long it lasts, how to revoke it, and what Alethia records.
- [Cluster commands](/reference/cli/clusters): every flag of `alethia cluster kubeconfig` and `alethia cluster token`.
- [Clusters](/guides/clusters): the clusters table, and the commands for people with their own cloud login.

records.title: Find a job
records.text: Find a job. Find a plan, deploy, destroy or scan job on the Jobs page, filter the list, and open the job's log.

records.title: Find a job
records.text:
Find a job and open it. Every plan, deploy, destroy, scan and runner change in Alethia is a job,
and the **Jobs** page lists them all for the organization.

records.title: Find a job
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text: - Your role can view jobs. Without it, the page says so and names who can give you access.

records.title: Find a job
records.heading: Steps
records.text:
1. Open **Jobs** in the sidebar. To see one project's jobs, open **Jobs** from the project's menu
 instead.
2. Narrow the list with the filter bar:

 Filter Matches 
 --- --- 
 Search Project name or slug, environment, runner name, or the error message 
 Date range A preset range or a custom range. The default is the last 12 months. 
 Authors The member who started the job 
 Environments, Projects The job's target. **Projects** is hidden in a project's own list. 
 Statuses `QUEUED`, `CLAIMED`, `PROCESSING`, `SUCCESS`, `FAILED`, `CANCELLED` 
 Types Any [job type](/guides/jobs/job-types) 

 Each option shows how many jobs it matches. The filters are kept in the page URL, so you can
 share a filtered list.
3. Select a row to open the job. See [Read a job](/guides/jobs/job-detail).

The table shows each job's **Type**, **Status** with its run time, **Project**, **Runner**,
**Environment**, and **Initiated** (when, and by whom). The list updates as jobs change, without a
reload.

From the CLI, `alethia jobs list` prints the same list. See [Job commands](/reference/cli/jobs).

records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The job you were looking for is in the list, and selecting it opens its log.

records.title: Read a job
records.text: Read a job. Open a job to follow its log, read what it found, and cancel, deploy or re-run it.

records.title: Read a job
records.text: Open a job to follow its log as it runs, see what it found, and act on it.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- Your role can view jobs. To cancel, deploy or re-run, your role needs the permission for that
 operation on the project. Without it, the button is disabled and says why.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Open the job
records.text: Select the job on the [Jobs](/guides/jobs) page, or follow a job link from the canvas.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Follow the log
records.text:
The log shows the runner's output as it arrives. Error output (`STDERR`) is styled as an error. The
log scrolls with new lines.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Read the result
records.text:
When the job ends, a banner under the header gives the outcome. For a successful plan or drift scan,
it says what the job found (see below). A failed job shows its error message.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Act on the job
records.text:
Use the buttons in the header:

 Button Shown when What it does 
 --- --- --- 
 **Cancel** The job is `QUEUED`, `CLAIMED` or `PROCESSING` Marks it cancelled. A job that has not started never runs. A running job's runner stops the run, but what it already applied stays. 
 **Deploy** The job is a successful `PLAN` Asks which runner to use (an online runner or **Any available**), then queues a `DEPLOY` of this plan. 
 **Re-run** The job has ended, and its type can be re-run A plan or deploy is queued again for the environment, with the project's **current** configuration, not the one this job used. An organization audit is copied as it was. 

A destroy is never re-run from a job: start it from the environment's settings. A runner job is
re-run from **Runners**. A cancelled job cannot be resumed.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Plan
records.text:
The heading gives the number of changes, such as "4 changes planned", or "No changes — the
infrastructure matches the configuration." Under it, a count for each action:

+1 to create · ~1 to update · −1 to destroy · ±1 to replace

If the job priced the plan, the block also shows the monthly cost change and the new total.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Drift scan
records.text:
The heading reads "N resources drifted" or "In sync — no managed resource has drifted." Under it,
the block can show:

- how many differences were dismissed as representational: a value written differently, not
 changed;
- whether unmanaged resources were checked. A refresh-only scan cannot see resources that are in
 the cloud but not in state, so the count leaves them out;
- the first five drifted resources, each with **Modified**, **Deleted** or **Other**, its address,
 and the attribute paths that differ. Values are never shown. Select **Show all N** for the rest.

See [Drift](/concepts/drift).

A job of another type shows "Job completed successfully." A stored result that cannot be read shows
"Plan summary unavailable" or "Drift summary unavailable"; the log still has the output.

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Details under the log
records.text:
Section Contents 
 --- --- 
 **Job details** Job ID, type, runner, project, and when it was created, started and completed 
 **Config snapshot** The project configuration when the job was created, as JSON 
 **Execution metadata** What the runner reported, as JSON: OpenTofu outputs, cost, cluster details, and for plans and deploys the verify report in `verify_result`

records.title: Read a job
records.heading: Check that it worked
records.text: The status badge in the header shows the job's final status, and the result banner matches it.

records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Plan and deploy from the console](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply)
- [Troubleshoot a deploy](/troubleshooting/deploy)
- [Real-time updates](/concepts/realtime): how the log streams.

records.title: Job types
records.text: Job types. Every job type Alethia runs, with its console label and what it does.

records.title: Job types
records.text:
Find what a job type does. The console shows each type by its label. Other pages link here instead
of repeating this list. Which runner handler runs each type is in
[Job execution](/concepts/runner/job-execution).

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
- You know where to see job types: the **Type** column and filter on the [Jobs](/guides/jobs) page,
 or `alethia jobs list`.

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Job types
records.text:
Type Label What it does 
 --- --- --- 
 `PLAN` Plan Runs `tofu plan` on the environment and the [verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) on the plan. Changes nothing. 
 `DEPLOY` Deploy Applies the reviewed plan. The verify gate runs again before `tofu apply`. 
 `DESTROY` Destroy Tears down the environment's infrastructure. 
 `DEPLOY_RUNNER` Deploy Runner Provisions a runner into your cloud account. 
 `UPDATE_RUNNER` Update Runner Updates a runner to a newer version. 
 `DESTROY_RUNNER` Destroy Runner Tears down a provisioned runner. 
 `ANALYZE_REPO` Analyze Repo Clones a repository and scans it for infrastructure configuration, to start a project from it. 
 `DETECT_DRIFT` Detect Drift Runs `tofu plan -refresh-only` and records drift. See [Drift](/concepts/drift). 
 `AUDIT` Audit Runs Elench on input that the job carries: a `show -json` plan or Kubernetes manifests. 
 `CHART_SCAN` Chart Scan Renders a bring-your-own Helm chart with `helm template`, with no secrets and no network, and checks the manifests with Elench. 
 `IAC_SCAN` IaC Scan Validates a bring-your-own IaC module and pins the commit it deploys from. 
 `STATE_SURGERY` State Surgery Repairs a broken OpenTofu

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Rules worth knowing
records.text:
- **Promotions** use `PLAN`, then `DEPLOY`. There is no separate type.
- **`IAC_SCAN` gates plans and deploys.** An environment with bring-your-own IaC needs a fresh scan
 that pinned the commit before a `PLAN` or `DEPLOY` can run. `DESTROY` is not gated: it uses the
 commit that made the deployed state, so a failed re-scan cannot trap live infrastructure.
- **`PROBE_CLUSTER` succeeds when the cluster is down.** It records `reachable=false`. The job fails
 only when the probe itself cannot run.
- **`BUILD`** reports one image digest per service in the job's execution metadata.
- **`STATE_SURGERY`** needs two people to approve it and is fully audited. The runner refuses it
 unless the runner sets `ALETHIA_BREAKGLASS_STATE_SURGERY_ENABLED`.
